## KVS 2026 recruitment status as of July 2026

The Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan (KVS) 2026 direct recruitment cycle under Notification 01/2025 has completed Tier 1 (10 to 11 January 2026) and Tier 2 (27 to 31 March 2026), with the Tier 2 result expected in July 2026 per secondary sources (prepp.in, freejobalert.com, testbook.com), though KVS and the conducting agency CBSE have not officially confirmed the date as of 15 July 2026. The current cycle covers 9,921 teaching and non-teaching vacancies, revised on 10 December 2025 from the original 9,126 through a corrigendum on kvsangathan.nic.in.

The 2026 cycle is now in its verification phase. Tier 1 acted as a screening filter shortlisting candidates to Tier 2 in a category-wise 1:10 ratio (revised down from the older 1:15 ratio). Tier 2 tested subject-specific knowledge across the four teaching cadres (PGT, TGT, PRT, Principal/VP) and the non-teaching cadres (Librarian, Assistant Section Officer, Hindi Translator, Senior Secretariat Assistant, Junior Secretariat Assistant, Stenographer). Once results release, the Skill Test / Interview / Demo Teaching phase begins for teaching-cadre candidates, expected in August-September 2026 based on typical KVS post-Tier 2 timelines.

For candidates who missed this cycle or are targeting the next round, the Ministry of Education has not yet announced when KVS Notification 02/2026 will open. However, contractual hiring is ongoing through the newly-launched **Samvida Sathi portal (samvida-sathi.kvs.gov.in)**, which replaces the earlier school-level walk-in model. Samvida Sathi is the primary route for teaching vacancies in Kendriya Vidyalayas for AY 2026-27 while the next direct recruitment cycle is planned.

The overall attractiveness of KVS teaching jobs in 2026 remains strong: All-India transferable service across 1,250 plus Kendriya Vidyalayas, 7th CPC Pay Level 6 to 8 basic pay, DA revised to 55% effective 1 January 2026, and central-government leave and CGHS benefits. Anticipation of 8th Central Pay Commission implementation (announced January 2025 by Ministry of Finance) adds a future-value component to the appointment.

---

## Vacancies breakdown across PGT, TGT, PRT, and other posts

The 9,921 vacancies (per Notification 01/2025 corrigendum, 10 December 2025) span teaching and non-teaching cadres across all 25 KVS Regional Offices.

| Post | Vacancies | Pay Level | Selection stages |
|---|---|---|---|
| Assistant Commissioner | 13 | Pay Level 12 | Tier 2 CBT + Interview |
| Principal | 161 | Pay Level 12 | Tier 2 CBT + Interview |
| Vice Principal | 69 | Pay Level 10 | Tier 2 CBT + Interview |
| PGT (all subjects) | 1,606 | Pay Level 8 | Tier 1 + Tier 2 + Demo + Interview |
| TGT (all subjects) | 3,069 | Pay Level 7 | Tier 1 + Tier 2 + Demo + Interview |
| PRT (including Music, Special Educator) | 3,630 | Pay Level 6 | Tier 1 + Tier 2 + Demo + Interview |
| Librarian | Included in non-teaching | Pay Level 7 | Tier 1 + Tier 2 + Skill Test |
| Finance Officer | Included in non-teaching | Pay Level 10 | Tier 2 + Interview |
| Assistant Section Officer (ASO) | Included in non-teaching | Pay Level 6 | Tier 1 + Tier 2 |
| Hindi Translator | Included in non-teaching | Pay Level 6 | Tier 1 + Tier 2 + Skill Test |
| Stenographer | Included in non-teaching | Pay Level 4 | Tier 1 + Tier 2 + Stenography |
| Senior Secretariat Assistant (SSA) | Included in non-teaching | Pay Level 4 | Tier 1 + Tier 2 + Skill Test |
| Junior Secretariat Assistant (JSA) | Included in non-teaching | Pay Level 2 | Tier 1 + Tier 2 + Typing |
| Total | 9,921 | | |

The 2024 previous cycle notified 13,404 vacancies, and pre-corrigendum 2026 was 9,126. The 10 December 2025 corrigendum added 795 posts (net), largely in PRT and TGT categories to align with new Kendriya Vidyalaya openings across the North-East and Ladakh.

PGT subjects covered: English, Hindi, Sanskrit, Physics, Chemistry, Biology, History, Geography, Economics, Commerce, Mathematics, Computer Science. TGT subjects: English, Hindi, Sanskrit, Social Science, Mathematics, Science, Computer Science, and regional languages. PRT includes Music teacher, Special Educator, and standard PRT.

---

## Application timeline and fee structure

The KVS 2026 application cycle followed this timeline:

| Milestone | Date | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Notification 01/2025 released | 13 November 2025 | kvsangathan.nic.in |
| Application window opens | 14 November 2025 | cbseit.in |
| Original last date | 4 December 2025 | |
| Extended last date | 11 December 2025 | Load-related extension |
| Corrigendum (vacancy revision to 9,921) | 10 December 2025 | +795 net posts |
| Correction window | Mid to late December 2025 | |
| Tier 1 admit card | Early January 2026 | Download from cbseit.in |
| Tier 1 CBT | 10 to 11 January 2026 | Two shifts daily |
| Tier 1 provisional answer key | Mid January 2026 | Objection window ~5 days |
| Tier 1 final answer key + result | 28 February 2026 | |
| Tier 2 admit card | Mid March 2026 | |
| Tier 2 CBT | 27 to 31 March 2026 | |
| Tier 2 provisional answer key | Early April 2026 | Objection window closed ~4 May 2026 |
| Tier 2 result | Expected July 2026 | Unconfirmed by KVS/CBSE |
| Skill Test / Interview / Demo Teaching | Expected August-September 2026 | For teaching posts |
| Joining orders (typical) | November 2026 to January 2027 | |

Application fee structure (Notification 01/2025):

| Post category | Application fee (Rs.) |
|---|---|
| PGT / TGT / PRT / Librarian / ASO / Hindi Translator | 1,500 |
| SSA / JSA / Stenographer | 1,200 |
| Assistant Commissioner / Principal / Vice Principal | 2,300 |
| SC / ST / PwBD / Ex-Servicemen / Women (as per DoPT norms) | Exempt or Rs. 500 processing fee (verify per notification wording) |

Payment mode: online only via cbseit.in, using net banking, credit/debit card, or UPI. No offline demand draft option. Fee is non-refundable except in cases of application rejection at the KVS end.

---

## Post-by-post eligibility

Eligibility varies materially by post. The comparison table below covers the three main teaching cadres.

| Attribute | PGT | TGT | PRT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Education | Master's in concerned subject with at least 50%, plus B.Ed | Bachelor's with at least 50% in concerned subject, plus B.Ed | Class 12 with at least 50%, plus D.El.Ed or B.El.Ed or 4-year BA-B.Ed or ITEP under NEP 2020 |
| CTET requirement | Not mandatory | Paper II qualified mandatory | Paper I qualified mandatory |
| Age limit (as on last date of application) | 40 years | 35 years | 30 years |
| Language proficiency | Teaching in both Hindi and English media | Teaching in both Hindi and English media | Teaching in Hindi and English media |
| Pay Level (7th CPC) | Level 8 | Level 7 | Level 6 |
| Basic pay range | Rs. 47,600 to Rs. 1,51,100 | Rs. 44,900 to Rs. 1,42,400 | Rs. 35,400 to Rs. 1,12,400 |
| Category age relaxation | SC/ST +5, OBC-NCL +3, PwBD +10 to +15 | Same | Same |

Note on NEP 2020 alignment: PRT eligibility now explicitly includes the 4-year Integrated Teacher Education Programme (ITEP) and 4-year BA-B.Ed, reflecting NCTE amendments. This is a 2025-26 update; older KVS notifications did not include ITEP.

For Principal, Vice Principal, and Assistant Commissioner: KVS Recruitment Rules require post-graduate qualifications plus teaching or administrative experience. Refer to the KVS Eligibility PDF at cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in (uploaded February 2026) for the exact eligibility clauses.

For Librarian: Bachelor's in Library Science plus B.Ed. For ASO / Hindi Translator: Master's degree plus DoPT-notified requirements. For SSA / JSA / Stenographer: Class 12 pass plus typing / stenography speed requirements.

---

## Two-tier CBT and the Skill Test structure

KVS 2026 uses a two-tier CBT plus a Skill Test / Interview / Demo Teaching for teaching cadres. This is the same pattern used from KVS 2024 onwards.

**Tier 1 (screening).** 100 objective MCQs across 300 marks in 120 minutes. Section breakdown:

- General English: 20 marks
- General Hindi: 20 marks
- General Awareness and Current Affairs: 40 marks
- Reasoning and Numerical Ability: 40 marks
- Computer Literacy: 20 marks
- Perspectives on Education (Pedagogy) and School Leadership: 160 marks

Marking: 3 marks per correct, 1 mark negative per incorrect. Tier 1 is qualifying only; it does not contribute to final merit. Shortlisting to Tier 2 happens in a category-wise 1:10 ratio (revised from 1:15 in earlier cycles).

**Tier 2 (subject-specific).** 180 marks in 180 minutes. Structure: 150 subject MCQs + 30 pedagogy MCQs. Marking: 1 mark per correct, 0.25 negative marking on objective sections. Tier 2 marks contribute to final merit.

Tier 2 subject papers by post:

- **PGT:** post-graduate level in concerned subject (English, Hindi, Sanskrit, Physics, Chemistry, Biology, History, Geography, Economics, Commerce, Mathematics, Computer Science)
- **TGT:** graduate level in concerned subject
- **PRT:** Class 12 level plus pedagogy, plus language proficiency in Hindi and English

**Skill Test / Demo Teaching / Interview (60 marks Professional Competency Test).** Teaching demonstration of 15 minutes in Hindi or English medium (candidate choice), followed by a 20 to 25 minute personal interview covering subject knowledge, pedagogy, KV ethos, and situational judgment. The Demo Teaching is done before a panel of subject expert and KV administrator.

Scores are normalised across shifts using CBSE's standard equipercentile method to ensure fairness across easier and harder question papers.

For non-teaching cadres, the Skill Test is post-specific: stenography for Stenographer, typing for JSA, book cataloguing for Librarian, etc.

---

## Syllabus per post with high-yield topics

**Tier 1 syllabus (common):**

- General English: reading comprehension, grammar (tenses, prepositions, subject-verb agreement), vocabulary (synonyms, antonyms, idioms), sentence rearrangement, error detection
- General Hindi: samas, sandhi, alankar, muhavare, viparyayarthi shabd, gadyansh
- General Awareness: history (freedom struggle emphasis), geography (Indian and world), polity (Constitution, governance), economics, science and technology, current affairs (past 12 months)
- Reasoning: verbal reasoning (analogy, series, coding-decoding, blood relations), non-verbal reasoning (mirror image, paper folding, figure completion), quantitative aptitude (arithmetic, DI, mensuration, algebra basics)
- Computer Literacy: MS Office, internet basics, hardware/software, ICT in teaching
- Perspectives on Education: pedagogy of Vygotsky, Piaget, Bruner, Kohlberg; assessment (formative, summative, CCE); inclusive education; NEP 2020 architecture; National Curriculum Framework (NCF) 2023; school leadership; RTE Act 2009

**Tier 2 syllabus (post-specific):**

- **PGT:** post-graduate depth in the chosen subject, aligned to CBSE Class 11-12 syllabus, plus pedagogy of secondary education, curriculum design, assessment strategies
- **TGT:** graduate-level depth in the chosen subject, aligned to CBSE Class 6-10 syllabus, plus middle-school pedagogy, ICT integration, formative assessment
- **PRT:** Class 12 depth in each subject taught at primary level (all subjects), plus early-childhood pedagogy, play-based learning, foundational literacy and numeracy (FLN), NCF-FS

High-yield areas across all posts: NEP 2020 provisions, NCF 2023 pillars, PARAKH assessment framework, CBSE circulars from 2025 onwards, current UNESCO / Education for All statistics on India.

---

## KVS salary structure with 7th CPC pay levels and DA at 55%

Salary follows 7th CPC pay levels. With DA revised to 55% effective 1 January 2026, the in-hand numbers below reflect the current 2026 gross for a new joiner.

| Post | Pay Level | Basic pay range | Gross (metro X city) | Gross (Y city) | Gross (Z city) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PGT | Level 8 | Rs. 47,600 to Rs. 1,51,100 | Rs. 88,000 to Rs. 92,000 | Rs. 78,000 to Rs. 82,000 | Rs. 71,000 to Rs. 75,000 |
| TGT | Level 7 | Rs. 44,900 to Rs. 1,42,400 | Rs. 83,000 to Rs. 87,000 | Rs. 74,000 to Rs. 78,000 | Rs. 67,000 to Rs. 71,000 |
| PRT | Level 6 | Rs. 35,400 to Rs. 1,12,400 | Rs. 68,000 to Rs. 72,000 | Rs. 61,000 to Rs. 65,000 | Rs. 55,000 to Rs. 59,000 |
| Vice Principal | Level 10 | Rs. 56,100 to Rs. 1,77,500 | Rs. 1,03,000 to Rs. 1,07,000 | Rs. 92,000 to Rs. 96,000 | Rs. 83,000 to Rs. 87,000 |
| Principal | Level 12 | Rs. 78,800 to Rs. 2,09,200 | Rs. 1,42,000 to Rs. 1,46,000 | Rs. 1,27,000 to Rs. 1,31,000 | Rs. 1,15,000 to Rs. 1,19,000 |

Gross components: Basic + DA (55% of basic effective 1 Jan 2026) + HRA (27% metro X, 18% Y city, 9% Z city) + Transport Allowance (Rs. 3,600 for metro, Rs. 1,800 elsewhere) + Children Education Allowance.

Deductions from gross to reach in-hand: NPS Tier-I contribution 10% of basic + DA, professional tax Rs. 200 per month (state-dependent), CGHS Rs. 250 per month, income tax per slab. Net in-hand is typically Rs. 8,000 to Rs. 12,000 below gross depending on tax slab and city.

The 8th Central Pay Commission was announced by the Ministry of Finance in January 2025 and is expected to be implemented in FY 2026-27 or FY 2027-28. Historical pattern (7th CPC over 6th CPC) suggests roughly a 14 to 20% basic pay increase on implementation.

---

## Benefits, allowances, and transferable service

KVS teaching jobs come with a full central-government benefits package that goes well beyond monthly salary. This is often underrated by first-time candidates.

- **CGHS medical coverage:** Central Government Health Scheme covering employee, spouse, dependent children, and parents. Cashless hospitalisation across CGHS-empanelled facilities nationwide.
- **Leave Travel Concession (LTC):** Two LTCs per 4-year block. One hometown LTC (rail fare reimbursement) and one All-India LTC (rail fare to any destination in India).
- **Children Education Allowance (CEA):** Rs. 2,250 per month per child (up to two children), fully tax-free under Section 10(14). For KVS staff, children in Kendriya Vidyalayas get free education plus this CEA cash allowance.
- **Hostel Subsidy:** Additional Rs. 6,750 per month per child if the child stays in a hostel.
- **Quarters (Type II to Type IV):** Subsidised on-campus quarters where available at rates around 5 to 10% of basic pay (much cheaper than market rent). Not guaranteed at every KV; allotment based on availability.
- **NPS (National Pension System):** Tier-I contribution 10% of basic + DA by employee, matched by government + 4% additional. Contributes to a lump-sum + monthly pension at retirement.
- **Gratuity:** Standard 7th CPC gratuity at 26 days basic per year of service, cap Rs. 25 lakh.
- **Leave:** 8 casual leaves, 20 earned leaves annually, 20 half-pay leaves, plus vacation leave (roughly 60 days during KV summer and winter vacations for teaching staff).
- **Transferable service:** All-India posting across 1,250 plus Kendriya Vidyalayas. Transfer eligibility opens after 5 years of service. Zone preference is honoured where possible.

The transferable service is a double-edged sword. It's stability across a large network (KVs exist in every state and most UTs), but it also means you can be posted to any KV in India after 5 years. For couples in dual-KVS careers, joint posting is prioritised where feasible.

Vacation leave for teaching staff is a major perk: KVs close for 60 days across summer and winter, and teaching staff can travel or take up self-study during this window. Non-teaching staff continue office hours during vacation.

---

## Cutoff trend from KVS 2018, 2022-23 and expected 2026 Tier 1 shortlist marks

Cutoff patterns changed with the shift from 150-mark single-tier to 300-mark Tier 1 in 2024. The concept of a merit cutoff moved from Tier 1 (now qualifying only) to Tier 2 (which contributes to final merit).

Approximate historical cutoff bands (secondary sources: prepp.in, testbook.com, ixambee):

| Cycle year | Post | Category | Cutoff (marks) |
|---|---|---|---|
| KVS 2018 (150 marks pattern) | PGT | UR | 90 to 110 |
| KVS 2018 | PGT | OBC | 85 to 100 |
| KVS 2018 | PGT | SC | 75 to 90 |
| KVS 2022-23 | PGT | UR | 95 to 115 |
| KVS 2022-23 | TGT | UR | 90 to 110 |
| KVS 2022-23 | PRT | UR | 80 to 100 |
| KVS 2024 (300 marks Tier 1) | All | Qualifying | 40% for UR / EWS, 33% for OBC-NCL, 33% for SC, 27% for ST |
| KVS 2026 Tier 1 (qualifying) | All | Same as 2024 pattern | Actual shortlist marks pending publication |
| KVS 2026 Tier 2 (contributes to merit) | PGT | UR | Expected in 130-150 out of 180 for competitive subjects |
| KVS 2026 Tier 2 | TGT | UR | Expected in 125-145 out of 180 |
| KVS 2026 Tier 2 | PRT | UR | Expected in 120-140 out of 180 |

The 2026 Tier 1 shortlist marks (category-wise minimum to move to Tier 2) will be published by KVS in the Tier 1 result document on kvsangathan.nic.in/en/results-misc-answer-keys/. Track this URL for the exact cutoff by post and category.

Historical pattern: subjects with fewer vacancies (like Sanskrit PGT, Music PRT) have lower cutoffs due to smaller candidate pool. Subjects with many vacancies (English TGT, Mathematics PGT) have higher cutoffs due to intense competition.

---

## Direct recruitment vs Samvida Sathi contractual hiring for AY 2026-27

KVS operates two parallel hiring streams. Understanding the distinction is critical.

| Attribute | Direct recruitment (Notification 01/2025) | Samvida Sathi (contractual) |
|---|---|---|
| Recruitment cycle | Every 2 to 3 years (last: 2024 cycle notified) | Continuous, need-based, AY 2026-27 |
| Selection process | Two-tier CBT + Skill Test / Interview / Demo | Interview + Demo (no CBT) |
| Portal | cbseit.in | samvida-sathi.kvs.gov.in |
| Tenure | Permanent regular appointment | Contractual, session-wise (July-March academic year) |
| Salary | 7th CPC pay level (basic + DA + HRA + benefits) | Contractual honorarium, roughly Rs. 27,500 to Rs. 32,000 per month depending on cadre and state |
| Pension and benefits | NPS + CGHS + LTC + CEA full package | No NPS, no CGHS, limited allowances |
| Transferable | All-India after 5 years | KV-specific, not transferable |
| Vacancy volume | 9,921 in current 2026 cycle | High volume across most KVs annually |
| Next notification | Not yet announced for 2026-27 | Continuous rolling recruitment |

Samvida Sathi is the primary teaching-vacancy fill route for AY 2026-27 while the next direct recruitment cycle is planned. Contractual teachers can and often do apply for the next direct recruitment cycle for regularisation.

If you're preparing for a KVS career: appear for Samvida Sathi to build KVS-specific teaching experience while preparing for the next direct recruitment CBT. Contractual experience is not a substitute for the direct recruitment merit list, but it does count as teaching experience for career growth.

---

## 150-day preparation timeline (worked example for TGT Social Science)

A 150-day KVS TGT Social Science plan, assuming 5 hours of daily study:

**Days 1 to 45 (fundamentals + syllabus mapping).**
- Weeks 1-2: Diagnostic test + syllabus mapping to your existing knowledge gaps. Buy NCERT History, Geography, Political Science, and Economics for Classes 6 to 10.
- Weeks 3-4: NCERT Class 6-8 History and Geography deep read. Note-taking with flashcards.
- Weeks 5-6: NCERT Class 9-10 History and Political Science.
- Weeks 7-8: Perspectives on Education pedagogy from R.P. Pathak, S.K. Kochhar. NEP 2020 + NCF 2023 official documents from ncert.nic.in.

**Days 46 to 90 (advanced content + pedagogy).**
- Weeks 9-10: Themes in Indian History (NCERT XI-XII), Fundamentals of Human Geography (NCERT XI), Constitutional History detailed.
- Weeks 11-12: Reasoning practice (R.S. Aggarwal, K. Kundan), Quant (M. Tyra shortcut methods).
- Weeks 13-14: General Awareness monthly current affairs (past 6 months). Wren and Martin for English grammar + KV-level vocabulary.
- Weeks 15-16: Computer Literacy from Lucent Computer Book + MS Office practice.

**Days 91 to 130 (mock tests + revision).**
- Weeks 17-19: Full-length mock tests (Testbook, Adda247, Oliveboard KVS TGT SST). Two mocks per week, weekly review.
- Weeks 20-22: Weakness-focused revision. Sectional practice on Perspectives on Education and Reasoning.

**Days 131 to 150 (final polish).**
- Weeks 23-25: Previous year KVS TGT SST papers (2018, 2022, 2023, 2024). Note-cards on high-yield topics. Two full-length mocks per week.
- Final week: Light revision, sleep well, exam confidence-building.

Recommended books: NCERT History and Geography for both grades 6-12, R. Prasad Indian Polity, R.P. Pathak Perspectives on Education, S.K. Kochhar Teaching of Social Studies, R.S. Aggarwal Reasoning, Lucent GK, Wren and Martin Grammar, Manorama Yearbook 2026.

Adapt the plan for other subjects: PGT Physics substitute NCERT XI-XII Physics + HC Verma + Resnick Halliday. TGT English substitute Wren and Martin + advanced literature (KV-specified authors).

---

## Frequently asked questions

**Is KVS 2026 notification out?**
Yes. KVS Notification 01/2025 was released on 13 November 2025 for 9,921 vacancies. Application window closed on 11 December 2025 (extended from 4 December 2025). Tier 1 CBT was held on 10-11 January 2026, and Tier 2 CBT ran on 27-31 March 2026. Tier 2 result is expected in July 2026 per secondary sources; not officially confirmed by KVS/CBSE as of 15 July 2026.

**How many vacancies are there in KVS 2026 recruitment?**
9,921 total vacancies (revised on 10 December 2025 through a corrigendum from the original 9,126). Breakdown: 13 Assistant Commissioners, 161 Principals, 69 Vice Principals, 1,606 PGT, 3,069 TGT, 3,630 PRT (including Music and Special Educators), plus Librarian, Finance Officer, ASO, Hindi Translator, Stenographer, SSA, and JSA.

**Is CTET mandatory for KVS PGT?**
No. CTET is not mandatory for PGT posts. However, CTET Paper II qualified is mandatory for TGT posts, and CTET Paper I qualified is mandatory for PRT posts. PGT eligibility requires a Master's degree in the concerned subject with at least 50% marks plus B.Ed.

**What is the age limit for KVS PGT TGT PRT 2026?**
PGT: 40 years. TGT: 35 years. PRT: 30 years. All measured as on the last date of application. Standard DoPT age relaxation applies: SC/ST +5 years, OBC-NCL +3 years, PwBD +10 to +15 years, ex-servicemen per rules, and KVS internal serving candidates per KVS Recruitment Rules.

**What is the KVS PRT in-hand salary in 2026?**
Approximately Rs. 55,000 to Rs. 72,000 per month depending on city HRA slab. Basic pay is Rs. 35,400 (7th CPC Pay Level 6) with 55% DA effective 1 January 2026, plus HRA (27% metro X, 18% Y city, 9% Z city), Transport Allowance, and Children Education Allowance. Deductions: NPS 10% of basic + DA, professional tax, CGHS Rs. 250, and income tax.

**What is Samvida Sathi under KVS?**
Samvida Sathi (samvida-sathi.kvs.gov.in) is KVS's contractual teaching portal launched for AY 2026-27 that replaces the earlier school-level walk-in hiring model. It provides session-wise contractual teacher appointments with honorarium of roughly Rs. 27,500 to Rs. 32,000 per month, no NPS/CGHS, and no transferability. Direct recruitment continues in parallel every 2-3 years.

**What is the KVS exam pattern in 2026?**
Two-tier CBT plus Skill Test / Interview / Demo Teaching for teaching cadres. Tier 1 (screening only, does not contribute to merit): 100 MCQs, 300 marks, 120 minutes with 3 marks per correct and 1 negative. Tier 2 (contributes to final merit): 180 marks in 180 minutes with 150 subject MCQs + 30 pedagogy MCQs, 1 mark per correct and 0.25 negative. Demo + Interview: 60 marks Professional Competency Test.

**What is the KVS Tier 2 shortlist ratio?**
1:10 category-wise (revised from the earlier 1:15 ratio, per Notification 01/2025). This means for every vacancy in a category, 10 candidates are shortlisted from Tier 1 to appear for Tier 2. Tighter shortlisting than earlier cycles increases the effective competition at Tier 2.

**When will KVS 2026 Tier 2 result release?**
Expected in July 2026 per secondary sources (prepp.in, freejobalert.com, testbook.com), following the Tier 2 CBT held on 27-31 March 2026 and the objection window that closed in early May 2026. KVS and the conducting agency CBSE have not officially confirmed the exact date as of 15 July 2026. Track kvsangathan.nic.in/en/results-misc-answer-keys/ for the official announcement.

**What is the KVS application fee for 2026?**
Rs. 1,500 for PGT, TGT, PRT, Librarian, ASO, and Hindi Translator posts. Rs. 1,200 for SSA, JSA, and Stenographer. Rs. 2,300 for Assistant Commissioner, Principal, and Vice Principal. SC/ST/PwBD/Ex-Servicemen/Women per DoPT norms may be exempt or pay only a Rs. 500 processing fee (verify per notification wording). Payment online only via cbseit.in.

**Is KVS transferable service and what are the benefits?**
Yes. All-India transferable across 1,250 plus Kendriya Vidyalayas with transfer eligibility after 5 years of service. Benefits: CGHS medical, LTC (hometown + All-India), Children Education Allowance (Rs. 2,250 per child per month, up to 2 children), NPS pension, gratuity, subsidised on-campus quarters where available (Type II to Type IV), 8 CL + 20 EL per year, and 60 days of vacation for teaching staff during summer/winter breaks.

**When is the next KVS direct recruitment notification expected?**
The next KVS direct recruitment notification (likely Notification 02/2026 or Notification 01/2027) has not been announced by KVS as of 15 July 2026. Historical pattern suggests direct recruitment every 2 to 3 years. For continuous teaching vacancy fill during the interim, contractual hiring via Samvida Sathi portal (samvida-sathi.kvs.gov.in) is the primary route for AY 2026-27.

---

content:
## NEET PG 2026: the edit window closes today

NEET PG 2026, conducted by the National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences, is on 30 August 2026. That is twenty days away at the time of writing.

Two things need attention immediately.

The selective edit window is open until 10 August 2026, which is today. If anything in your application needs correcting, that closes now and does not reopen. Registration itself closed on 21 July 2026.

And the exam pattern has changed for 2026. NBEMS reduced the paper from 200 questions to 180, and the total from 800 marks to 720. Candidates preparing from older material, or working through mock papers built on the previous structure, are practising a paper that no longer exists.

## Important dates

| Event | Date |
|---|---|
| Registration closed | 21 July 2026 |
| Selective edit window | Until 10 August 2026 |
| Examination | 30 August 2026 |
| Result | Expected within a fortnight of the exam, around 15 September 2026 |
| Counselling | Conducted by MCC in multiple rounds after the result |

The fortnight turnaround between exam and result is characteristic of NEET PG and worth planning around. Unlike examinations where results take months, you will know your position by mid-September, and counselling registration follows quickly. Candidates who treat the period after 30 August as a break often find themselves unprepared for counselling choices that need research.

## The revised 2026 exam pattern

| Element | 2026 | Previously |
|---|---|---|
| Questions | 180 | 200 |
| Total marks | 720 | 800 |
| Duration | 3 hours 30 minutes | 3 hours 30 minutes |
| Mode | Computer based | Computer based |
| Marking | +4 correct, −1 wrong | +4 correct, −1 wrong |

Twenty fewer questions in the same time changes the arithmetic of the paper more than it appears. You now have about 70 seconds per question rather than 63, which is a meaningful increase in thinking time on a paper where the questions are clinically dense.

The practical consequence is that the 2026 paper rewards accuracy slightly more and raw speed slightly less. With fewer questions carrying the same weight each, every individual question matters more to the final score: one question is now worth about 0.56 per cent of the total rather than 0.5 per cent.

Candidates should also check that their mock test material has been updated. A 200-question mock taken in 210 minutes trains a pace that is now unnecessarily fast, and one built to the old marks total gives a misleading sense of where you stand.

## Marking, and the negative marking calculation

Four marks for a correct answer, one deducted for a wrong one, nothing for an unattempted question.

That is a 4 to 1 ratio, which is more forgiving than it first sounds. Guessing blindly among four options yields on average one correct at plus 4 against three wrong at minus 3, a net gain of 1 mark. So blind guessing carries positive expected value.

Eliminating even one option improves that substantially. With two plausible options remaining, the expected value of attempting is strongly positive.

The implication for a 180-question paper is that you should leave very few blanks. A candidate finishing with twenty unattempted questions has forgone roughly 20 marks of expected value, which on a percentile-ranked examination with a dense field is a material loss.

That said, NEET PG is scored against a percentile rather than an absolute standard, so the goal is relative performance. Reckless attempting that produces many wrong answers still costs marks against candidates who are more selective, so the balance is to attempt everything you can reason about at all and leave only the questions where you genuinely cannot narrow the field.

## What the paper covers

NEET PG tests the MBBS syllabus across pre-clinical, para-clinical and clinical subjects, weighted towards the clinical subjects that dominate postgraduate practice.

The pre-clinical subjects are Anatomy, Physiology and Biochemistry. The para-clinical subjects are Pathology, Pharmacology, Microbiology and Forensic Medicine, along with Community Medicine or Preventive and Social Medicine. The clinical subjects are Medicine, Surgery, Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Paediatrics, Orthopaedics, Ophthalmology, Ear Nose and Throat, Dermatology, Psychiatry, Anaesthesia and Radiology.

Medicine, Surgery, Obstetrics and Gynaecology and Paediatrics carry the heaviest weight between them, and Community Medicine has grown in prominence in recent cycles. Questions are increasingly clinical in framing rather than recall-based, presenting a case and asking for diagnosis, next investigation or management.

Because the paper draws on the entire MBBS curriculum, the realistic preparation strategy in the final twenty days is revision and question practice rather than fresh study of any subject.

## Percentile, and what qualifying means

NEET PG results are reported as a score and a percentile, and the qualifying standard is set as a percentile rather than a fixed mark.

The usual qualifying percentiles are the 50th percentile for General and EWS candidates, the 40th percentile for SC, ST and OBC candidates, and the 45th percentile for General category candidates with a benchmark disability. NBEMS and the Medical Counselling Committee confirm the applicable cutoffs after each result, and they have on occasion been revised downward in a given cycle when seats remained unfilled, so the announced figures for your cycle govern.

Qualifying is not the same as getting a seat. Clearing the percentile makes you eligible to participate in counselling; what determines whether you get a seat, and in which speciality and college, is your rank against the field and the choices you make in counselling.

That distinction matters because the gap between the qualifying percentile and the score needed for a competitive speciality in a good college is very large. A candidate at the 50th percentile has qualified and will realistically be choosing among the less contested options.

## Counselling: how seats are actually allotted

After the result, the Medical Counselling Committee conducts counselling online across multiple rounds.

Seats are divided broadly into the All India Quota, administered centrally by MCC, and the State Quota, administered by individual state authorities through their own counselling processes. Deemed and central universities, and certain institutional seats, are handled within the MCC process.

The practical implication is that most candidates participate in two parallel processes: the MCC counselling for All India Quota and central institutions, and their state's counselling for state quota seats. Registering for both, where eligible, widens the options considerably, and candidates who engage only with one reduce their chances without realising it.

Counselling proceeds in rounds. In each round you register, pay the fee, fill and lock a preference list of college and speciality combinations, and receive an allotment based on rank and preferences. You may then accept and report, or in some rounds choose to participate again for a better allotment, subject to the rules on resignation, forfeiture and security deposits, which differ by round.

Those rules are where candidates lose seats through procedural error rather than rank. Reading the MCC information bulletin for the current cycle before the first round opens is genuinely important, because decisions about whether to freeze an allotment or float for a better one carry consequences that cannot be undone.

## Choice-filling: the decision that shapes a career

The preference list is the most consequential thing a candidate does after the examination, and it gets far less attention than the exam itself.

You are choosing combinations of speciality and college, and the two trade off against each other. A more competitive speciality at a less prestigious institution, or a less contested speciality at a better one, are genuinely different career paths rather than better and worse versions of the same thing.

Some practical considerations. Clinical specialities with strong practice prospects are contested hardest, which means the same rank buys a much better college in a less contested branch. Non-clinical and para-clinical specialities are available at ranks where clinical branches are not, and they lead to academic, laboratory and public health careers that suit some doctors better than clinical practice does. Bond conditions, stipends and service obligations vary enormously between states and institutions and should be checked before preferencing, since a bond can bind several years of your life.

Research previous years' closing ranks for the combinations you are considering. They are published and they tell you far more about your realistic options than any general advice can.

## What happens on exam day

Practical details, since a computer-based clinical paper has its own logistics.

Your admit card specifies the reporting time, which is well ahead of the examination start, and NBEMS does not admit candidates who arrive after the stated closing time. Biometric verification and document checks take time, which is why the window opens early.

Carry the printed admit card and the photo identity document specified on it, and ensure the name matches your application exactly. NBEMS is strict on identity verification.

Electronic items are prohibited: mobile phones, smart watches, calculators, Bluetooth devices and storage media. So are bags and written material. Centres do not reliably provide storage.

The examination runs for 210 continuous minutes with no scheduled break, which is a genuine endurance requirement. Candidates who have not sat a full 210-minute mock discover this on the day, which is a poor time to learn it.

Because the paper is computer based, spend the first minute familiarising yourself with the navigation, the review and marking tools, and where the question palette shows attempted and unattempted items. Knowing how to jump quickly to flagged questions matters when you return to fill blanks at the end.

## Where NEET PG sits among the medical PG routes

NEET PG is the main route to postgraduate medical seats, but it is not the only examination a medical graduate encounters.

| Route | For | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| NEET PG | MD, MS and PG Diploma seats across India | The principal route, conducted by NBEMS |
| INI CET | Postgraduate seats at Institutes of National Importance such as AIIMS, PGIMER, JIPMER and NIMHANS | A separate examination with its own cycle and counselling |
| [NEET SS](/entrance-exams/neet-ss-2026) | Super-speciality courses, DM and MCh, after completing a postgraduate degree | Taken later, after PG |
| State-level processes | State quota seats | Administered through state counselling using NEET PG scores |

The distinction worth noting is that INI CET is a genuinely separate examination for the institutes of national importance, so a candidate targeting AIIMS or PGIMER needs to sit that as well as NEET PG rather than instead of it. The two have separate registrations, separate dates and separate counselling.

NEET SS comes later in a career, after a postgraduate degree, for super-speciality training.

## Eligibility

Candidates must hold an MBBS degree recognised by the National Medical Commission, or be due to complete the internship by the cutoff date specified in the information bulletin for the cycle.

Registration with the National Medical Commission or a State Medical Council is required, whether provisional or permanent.

Completion of the compulsory rotating internship by the prescribed date is the condition that most commonly affects eligibility, and the date is set in the bulletin each year.

There is no age limit and no cap on the number of attempts.

## The final twenty days

With the examination on 30 August, the useful work is narrow.

Revise rather than study new material. Twenty days before a paper drawing on the whole MBBS curriculum, the return on opening a new subject is close to zero while the cost in revision time is real.

Work questions, not chapters. Clinical vignette questions train the reasoning the paper actually tests, and they surface gaps far faster than reading does, because a gap you cannot answer around is immediately visible in a way that a chapter you have read passively is not.

Take full-length mocks built to the 180-question, 720-mark pattern, under the 210-minute clock, and analyse each one properly. If your mock material is still on the 200-question structure, the timing it trains is now wrong.

Prioritise the high-weight clinical subjects and Community Medicine in revision, since that is where the marks concentrate, and resist the temptation to spend the final fortnight shoring up a pre-clinical subject that carries few questions.

Rehearse the attempt strategy: with a 4 to 1 marking ratio, decide in advance that you will attempt anything you can narrow at all, and reserve the final minutes to fill remaining blanks.

And begin reading about counselling now, in the gaps. The result arrives around mid-September and the choices come quickly after, so the research you do in August is research you will not have time for later. Pull the closing ranks for the speciality and college combinations you would realistically consider, note the bond conditions attached to each, and keep the list somewhere you can return to once you have a rank.

One more thing worth doing today rather than later: check your application in the edit window before it closes. A misspelled name, a wrong category entry or an incorrect photograph can create problems at the centre or at counselling verification, and the correction window is the only opportunity to fix any of it.

## Frequently asked questions

**When is NEET PG 2026 and has registration closed?**
NEET PG 2026 is on 30 August 2026, conducted by NBEMS in computer-based mode. Registration closed on 21 July 2026. The selective edit window remains open until 10 August 2026, after which no corrections to the application are possible.

**What is the new NEET PG 2026 exam pattern?**
NBEMS revised the pattern for 2026: the paper now has 180 questions for 720 marks, reduced from 200 questions and 800 marks, over the same duration of 3 hours 30 minutes. Marking remains +4 for a correct answer and −1 for a wrong one. Candidates should check that their mock material reflects the new structure, since a 200-question mock trains a pace that is now unnecessarily fast.

**How many marks is NEET PG 2026 out of?**
720 marks, from 180 questions at 4 marks each. This is down from the previous 800 marks across 200 questions. Each question is now worth about 0.56 per cent of the total rather than 0.5 per cent, so individual questions carry slightly more weight.

**Is there negative marking in NEET PG?**
Yes, one mark is deducted for each wrong answer against four awarded for a correct one. That 4 to 1 ratio means blind guessing among four options carries positive expected value, netting about one mark on average, so very few questions should be left blank. Unattempted questions score nothing.

**When will the NEET PG 2026 result be declared?**
NBEMS releases the result within a fortnight of the examination, so with the exam on 30 August 2026 the result is expected around 15 September 2026. Counselling by the Medical Counselling Committee follows shortly afterwards, which is why counselling research is best done in August rather than after the result.

**What are the NEET PG qualifying percentiles?**
Usually the 50th percentile for General and EWS candidates, the 40th percentile for SC, ST and OBC candidates, and the 45th percentile for General category candidates with a benchmark disability. NBEMS and MCC confirm the applicable cutoffs after each result, and they have occasionally been revised downward in a cycle when seats remained unfilled, so the announced figures for your cycle govern.

**Does qualifying NEET PG mean I get a seat?**
No. Clearing the qualifying percentile makes you eligible to participate in counselling. Whether you receive a seat, and in which speciality and college, depends on your rank against the field and the choices you make during counselling. The gap between the qualifying percentile and the score needed for a competitive speciality at a good college is very large.

**How does NEET PG counselling work?**
The Medical Counselling Committee conducts online counselling in multiple rounds after the result. Seats divide broadly into the All India Quota administered by MCC and the State Quota administered by individual states, with deemed and central university seats handled within the MCC process. Most candidates should register for both MCC counselling and their state's counselling where eligible, since engaging with only one narrows the options.

**What should I consider when filling NEET PG choices?**
That speciality and college trade off against each other. Competitive clinical branches are contested hardest, so the same rank buys a better college in a less contested branch. Non-clinical and para-clinical specialities are available at ranks where clinical branches are not and lead to academic, laboratory and public health careers. Check bond conditions, stipends and service obligations before preferencing, since these vary enormously and a bond can commit several years. Research published closing ranks for the combinations you are considering.

**What is the eligibility for NEET PG 2026?**
An MBBS degree recognised by the National Medical Commission, or completion of the compulsory rotating internship by the cutoff date specified in the information bulletin, along with registration with the NMC or a State Medical Council, whether provisional or permanent. The internship completion date is the condition that most commonly affects eligibility. There is no age limit and no cap on attempts.

**How should I use the last twenty days before NEET PG?**
Revise rather than start new subjects, since the return on opening fresh material this close is minimal. Work clinical vignette questions rather than reading chapters, as they train the reasoning the paper tests and surface gaps faster. Take full-length mocks built to the new 180-question, 720-mark pattern under the 210-minute clock. Prioritise the high-weight clinical subjects and Community Medicine. And start reading about counselling now, because the result lands in mid-September and the choices follow quickly.

**Which subjects carry the most weight in NEET PG?**
Medicine, Surgery, Obstetrics and Gynaecology and Paediatrics carry the heaviest weight between them, with Community Medicine having grown in prominence in recent cycles. Questions are increasingly clinical in framing rather than recall-based, presenting a case and asking for the diagnosis, the next investigation or the management, which is why question practice serves better than chapter reading at this stage.

content:
## JEE Main 2027: what is settled and what is not

JEE Main 2027 will be conducted by the National Testing Agency, with the notification expected in October 2026 and Session 1 expected in January 2027.

Both of those are expectations rather than announcements. NTA has not published the information bulletin for 2027, which means the registration window, the exact examination dates, the fee and the centre list are all unconfirmed. Any specific date you see quoted for JEE Main 2027 at present is a projection from the recent cycles, not a published schedule.

What is settled is the structure, because NTA has run it consistently and the examination's design is well established. That is what this page covers in detail, along with one change from recent cycles that older preparation material still gets wrong.

The change: from 2025, the numerical answer questions in Section B became compulsory. Previously each subject offered ten numerical questions of which candidates attempted any five. Now there are five and all five must be attempted. Anyone practising from books or question banks built before that change is training against a paper that allowed a choice which no longer exists.

## Expected schedule

| Event | Expected timing |
|---|---|
| Notification and information bulletin | October 2026 |
| Session 1 registration | October to November 2026 |
| Session 1 examination | January 2027 |
| Session 2 registration | February 2027 |
| Session 2 examination | April 2027 |

These follow the pattern of recent cycles. Watch jeemain.nta.nic.in for the bulletin rather than relying on secondary sites, since NTA fixes the dates there and has occasionally shifted them.

## Two sessions, and how the best score works

JEE Main runs in two sessions, and this is one of the most useful features of the examination for a candidate.

You may appear in one session or both. If you appear in both, the better of your two NTA scores is the one used for your rank and for JEE Advanced eligibility. The weaker score is discarded.

That structure removes much of the single-day risk that makes other entrance examinations stressful. A candidate who is unwell in January, or who mismanages the paper, has a full second attempt in April with nothing lost.

The strategic implication is worth stating clearly. Session 1 should be treated as a real attempt rather than a rehearsal, because a good score there removes pressure entirely and lets you use February and March on JEE Advanced preparation instead. But it should be sat without the anxiety of finality, because it is not final.

Candidates who deliberately skip Session 1 to prepare more for Session 2 usually get this wrong. They forgo a free attempt, arrive in April with no live examination experience, and carry all the pressure into a single day.

## Exam pattern for Paper 1 (BE and BTech)

| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| Subjects | Physics, Chemistry, Mathematics |
| Questions per subject | 25, being 20 multiple choice and 5 numerical answer |
| Total questions | 75 |
| Total marks | 300 |
| Duration | 3 hours |
| Mode | Computer based |
| Marking | +4 for correct, −1 for incorrect |

Section A of each subject holds the 20 multiple choice questions. Section B holds the 5 numerical answer questions, where you type a numerical value rather than selecting an option, and all five are compulsory.

Negative marking applies to both sections at one mark, which is another change worth noting: numerical questions previously carried no penalty in some cycles, and they now do.

## Papers 2A and 2B

JEE Main is not only an engineering entrance. Paper 2A is for BArch and Paper 2B for BPlanning admissions.

Paper 2A covers Mathematics, an Aptitude Test, and a Drawing Test, with the drawing component assessed separately. Paper 2B covers Mathematics, an Aptitude Test, and a Planning-based section.

Candidates may appear for Paper 1 and Paper 2 in the same session if applying to both engineering and architecture or planning programmes, which requires selecting both at application and paying the applicable fee.

## Marking strategy

At +4 and −1 the ratio is 4 to 1, which is comparatively forgiving.

Guessing blindly among four options in Section A yields on average one correct at plus 4 against three wrong at minus 3, netting plus 1. So blind guessing has positive expected value, and eliminating even one option makes attempting clearly correct.

Section B is different in character. A numerical answer question has no options to eliminate, so a guess is not a one-in-four proposition; it is effectively a shot in the dark with a one-mark penalty attached. There, attempt only where you have actually worked the problem or can bound the answer sensibly. Since all five are compulsory in the sense that no choice is offered, that does not mean all five must be answered.

Across the paper, the practical rule is to be liberal with attempts in Section A once you can narrow options, and disciplined in Section B where a wrong value costs a mark with no compensating probability.

## Percentile and normalisation

JEE Main results are reported as NTA scores, which are percentile scores, rather than as raw marks.

Because the examination runs across multiple days and shifts, NTA normalises across sessions so that a candidate who sat a harder shift is not disadvantaged. Your NTA score reflects your relative position among candidates in your session, computed to several decimal places.

The All India Rank is then derived from the combined best NTA scores of both sessions, with a defined tie-breaking procedure applied where scores are identical.

Two consequences follow. There is no advantage in choosing a particular shift or date in the hope of an easier paper, since normalisation removes it. And a high percentile in a shift with strong candidates is worth the same as a high percentile anywhere else.

## Eligibility, and the separate Class 12 condition

For appearing in JEE Main, a candidate must have passed Class 12 or an equivalent examination, or be appearing in it in the current year. Candidates who passed in the two preceding years are also eligible, giving effectively three consecutive years of eligibility.

There is no age limit for appearing in JEE Main itself.

The condition that catches candidates out is separate from examination eligibility. For admission to the NITs, IIITs and centrally funded technical institutions through JoSAA counselling, a candidate needs either 75 per cent aggregate in Class 12, relaxed to 65 per cent for SC and ST candidates, or to be within the top 20 percentile of their Class 12 board.

So it is entirely possible to score well in JEE Main and be ineligible for an NIT seat on Class 12 marks. That requirement is set by the admitting institutions rather than by NTA, and candidates in Class 12 should treat their board examination as part of the engineering admission process rather than as a separate matter.

## What JEE Main leads to

| Destination | Route |
|---|---|
| NITs, IIITs and GFTIs | JoSAA counselling on the basis of JEE Main rank, subject to the Class 12 condition |
| IITs | JEE Main is the qualifying stage; the top candidates, around 2.5 lakh, become eligible for JEE Advanced |
| State engineering colleges | Many states use JEE Main scores for admission to their institutions |
| Private and deemed universities | A large number accept JEE Main scores |
| BArch and BPlanning programmes | Through Papers 2A and 2B |

The JEE Advanced link is the one candidates focus on most. Qualifying JEE Main at a rank within the announced cutoff, generally around the top 2.5 lakh, makes a candidate eligible to sit JEE Advanced, which is the examination for admission to the IITs. Session performance therefore matters twice: for your own NIT and state options, and for whether you reach JEE Advanced at all.

## Preparing for JEE Main 2027

Working back from an expected January 2027 Session 1, there are roughly five months.

Build from the NCERT texts for Class 11 and 12 across all three subjects, since the syllabus is drawn from them and NTA questions stay within that scope. Standard reference books add depth for the harder questions but do not replace the NCERT base.

Practise numerical answer questions specifically. They are compulsory now, they carry negative marking, and they require exact values rather than recognisable options, which is a different skill from multiple choice work. Candidates who prepare only on MCQs are underprepared for a third of each subject's question count.

Work previous years' papers, which are freely available and remain the best guide to how NTA frames questions.

Take full computer-based mocks under the three-hour clock, including on NTA's own mock platform when it opens, so the interface is familiar. A candidate meeting the numerical entry field for the first time on exam day loses time to it.

Do not neglect Class 12 board preparation. The 75 per cent condition for NIT admission makes the board examination part of the same project, and candidates who treat it as an afterthought can find a good JEE rank unusable.

Plan to sit both sessions from the outset.

## Subject-wise approach

Because the three subjects reward different things, a single study method applied uniformly wastes effort.

Physics rewards conceptual clarity over memorisation. Mechanics, electrostatics, current electricity, magnetism, optics and modern physics carry consistent weight, and the questions typically require applying two or three concepts together rather than recalling a formula. Working problems is the only method that builds this; reading theory produces a false sense of readiness.

Chemistry splits into three parts that behave differently. Physical chemistry is numerical and rewards practice in the same way physics does. Inorganic chemistry is substantially memory-based, covering periodic properties, chemical bonding, coordination compounds and the p-block and d-block elements, and it responds directly to systematic revision, which makes it the most reliably scoring portion for a disciplined candidate. Organic chemistry rewards understanding reaction mechanisms rather than memorising individual reactions, since the same mechanism explains many transformations.

Mathematics is the most time-expensive subject in the examination. Calculus, coordinate geometry, algebra, trigonometry, vectors and three-dimensional geometry, and probability carry the bulk of the questions, and speed comes from recognising question types rather than from working faster. Candidates who run short of time on the paper are usually losing it here.

A practical allocation, for a candidate with all three at a comparable level, is to protect inorganic chemistry revision as the cheapest marks available, invest most problem-solving time in mathematics and physics, and treat organic chemistry mechanisms as a distinct project rather than as reaction lists to memorise.

## Mistakes that cost JEE Main candidates

Skipping Session 1. It is a free attempt with the better score counting, and forgoing it concentrates all the risk on a single April date with no live examination experience behind you.

Practising numerical questions as though they were optional. They are compulsory now and carry negative marking, and a candidate who has only drilled multiple choice is unprepared for a third of each subject's questions.

Guessing in Section B. With no options to eliminate, a numerical guess is a shot in the dark with a one-mark penalty. Discipline there is worth more than volume.

Treating the Class 12 board examination as separate. The 75 per cent condition for NIT admission makes it part of the same project, and a strong JEE rank with insufficient board marks is a genuinely wasted year.

Preparing beyond the NCERT scope. Reference books add depth on hard questions, but candidates who abandon the NCERT base for advanced material often find they have gaps in exactly the straightforward questions that make up most of the paper.

Meeting the computer interface on exam day. NTA publishes a mock platform, and the numerical entry field in particular costs time to anyone using it for the first time under pressure.

## How to apply, when the window opens

Applications will be filed on jeemain.nta.nic.in.

1. Register with a valid email address and mobile number, both used for all communication including the admit card.
2. Complete the application with personal and academic details exactly as on your certificates.
3. Select the paper or papers you are applying for: Paper 1 for BE and BTech, Paper 2A for BArch, Paper 2B for BPlanning, or a combination.
4. Choose your examination city preferences in order.
5. Upload photograph, signature and the required documents in the specified format and dimensions, which NTA specifies precisely and rejects if not met.
6. Pay the application fee, which varies by paper combination and category.
7. Submit and save the confirmation page and application number.

NTA usually provides a correction window after the close of applications, but it is limited in what it allows to be changed, so accuracy at submission matters.

## Frequently asked questions

**When is JEE Main 2027?**
Session 1 is expected in January 2027 and Session 2 in April 2027, with the NTA notification expected in October 2026. None of these are confirmed: NTA has not published the 2027 information bulletin, so registration dates, exact examination dates, fees and centres are all unannounced. Any specific date circulating now is a projection from recent cycles rather than a published schedule.

**What is the JEE Main 2027 exam pattern?**
Paper 1 for BE and BTech has 75 questions for 300 marks over 3 hours, computer based, with 25 questions in each of Physics, Chemistry and Mathematics. Each subject has 20 multiple choice questions in Section A and 5 numerical answer questions in Section B. Marking is +4 for a correct answer and −1 for an incorrect one in both sections.

**Are the numerical questions in JEE Main optional?**
No, not since 2025. Previously each subject offered ten numerical questions of which candidates attempted any five. From 2025 there are five and no choice is offered. Preparation material published before that change trains against a paper that allowed an option which no longer exists, so check the edition of any question bank you are using.

**How do the two JEE Main sessions work?**
JEE Main runs in two sessions and you may appear in one or both. If you appear in both, the better of your two NTA scores is used for your rank and for JEE Advanced eligibility, and the weaker is discarded. This removes most of the single-day risk, which is why deliberately skipping Session 1 to prepare longer for Session 2 is usually a mistake: it forgoes a free attempt and puts all the pressure on one day.

**Is there negative marking in JEE Main?**
Yes, one mark for each incorrect answer against four for a correct one, in both the multiple choice and the numerical sections. In Section A that 4 to 1 ratio makes guessing positively valued once you can eliminate an option. In Section B there are no options to eliminate, so a guess is a shot in the dark carrying a one-mark penalty, and those questions should be attempted only where you have worked the problem.

**What is the Class 12 percentage requirement for JEE Main?**
There is no percentage requirement to appear in JEE Main. But for admission to the NITs, IIITs and centrally funded technical institutions through JoSAA counselling, a candidate needs 75 per cent aggregate in Class 12, relaxed to 65 per cent for SC and ST candidates, or to be within the top 20 percentile of their board. That condition is set by the admitting institutions, so it is possible to score well in JEE Main and still be ineligible for an NIT seat.

**How many attempts do I get at JEE Main?**
Candidates who passed Class 12 in the current year or either of the two preceding years are eligible, which gives effectively three consecutive years of eligibility, with two sessions in each year. There is no age limit for appearing in the examination itself.

**How does JEE Main lead to the IITs?**
JEE Main is the qualifying stage. Candidates ranked within the announced cutoff, generally around the top 2.5 lakh, become eligible to sit JEE Advanced, which is the examination used for admission to the IITs. So JEE Main performance matters twice: for your own NIT, IIIT and state college options through JoSAA, and for whether you reach JEE Advanced at all.

**What is the NTA score and how is it different from marks?**
The NTA score is a percentile score reflecting your relative position among candidates in your session, computed to several decimal places, rather than your raw marks. Because the examination runs across multiple days and shifts, NTA normalises across them so a candidate who sat a harder shift is not disadvantaged. There is therefore no advantage in choosing a particular date or shift hoping for an easier paper.

**What are Paper 2A and Paper 2B in JEE Main?**
Paper 2A is for BArch admissions and covers Mathematics, an Aptitude Test and a Drawing Test. Paper 2B is for BPlanning admissions and covers Mathematics, an Aptitude Test and a Planning-based section. Candidates applying to both engineering and architecture or planning programmes may appear for Paper 1 and Paper 2 in the same session by selecting both at application and paying the applicable fee.

**How should I prepare for JEE Main 2027 from now?**
With roughly five months to an expected January session, build from the NCERT texts for Classes 11 and 12 since the syllabus is drawn from them, using reference books for depth rather than as a replacement. Practise numerical answer questions specifically, as they are compulsory, carry negative marking and demand exact values. Work previous years' papers, take full computer-based mocks under the three-hour clock including on NTA's own mock platform, and keep Class 12 board preparation running given the 75 per cent condition for NIT admission.

**Where will JEE Main 2027 applications be filed?**
On jeemain.nta.nic.in, once NTA publishes the information bulletin expected in October 2026. Watch that site directly rather than aggregator pages, since the dates, fees, centre list and document specifications are all fixed there, and NTA rejects uploads that do not meet its stated format and dimension requirements.
