content:
NEET UG 2026 has had an unusual cycle. The examination originally scheduled for 3 May 2026 was cancelled by the National Testing Agency following question paper leak allegations, and a re-examination was held on 21 June 2026 from 2:00 PM to 5:00 PM. The result followed, and counselling is now underway.

If you sat the re-exam, the part that decides where you study is happening now, and it is administratively demanding in a way the examination itself is not.

## Where this cycle stands

| Stage | Status |
|---|---|
| Original exam, 3 May 2026 | Cancelled by NTA |
| Re-examination | Held 21 June 2026, 2:00 PM to 5:00 PM |
| Re-registration | Not required for already-registered candidates |
| Fees already paid | Confirmed for refund by NTA |
| Result | Declared following the re-exam |
| Counselling | Underway through MCC and state authorities |

Candidates who had registered for the May examination were carried forward automatically. NTA did not require a fresh application, and confirmed that fees already paid would be refunded.

## Counselling is two separate processes, not one

This is the single thing candidates most often misunderstand, and getting it wrong costs seats.

The Medical Counselling Committee conducts counselling for the All India Quota, which is 15 per cent of state government medical college seats, together with deemed universities, central universities, and institutions such as AIIMS and JIPMER.

State counselling authorities separately conduct counselling for the remaining 85 per cent of state government college seats, plus private colleges within that state.

These run on different portals, with different registration, different schedules and different fee structures. Registering with MCC does not register you for state counselling, and registering with your state does not register you for the All India Quota.

Candidates who want to be considered for both, which is most candidates, must register separately for both and track both schedules independently. Missing a state registration window while focused on MCC is a common and entirely avoidable loss.

If you are willing to study outside your home state, the All India Quota widens your options considerably. If you are not, state counselling is where nearly all your realistic seats sit.

## How seat allotment actually works

Counselling runs in rounds. In each round you fill and lock a list of choices in order of preference, the authority runs an allotment against your rank and your choices, and seats are allocated to whoever ranks highest among those who chose them.

Your choice list is the decision that matters. The allotment cannot give you something you did not list, and it will give you the highest thing on your list that your rank reaches. That means two errors are possible and they cut in opposite directions.

List too few choices and you may be allotted nothing in a round where a lower preference was available to you. List them in the wrong order and you may be allotted a college you would have ranked below another one you also qualified for.

Order the list by genuine preference, not by predicted cutoff. The system already handles the cutoff question by only reaching what your rank allows. Your job is to state what you actually want first.

Understand the rules on accepting, declining and upgrading before a round rather than during it. Free exit, seat forfeiture and security deposit rules vary between MCC and individual states, and the consequences of declining a seat in a later round are different from the consequences in an earlier one. This is where candidates lose money and options through decisions taken under time pressure without reading the rules.

## What the qualifying percentile means

NEET qualification is set by percentile, not by a fixed mark. The qualifying percentile is defined against the performance of everyone who sat the examination, which is why the corresponding raw mark moves every year.

Qualifying is a threshold for eligibility, and it is not the same as being competitive for a seat. A candidate who qualifies at the threshold percentile is eligible to participate in counselling but will find that very few seats are reachable at that rank. The gap between qualifying and securing a government college seat is wide.

That distinction is worth being clear-eyed about when planning. Private and deemed institutions have fees that differ by an order of magnitude from government colleges, and a candidate whose rank reaches only those options is facing a financial decision rather than an academic one.

Category-wise qualifying percentiles differ, with reserved categories and candidates with benchmark disabilities qualifying at lower thresholds as specified by the authorities.

## Exam pattern, for candidates planning a future attempt

NEET UG is a single paper covering Physics, Chemistry and Biology, the last split into Botany and Zoology.

The paper carries 180 questions to be answered for 720 marks. Marking is four marks for a correct answer and minus one for an incorrect one, with nothing deducted for a question left unattempted.

That negative marking shapes strategy directly. With a four-to-one ratio, an educated guess between two remaining options has positive expected value, while a blind guess across four does not. Blanket guessing to fill the sheet is a losing approach, and so is excessive caution that leaves marks on the table where you had genuinely narrowed the options.

Biology carries the largest share of questions, which is why it disproportionately determines outcomes, and it is also the section where accuracy is most achievable because the content rewards recall over derivation.

The syllabus follows the standard Class 11 and Class 12 science curriculum. Confirm the syllabus and pattern for your cycle from the NTA information bulletin, since NTA has revised both between cycles.

## What the cancellation means for candidates

A cancelled and re-held examination is disruptive in ways that go beyond the calendar, and it is worth naming them honestly.

The gap between 3 May and 21 June forced candidates to hold preparation at peak for an additional seven weeks, which is difficult and which affects people unevenly. Candidates with stable study conditions absorbed it better than those without.

The re-examination was a fresh paper. Candidates who had walked out of the May examination with a sense of how they had done had that reset entirely.

The compressed timeline afterwards, with result and counselling following in sequence, left less room than usual between stages.

None of that changes what you can do now, which is to focus on counselling, because that is the part still within your control. But candidates who found the cycle harder than expected should understand that the disruption was real and shared rather than a personal failure of preparation.

## Round strategy, and the mistakes that cost seats

Counselling runs across several rounds, and each has different rules about what happens if you accept, decline or do nothing. Understanding the sequence before it starts is worth more than any amount of cutoff prediction.

In early rounds the risk of holding out is lower, because further rounds remain and vacated seats return to the pool. In later rounds the same decision becomes irreversible, and a candidate who declines a seat expecting another round may find there is not one, or that the deposit is forfeited.

Free exit provisions, security deposit rules and seat forfeiture penalties differ between MCC and individual state authorities, and they differ between rounds within the same process. Read the information brochure for the specific round you are in rather than relying on how it worked last year or in another state.

Upgrading deserves particular care. Accepting a seat while remaining in the running for a better one is possible in defined circumstances, and the conditions attached vary. Candidates who assume upgrading is automatic, or that it carries no risk to the seat already held, sometimes lose both.

The mop-up and stray vacancy rounds at the end operate under tighter rules and shorter notice. Candidates still unplaced at that stage should be watching daily rather than weekly, because the windows are short and missing one ends the cycle.

## Government, private and deemed institutions

The financial difference between these is large enough that it should shape your choice list rather than being discovered afterwards.

Government medical colleges charge fees that are modest by any comparison, which is why competition for them is intense and why the ranks that reach them are far better than the ranks that merely qualify.

Private colleges charge substantially more, with the exact figure varying by state and institution, and state counselling authorities generally publish the fee structure for private colleges within their process.

Deemed universities, which come under MCC, are typically the most expensive option, and candidates sometimes reach them in later rounds without having considered the cost.

The practical advice is to work out what you can actually afford before you fill a choice list, not after an allotment. An allotment you cannot take up wastes a round and, depending on the rules in force, may cost a deposit as well. Discussing the financial position with family before counselling starts is a more useful preparation than refreshing cutoff predictions.

## If this cycle did not go the way you hoped

Some candidates in every cycle finish counselling without a seat they want, and this cycle's disruption will have made that harder for some.

The options are narrower than internet advice suggests. Repeating the year and attempting NEET again is the main route, and it is a serious commitment: a full year with an uncertain outcome, at an age where peers are progressing.

Allied health sciences, biotechnology, pharmacy, nursing, veterinary science and other biology-based degrees are real careers rather than consolation prizes, and some accept NEET scores while others have their own admission routes. Candidates who dismiss them in June sometimes find them appealing in September.

Studying medicine abroad is heavily marketed and deserves scrutiny rather than enthusiasm. The relevant questions are recognition of the qualification in India, the screening examination required to practise here, and the actual pass rates of graduates from the specific institution being sold to you.

Whatever the decision, make it deliberately rather than by drifting into a repeat year because it felt like the default. A year is a real cost and it should be spent on a plan rather than on momentum.

## Documents to have ready for counselling

Counselling verification is where administrative problems surface, and they surface at a point where there is no time to fix them.

Assemble the full set before your first round: the NEET scorecard and rank letter, admit card, Class 10 certificate for date of birth, Class 12 mark sheet and passing certificate, identity proof, passport photographs matching the one used in the application, and a category certificate in the prescribed format where applicable.

Candidates claiming benefits under any reserved category need that certificate in the exact format the authority specifies, issued within any validity window it defines. An outdated format is a common cause of rejection at verification, and it is not something the authority will waive.

Keep several photocopies alongside the originals. Verification processes ask for both, and the queue is not the place to discover you have one set.

Check every document against your application details. A name spelled differently on a certificate than in your NEET registration is a real problem at verification, however obviously it is the same person.

## How the reservation and quota structure fits together

Counselling allocates seats through several overlapping categories, and candidates frequently misread which ones they can benefit from.

The All India Quota is 15 per cent of seats in state government medical colleges, pooled nationally and administered by MCC. Any qualified candidate can compete for it regardless of home state, which is what makes it the route to studying outside your own state.

The state quota is the remaining 85 per cent of state government college seats, administered by each state. Eligibility for it generally depends on domicile or schooling within that state, and the rules differ between states in ways that matter: some require years of residence, some require Class 10 and 12 within the state, and some recognise other conditions.

Category reservation applies within both, at the percentages defined by the relevant authority, and reserved category candidates compete both in their category and in the open pool, taking whichever gives the better outcome.

There are further categories in some processes, including seats for candidates with benchmark disabilities, and institutional or management quotas in private and deemed institutions with their own rules.

The practical implication is that your eligibility for state counselling is a question of fact about your domicile and schooling that you should settle definitively before counselling begins. Candidates occasionally assume eligibility in a state they no longer qualify for, or fail to realise they qualify in one they left years ago.

## What to do while counselling runs

Counselling is administratively demanding and it rewards organisation more than anything else at this stage.

Track both processes on a calendar with every registration deadline, choice-filling window, locking deadline, allotment date and reporting deadline written down. Missing a locking deadline means your choices are not considered in that round, and no authority will make an exception.

Check the official portals rather than social media for schedule changes. Counselling dates shift, and they shift with short notice.

Keep your documents assembled and your fees ready, because reporting deadlines after an allotment are short and a candidate scrambling for a demand draft or a certificate can lose a seat they were allotted.

Decide your preference order calmly, in advance, with the people whose views matter to you. Filling a choice list under time pressure on the final evening is how candidates end up with orders they did not intend.

And keep a written record of what you did in each round. Across several rounds and two processes, it is genuinely easy to lose track of what you have accepted, declined or are still waiting on.

## Frequently asked questions

**Was the NEET UG 2026 exam cancelled?**

Yes. The examination originally scheduled for 3 May 2026 was cancelled by the National Testing Agency following question paper leak allegations. A re-examination was conducted on 21 June 2026 from 2:00 PM to 5:00 PM.

**Did candidates have to re-register for the NEET re-exam?**

No. Candidates who had already registered for the May examination were carried forward automatically, and NTA confirmed that application fees already paid would be refunded. Admit cards for the re-examination were released around 14 June 2026.

**When was the NEET UG 2026 result declared?**

The result followed the 21 June re-examination, and counselling through the Medical Counselling Committee and state authorities is underway. Scorecards are downloaded from the NTA portal at neet.nta.nic.in.

**What is the difference between MCC and state counselling?**

MCC conducts counselling for the 15 per cent All India Quota, deemed universities, central universities and institutions such as AIIMS and JIPMER. State authorities separately conduct counselling for the remaining 85 per cent of state government college seats and private colleges in that state. They are different portals with different registrations and schedules, and registering for one does not register you for the other.

**Do I need to register separately for both?**

Yes, if you want to be considered for both. Most candidates do. Missing a state registration window while focused on MCC is a common and avoidable loss, so track both schedules independently.

**How does seat allotment work?**

Counselling runs in rounds. You fill and lock a preference list, and the authority allots the highest choice on your list that your rank reaches. The system cannot allot something you did not list, so order the list by genuine preference rather than by predicted cutoff, and list enough choices to avoid going unallotted in a round.

**What is the NEET UG exam pattern?**

A single paper of 180 questions for 720 marks, covering Physics, Chemistry and Biology, with Biology split into Botany and Zoology. Four marks are awarded for a correct answer and one is deducted for an incorrect one, with no penalty for an unattempted question.

**Does qualifying NEET guarantee a medical seat?**

No. The qualifying percentile is an eligibility threshold, not a competitive position. A candidate qualifying at the threshold is eligible to participate in counselling but will find very few seats reachable at that rank, and the gap between qualifying and securing a government college seat is wide.

**Why does the NEET qualifying mark change every year?**

Because qualification is set by percentile rather than by a fixed score. The percentile is defined against the performance of everyone who sat the examination that year, so the raw mark corresponding to it moves with the difficulty of the paper and the candidate pool.

**What documents do I need for NEET counselling?**

The scorecard and rank letter, admit card, Class 10 certificate for date of birth, Class 12 mark sheet and passing certificate, identity proof, matching passport photographs, and a category certificate in the prescribed format where applicable. Keep originals and photocopies, and check every detail against your NEET registration, since a name mismatch is a genuine problem at verification.

**Can I appear for NEET again next year?**

Yes. There is no cap on the number of attempts, and eligibility is governed by the qualifying conditions rather than by an attempt limit. Candidates repeating should treat it as a deliberate year-long commitment with a plan rather than as the default response to a disappointing result.

**Is the All India Quota open to candidates from any state?**

Yes. The 15 per cent All India Quota is pooled nationally and administered by MCC, and any qualified candidate can compete for it regardless of home state. It is the route to studying outside your own state. The remaining 85 per cent state quota generally depends on domicile or schooling conditions that differ between states.

**What happens if I do not report after being allotted a seat?**

The seat is released back into the pool and, depending on the round and the authority's rules, you may forfeit a security deposit or lose eligibility for subsequent rounds. Reporting deadlines after an allotment are short, which is why documents and fees should be ready before the allotment rather than after it.

## Official sources

- National Testing Agency NEET portal: https://neet.nta.nic.in
- Medical Counselling Committee: https://mcc.nic.in
- Your state counselling authority, which is the authority on the 85 per cent state quota and private colleges within the state

NTA is the authority on your score. MCC and your state authority are the authorities on your seat. Where this page conflicts with any of them, they are correct.

content:
## Is there a BTET 2026 exam? The honest answer

There is no live, officially notified Bihar Teacher Eligibility Test (BTET) for 2026 for primary classes. If you searched for a BTET 2026 notification date or application form, the pages promising one are recycling old templates with invented dates, and you can tell because they contradict each other: one lists the exam in December 2026, another in November, a third quotes a February registration. None of these traces to a Bihar School Examination Board notice, because the Board is not running a standalone primary TET this cycle.

Here is what actually decides teacher eligibility in Bihar in 2026. For teaching classes 1 to 8, the operative test is [CTET](/entrance-exams/ctet-september-2026), the Central Teacher Eligibility Test conducted by CBSE. For teaching classes 9 to 12, the state test is BSEB STET, the Secondary Teacher Eligibility Test. The actual recruitment, the exam that gives you the job rather than just the eligibility, is BPSC TRE 4.0, run by the Bihar Public Service Commission. The old BTET, last held in 2011, is not part of this picture anymore.

So if you are chasing a Bihar government teaching job in 2026, the question is not when BTET happens. It is which of CTET, STET, and BPSC TRE you actually need, and this guide answers exactly that.

The confusion is understandable, because the names sound alike and the rules have changed more than once in the last decade. A candidate can waste an entire preparation season waiting for a BTET form that will never open, while the CTET or STET window they actually needed comes and goes. The rest of this page untangles the four exams, maps each to the class level it serves, and walks through the eligibility and the degree you need for each, so you spend your time on the exam that leads to an appointment rather than the one that does not exist.

## BTET vs STET vs CTET vs BPSC TRE at a glance

This is the distinction the entire search results page gets wrong. Read this table first, then the sections below explain each one.

| Exam | What it is | Classes | Conducted by | Status in 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BTET / BETET | Legacy Bihar primary TET | 1 to 8 | Bihar School Examination Board | Discontinued, last held 2011 |
| CTET | Central eligibility test | 1 to 8 | CBSE | Live, the route for Bihar primary |
| STET | State secondary eligibility test | 9 to 12 | Bihar School Examination Board | Live |
| BPSC TRE 4.0 | Teacher recruitment exam | 1 to 12 | Bihar Public Service Commission | The actual recruitment |

The one-line summary: TET exams (CTET and STET) make you eligible. BPSC TRE hires you. BTET is history.

## The legacy BTET, and why it confuses people

The Bihar Elementary Teacher Eligibility Test, written variously as BTET or BETET, was last conducted on 20 and 21 December 2011, with certificates issued in May 2012. It followed the standard two-paper TET format, Paper 1 for primary teaching and Paper 2 for the upper primary level. After that cycle, Bihar did not run its own primary TET again, and the state routed classes 1 to 8 eligibility through CTET instead.

The reason old BTET pages still rank is that search demand for the term never died, so content farms keep publishing fresh-looking BTET pages with made-up dates to capture the traffic. If you hold a genuine 2012 BTET or BETET certificate, it still matters, because TET certificate validity is now lifetime (covered further down). But there is no new BTET exam to sit.

## CTET: the route for classes 1 to 8

For anyone aiming to teach at the primary (classes 1 to 5) or upper primary (classes 6 to 8) level in a Bihar government school, CTET is the eligibility test that counts. CBSE conducts CTET in two papers. Paper 1 is for candidates who want to teach classes 1 to 5, and Paper 2 is for classes 6 to 8. A candidate who wants to teach across both levels sits both papers.

CTET is held at national level, usually twice a year, and its certificate is accepted by Bihar for the primary and upper primary eligibility requirement in BPSC TRE. So if your target classes are 1 to 8, plan for CTET, not a Bihar-specific primary TET.

## How CTET fits a Bihar candidate's plan

CTET deserves a closer look because it is the workhorse eligibility test for the largest pool of Bihar teaching aspirants, those targeting classes 1 to 8. Since CBSE holds it at national level, a Bihar candidate sits the same paper as candidates from every other state, and the certificate is portable across states that accept CTET. Paper 1 covers Child Development and Pedagogy, two languages, Mathematics, and Environmental Studies for the primary level. Paper 2 covers Child Development and Pedagogy, two languages, and then either Mathematics and Science or Social Studies, depending on the subject group you intend to teach at the upper primary level. The general-category qualifying mark is 60 percent, with relaxation for reserved categories, and the certificate, like STET, is now valid for life. For a Bihar candidate, the practical plan is to clear the CTET paper matching the level you want, keep the certificate safe, and use it to apply when the next BPSC TRE cycle for that level opens.

## STET: the route for classes 9 to 12

BSEB STET is the live Bihar state eligibility test, and it covers the secondary and senior secondary levels. STET has two papers: Paper 1 qualifies you to teach classes 9 and 10, and Paper 2 qualifies you for classes 11 and 12. Each paper is an online computer based test of 150 objective questions for 150 marks, with a duration of 150 minutes and no negative marking.

Each paper mixes subject-specific questions with teaching and general awareness questions. Paper 1 typically carries 100 subject questions plus 50 on pedagogy and general awareness. The qualifying bar is 50 percent for the general category and 45 percent for reserved categories such as SC, ST, and others, per BSEB norms.

On the recent cycle: the STET 2025 exam ran from 14 October to 16 November 2025, and its result was declared on 5 January 2026, per BSEB. A fresh STET 2026 notification is expected around late 2026 on secondary.biharboardonline.com, though the exact date is not yet fixed, so treat any circulating STET 2026 date as tentative until BSEB confirms it.

## BPSC TRE 4.0: the exam that gives you the job

This is the one candidates should actually be planning for. BPSC TRE, the Teacher Recruitment Examination run by the Bihar Public Service Commission, is the recruitment that fills Bihar government teaching posts across all class levels. The fourth cycle, TRE 4.0, is the current one.

TRE 4.0 is reported to carry over 45,000 vacancies (trackers cite figures between about 45,000 and 47,000, and the exact number will be confirmed in the official notification, so treat it as tentative). The exam is reported to be scheduled for the 22 to 27 September 2026 window. Application fee is around Rs 750 for general and other candidates and Rs 200 for SC, ST, female, and PwD candidates, per BPSC norms. Selection is a written computer based test with no interview, followed by document verification, and the merit is drawn from the written score.

The exam pattern varies by the class level you apply for.

| Level | Paper structure |
|---|---|
| Classes 1 to 5 | Paper 1 Language (30 Q, qualifying) plus Paper 2 General Studies (120 Q) |
| Classes 6 to 12 | Paper 1 Language (30 Q, qualifying) plus Paper 2 General Studies (40 Q) plus Paper 3 Subject (80 Q) |

The important link between the exams is eligibility. BPSC TRE requires you to already hold the matching TET qualification. For classes 1 to 8 that means CTET or STET, and for classes 9 to 12 that means STET in the relevant subject, alongside the teaching degree the level requires.

## Which exam do you actually need

Match your target class level to the exams you must clear.

| You want to teach | Eligibility test | Recruitment exam |
|---|---|---|
| Classes 1 to 5 | CTET Paper 1 (or STET Paper 1) | BPSC TRE, primary level |
| Classes 6 to 8 | CTET Paper 2 (or STET) | BPSC TRE, middle level |
| Classes 9 to 10 | STET Paper 1 | BPSC TRE, secondary level |
| Classes 11 to 12 | STET Paper 2 | BPSC TRE, senior secondary level |

So the path is always two steps. First clear the eligibility test for your level, then clear BPSC TRE to get appointed. There is no single BTET exam that does both.

## Eligibility by level, with the degree you need

The teaching qualification changes with the level, and this trips up candidates who assume a B.Ed covers everything.

For classes 1 to 5, you need Class 12 with at least 50 percent (45 percent for reserved categories) plus a two-year Diploma in Elementary Education (D.El.Ed), or a four-year B.El.Ed, along with CTET or STET Paper 1. For classes 6 to 8, you need graduation plus D.El.Ed or B.Ed, along with CTET Paper 2 or STET. For classes 9 to 10, you need graduation with 50 percent plus B.Ed, along with STET Paper 1 in the subject. For classes 11 to 12, you need a master's degree with 50 percent in the subject plus B.Ed, along with STET Paper 2.

A frequent confusion: a B.Ed alone does not make you eligible for classes 1 to 5. Post-2023 rules restrict primary teaching to D.El.Ed and equivalent diploma routes, so a B.Ed holder aiming at the primary level should confirm the current qualification list in the BPSC TRE notification before applying.

## Worked eligibility examples

Concrete cases make the rules clearer.

Take a candidate with Class 12 at 48 percent plus a D.El.Ed and CTET Paper 1. Are they eligible for BPSC TRE classes 1 to 5? Not on the marks. Primary eligibility needs 50 percent in Class 12 for the general category, or 45 percent for reserved categories, so a 48 percent general candidate falls short, while a reserved candidate at 48 percent clears the bar.

Take a candidate who wants to teach class 10 science. They need graduation in science with 50 percent, a B.Ed, and a pass in STET Paper 1 in the science subject. To qualify STET they must score at least 75 out of 150, which is the 50 percent general-category cutoff. A CTET pass would not substitute here, because classes 9 and 10 are STET territory, not CTET.

## TET certificate validity is now lifetime

One piece of genuinely useful news that competitor pages bury: TET certificates, including Bihar TET and STET, are valid for life, not seven years. The Union Government announced the change on 3 June 2021, extending validity from 7 years to lifetime with retrospective effect from 2011, and Bihar's Education Department applied it retroactively from 2012.

The practical result is that a candidate holding a 2012 BTET or STET certificate still holds a valid lifetime qualification and does not need to re-sit the eligibility test. That old certificate can support a BPSC TRE application for the matching level, subject to the notification's qualification list.

## STET in depth: subjects and how to prepare

STET is the exam most Bihar candidates aiming at secondary teaching underestimate. Each paper pairs subject mastery with teaching knowledge, so a strong subject graduate can still miss the cutoff by neglecting pedagogy. Paper 1 covers the subject you intend to teach for classes 9 and 10, from a list that includes Hindi, English, Sanskrit, Urdu, Mathematics, Science, and Social Science, alongside a pedagogy and general awareness block. Paper 2 does the same for classes 11 and 12 across senior secondary subjects.

Because there is no negative marking, every question is worth attempting, and the qualifying nature of the exam means your goal is to clear the cutoff cleanly rather than top a merit list. The subject block rewards revising your graduation or post-graduation syllabus to the depth of the school curriculum you will teach, while the pedagogy and general awareness block rewards familiarity with the Right to Education framework, child psychology basics, and current affairs. Previous STET papers are the best guide to the balance the Board strikes between subject and pedagogy questions.

## BPSC TRE 4.0 in depth: posts and selection

BPSC TRE 4.0 recruits teachers across four broad levels: primary (classes 1 to 5), middle (classes 6 to 8), secondary (classes 9 to 10), and senior secondary (classes 11 to 12). You apply for the level that matches your qualification and TET pass, and you compete within that level's vacancy pool and subject.

The selection is refreshingly simple compared with most government exams: a single written computer based test decides the merit, there is no interview, and document verification confirms your eligibility afterward. Paper 1 tests language and is only qualifying, so it does not add to your merit score. The scoring paper is General Studies for primary and middle levels, with an added subject paper for the secondary and senior secondary levels. Reservation and domicile rules follow Bihar state policy, and candidates should read the reservation roster in the notification, since the vacancy split by category and subject decides how competitive each slot really is.

## Teacher pay under BPSC TRE

Pay rises with the level you teach. Bihar government teachers recruited through TRE draw a state pay scale with basic pay, dearness allowance, house rent allowance, and other allowances on top. Reported starting pay runs roughly from the mid-20,000s per month for primary teachers to the low-30,000s for senior secondary teachers, before allowances, per BPSC TRE recruitment terms. Treat these as indicative, because the exact pay scale and allowance rates are set out in the official notification and revised periodically. Beyond the cash pay, a permanent state teaching post carries job security, pension benefits under the applicable scheme, and a defined promotion path, which is why TRE draws lakhs of applicants each cycle.

## Common mistakes candidates make

The first and biggest mistake is preparing for a BTET exam that does not exist, and losing weeks on fake notification dates instead of registering for CTET or STET. The second is assuming a B.Ed qualifies you for every level, when primary teaching now runs through the D.El.Ed route. The third is treating the TET as the finish line, when it is only the eligibility gate and BPSC TRE is the exam that actually appoints you. The fourth is trusting a vacancy number or exam date from a coaching page rather than the BPSC or BSEB portal, which leads to missed deadlines when the real notification lands. Getting these four straight puts you ahead of most of the field before you have answered a single practice question.

## Where to track the real notifications

Ignore the content-farm BTET pages and follow the primary sources. BPSC TRE notifications appear on bpsc.bihar.gov.in. STET notifications and results appear on secondary.biharboardonline.com. CTET is on ctet.nic.in. These three, not a mythical BTET portal, are where the 2026 teaching-recruitment action actually happens. Any date not published on one of these should be treated as unconfirmed.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is there a BTET 2026 exam?**

No. There is no live, officially notified Bihar TET (BTET) for primary classes in 2026. The Bihar School Examination Board last held the standalone primary BTET in 2011. For classes 1 to 8, eligibility now runs through CTET; for classes 9 to 12, through BSEB STET.

**What is the difference between BTET and STET?**

BTET was the legacy Bihar primary eligibility test (classes 1 to 8), last held in 2011 and now discontinued. STET is the live Bihar Secondary Teacher Eligibility Test for classes 9 to 12, conducted by BSEB, with Paper 1 for classes 9 to 10 and Paper 2 for classes 11 to 12.

**Do I need CTET or STET to become a Bihar teacher?**

It depends on the class level. For classes 1 to 8 you need CTET (or STET Paper 1). For classes 9 to 10 you need STET Paper 1, and for classes 11 to 12 you need STET Paper 2. You then clear BPSC TRE to get appointed.

**Is BTET the same as BPSC TRE?**

No. A TET (CTET or STET) is an eligibility test that qualifies you to be considered for a teaching post. BPSC TRE is the actual recruitment exam that fills Bihar government teacher vacancies. You need the TET qualification first, then you sit BPSC TRE for the job.

**Is a Bihar TET or STET certificate valid for lifetime?**

Yes. TET certificate validity was extended from 7 years to lifetime by the Union Government on 3 June 2021, with retrospective effect from 2011. Bihar applied it from 2012, so a candidate holding a 2012 or later BTET or STET certificate still holds a valid lifetime qualification.

**Which exam do I need for BPSC TRE classes 1 to 5?**

For BPSC TRE at the classes 1 to 5 level, you need CTET Paper 1 (or STET Paper 1), plus Class 12 with at least 50 percent (45 percent for reserved categories) and a two-year D.El.Ed or a four-year B.El.Ed.

**How many vacancies are in BPSC TRE 4.0 2026?**

BPSC TRE 4.0 is reported to carry over 45,000 vacancies, with trackers citing figures between about 45,000 and 47,000. The exact number will be confirmed in the official BPSC notification on bpsc.bihar.gov.in, so treat circulating figures as tentative until then.

**Can a B.Ed holder teach classes 1 to 5 in Bihar?**

Generally no. Post-2023 rules restrict primary teaching (classes 1 to 5) to D.El.Ed and equivalent diploma holders, so a B.Ed alone usually does not qualify for the primary level. Confirm the current qualification list in the BPSC TRE notification before applying.

content:
## MAHATET 2026 status: the June exam was postponed

The Maharashtra Teacher Eligibility Test, MAHATET (often searched as MHTET), is a real, long-running exam conducted by MSCE Pune, the Maharashtra State Council of Examination, through its portal mahatet.in. But the current status matters more than anything else on this page: the June 2026 MAHATET was postponed. As of 28 July 2026, the mahatet.in homepage carries an official notice postponing the June 2026 exam, and no revised date has been announced.

Per reporting by Testbook and Adda247, the postponement followed a suspected paper leak. Police in Bhiwandi recovered confidential exam material in a raid on the morning of 27 June 2026, MSCE preliminarily matched some recovered questions to the June paper, and the exam that had been scheduled for 28 June 2026 was called off. MSCE has said a new schedule will be announced only after the investigation, and only on the official portal. So treat every forward date you see, including whether the exam is held later in 2026 at all, as unconfirmed until MSCE publishes it.

This matters because low-quality sites still show three different exam dates for June 2026, namely 21, 26, and 28 June, none of which is now valid. That contradiction is a sign the pages were never updated after the postponement, not that the exam does not exist.

## A note on the name: MHTET, MAHATET, and MHT CET

The correct name is MAHATET or MAHA TET, the Maharashtra Teacher Eligibility Test. Many people type MHTET, which is a shortened form of the same teacher test. Do not confuse either of these with MHT CET, the Maharashtra Common Entrance Test for engineering and pharmacy admissions, which is a completely different exam for a completely different purpose. If you want to become a teacher in Maharashtra, MAHATET, also written as MHTET, is the exam you need, not MHT CET.

## MAHATET vs TAIT vs CTET: which exam do you need

This is the distinction that decides your whole plan, and almost every competitor page muddles it. Three separate things sit behind a Maharashtra teaching job, and passing MAHATET alone does not get you hired.

| Exam | What it is | Conducted by | What it gives you |
|---|---|---|---|
| MAHATET | Maharashtra teacher eligibility test | MSCE Pune | Eligibility to be a teacher in Maharashtra |
| TAIT | Teacher Aptitude and Intelligence Test | MSCE Pune | Your merit rank for recruitment |
| CTET | Central teacher eligibility test | CBSE | Eligibility, mainly for central schools, also accepted in Maharashtra |

The one-line summary: MAHATET makes you eligible, TAIT ranks you, and the Pavitra portal places you. MAHATET is only the first gate. A candidate who passes MAHATET but skips TAIT has an eligibility certificate and no path to a job, which is the single most common misunderstanding about teacher recruitment in Maharashtra, so it is worth fixing in your mind before you plan your preparation around the wrong exam.

## The three-stage recruitment flow

Becoming a government or aided-school teacher in Maharashtra works in three steps, and knowing the sequence saves you from thinking a single exam gets you a job.

First, you clear MAHATET (or CTET), which certifies that you meet the eligibility standard to teach. This gets you no job by itself.

Second, you appear for MAHA TAIT, the Teacher Aptitude and Intelligence Test, which is the actual selection exam conducted by MSCE Pune for the state. TAIT is a 200-mark test of aptitude and intelligence, and your score here builds your merit rank. A MAHATET or CTET pass is a prerequisite to be recruited through TAIT.

Third, vacancies and placements are handled through the Pavitra portal, the state's teacher-recruitment portal, which allocates candidates to schools based on their TAIT merit and their preferences. So the job comes from TAIT merit plus Pavitra allocation, with MAHATET or CTET as the eligibility you needed to get there.

## Why MAHATET matters for a teaching career in Maharashtra

For anyone aiming to teach in a Maharashtra government or aided school, MAHATET is the foundation the whole career stands on. The Right to Education framework made a teacher-eligibility test mandatory for teaching appointments, and MAHATET is Maharashtra's version of that test for Classes 1 to 8. Without a valid MAHATET or CTET certificate, you cannot be recruited through the state's process, no matter how strong your degree or your TAIT score. That is why lakhs of aspirants sit MAHATET each cycle: it is the non-negotiable first step. The exam is deliberately pitched at the level a school teacher must actually master, testing whether you understand how children learn and can teach the school syllabus clearly, rather than testing advanced academic content. Passing it signals that you meet the professional standard the state sets for its classrooms.

## Documents you will need

Keep these ready when the application window opens.

1. A recent passport-size photograph and a scanned signature in the specified format.
2. Your Higher Secondary (Class 12) marksheet and your graduation marksheet where Paper II eligibility requires it.
3. Your teacher-training qualification certificate, such as the D.Ed, D.El.Ed, B.El.Ed, or B.Ed.
4. A category certificate where you claim the reserved qualifying marks or a fee concession.
5. A valid photo ID and an active email and mobile number for exam alerts.

## MAHATET exam structure

MAHATET has two papers, matched to the level you want to teach.

Paper I is for candidates who want to teach the primary level, that is Classes 1 to 5. Paper II is for candidates who want to teach the upper primary level, that is Classes 6 to 8. A candidate who wants to be eligible for both levels sits both papers, and the two papers are held in separate sessions so you can attempt both in the same cycle if you meet the eligibility for each.

## MAHATET exam pattern

The exam is offline and OMR based, with objective multiple-choice questions.

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Questions | 150 |
| Marks | 150 |
| Duration | 2 hours 30 minutes |
| Negative marking | None |

Paper I has five sections of 30 marks each: Child Development and Pedagogy, Language I, Language II, Mathematics, and Environmental Studies. Paper II has Child Development and Pedagogy, Language I, Language II, and then either Mathematics and Science or Social Studies, depending on the subject group. Confirm the exact per-section split against the official 2026 syllabus, as the 150-mark total is firm while the internal split follows the standard eligibility-test template.

## Qualifying marks, with a worked example

To pass MAHATET you must reach the qualifying score, which differs by category. General and open candidates need 90 out of 150, which is 60 percent. Reserved candidates, that is SC, ST, OBC, PwD, and EWS, need 82 out of 150, which is 55 percent.

A worked example makes the rule concrete. Suppose two candidates both score 88 out of 150. An open-category candidate with 88 fails, because the bar is 90. A reserved-category candidate with the same 88 passes, because the bar is 82. So the same raw score can be a pass or a fail depending on category, which is why knowing your exact qualifying mark matters.

## Eligibility for MAHATET

Eligibility depends on the paper and follows the national teacher-education norms.

For Paper I, you need Higher Secondary (Class 12) with at least 50 percent, plus a two-year Diploma in Education, such as D.Ed or D.El.Ed, or a four-year Bachelor of Elementary Education, or an equivalent teacher-training qualification. For Paper II, you need graduation plus a Bachelor of Education, or Higher Secondary with a four-year integrated B.El.Ed or B.A.Ed. Reserved categories typically get a five percent relaxation on the qualifying degree marks. Confirm the exact accepted qualifications in the official notification, since the teacher-education rules have been revised over the years.

## Certificate validity is now lifetime

One genuinely useful point that competitor pages bury: the MAHATET certificate is valid for life, not for seven years. This aligns with the national move to lifetime validity for teacher-eligibility certificates. So once you pass MAHATET, the certificate stays valid for future recruitment cycles and you do not need to re-sit the eligibility test.

## The paper-leak postponement in context

The June 2026 postponement is worth understanding beyond the bare fact, because it shapes what candidates should expect next. Teacher-eligibility and recruitment exams in several states have faced integrity problems in recent years, and the standard response is to cancel the affected sitting, investigate, and hold a fresh exam with tighter safeguards. That is the path MSCE has signalled here: the 28 June 2026 sitting was called off after material was recovered in the Bhiwandi raid on 27 June and preliminarily matched to the paper, and a new schedule will follow the investigation. For a candidate, the honest reading is that the delay is real and the new date is genuinely not fixed, so planning around any specific rescheduled date right now would be guesswork. The safer approach is to assume the exam will return with a fresh, secure paper at a date MSCE announces later, and to keep preparing rather than waiting for certainty. The one thing not to do is rely on the pre-postponement dates that many sites still display, since those are now firmly out of date.

## Application fee and process

Application is online at mahatet.in: register, fill the form, upload your photograph and signature, pay the fee online, and submit. The fee for the current cycle was reported as around Rs 700 for reserved categories and Rs 1000 for others for a single paper, and higher for both papers, but treat these as reported figures and confirm them on the official notice, since fees change between cycles. The June 2026 application window has already run and closed, so the next window will open only when MSCE announces a fresh schedule.

## MAHA TAIT explained

Because MAHATET is only the eligibility gate, the exam that actually decides recruitment deserves a closer look. MAHA TAIT, the Teacher Aptitude and Intelligence Test, is conducted by MSCE Pune for the Maharashtra government, and your score on it builds the merit rank used to allocate teaching posts. It is a 200-mark test of 200 objective questions in two hours, with no negative marking, split broadly into an aptitude portion and an intelligence portion, and it is offered bilingually. To be recruited through TAIT, you must already hold a MAHATET or CTET pass, so the two exams work together: eligibility first, then the merit test. A strong TAIT score is what puts you near the top of the queue when vacancies are allotted, which is why serious candidates treat TAIT preparation as the real contest and MAHATET as the qualifying step to reach it.

## The Pavitra portal explained

The final piece is placement, and in Maharashtra that runs through the Pavitra portal, the state's transparent teacher-recruitment portal. Pavitra publishes the available vacancies across government and aided schools and allocates candidates to schools based on their TAIT merit and the preferences they submit. The idea is to remove discretion from teacher postings by making the process merit-and-preference driven and visible. For a candidate, this means the job you finally get depends on three things in sequence: holding the MAHATET or CTET eligibility, scoring well on TAIT, and then choosing your school preferences wisely on Pavitra when your rank comes up. Understanding this flow early helps you plan, because a candidate who clears MAHATET but neglects TAIT has cleared only the first of three gates.

## Where CTET fits, and which to take

Maharashtra accepts both MAHATET and CTET as the eligibility qualification for teaching, which raises a real question for candidates: which should you take. [CTET](/entrance-exams/ctet-september-2026), conducted by CBSE, is a national exam mainly used for central schools such as Kendriya Vidyalayas and Navodaya Vidyalayas, and it is also accepted for Maharashtra recruitment. MAHATET is the state exam, tuned to the Maharashtra context and languages. If your goal is squarely a Maharashtra state or aided-school job, MAHATET is the natural fit, and many candidates take it as their primary eligibility test. If you also want to keep central-school options open, adding CTET widens your reach, since a CTET pass is accepted both nationally and in Maharashtra. Neither exam gives you a job by itself, so the decision is about which doors you want to keep open, not about which one is a shortcut to a posting.

## What the postponement means for you

If you had applied for the June 2026 MAHATET, the postponement is frustrating but does not cancel your candidature. Your application stands, and MSCE has said it will announce a fresh schedule after the investigation into the suspected leak, published on mahatet.in. The practical advice is to keep your documents and admit-card login details ready, watch only the official portal for the new date rather than trusting the old 21, 26, or 28 June dates still floating on other sites, and use the extra time to strengthen your preparation, particularly for TAIT, which is the exam that actually decides recruitment. A postponement caused by a leak also usually means tighter security and a genuinely fresh paper, so the extra weeks are best spent revising rather than waiting.

## How to prepare for MAHATET

MAHATET rewards command of teaching pedagogy and school-level subject knowledge rather than advanced content, so the preparation is about breadth and clarity, not depth. Child Development and Pedagogy carries a full section in both papers and is the highest-return area, since it is scoring and repeatable, so build a strong foundation in learning theories, child psychology, inclusive education, and assessment. The language sections reward comprehension and grammar practice plus a grasp of language teaching methods. For Paper I, the Mathematics and Environmental Studies sections stay at the primary-school level, so revise the concepts a Class 5 teacher must explain clearly. Because there is no negative marking, attempt every question, and practise full-length papers under the 2 hour 30 minute limit to build stamina and pacing. Previous MAHATET papers, which are available on the official site, are the best guide to the balance and difficulty the exam sets.

## Common points of confusion

Several recurring confusions trip up candidates, and clearing them early saves wasted effort. The first is thinking MAHATET is a recruitment exam that leads directly to a job, when it is only the eligibility gate before TAIT and Pavitra. The second is mixing up MHTET with MHT CET, which are entirely different exams. The third is assuming the certificate expires after seven years, when it is now valid for lifetime. The fourth is trusting the exam dates on aggregator sites, which still show the stale June dates that the postponement overtook. The fifth is treating MAHATET and CTET as either-or rivals, when they are both accepted eligibility routes in Maharashtra and taking both simply widens your options. Getting these five straight puts you well ahead of a candidate working from the muddled information most sites still publish.

## How to track the real notifications

Given the postponement and the stale dates on aggregator sites, follow the primary sources. MAHATET notifications, admit cards, and results appear on mahatet.in. MAHA TAIT is on the MSCE Pune portal. Teacher vacancies and placements appear on the Pavitra portal. CTET is on ctet.nic.in. Any MAHATET date not published on mahatet.in should be treated as unconfirmed, especially now that the June 2026 exam has been postponed without a new date.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is MAHATET 2026 postponed?**

Yes. As of 28 July 2026, MSCE Pune has postponed the June 2026 MAHATET and has not announced a new date. Per Testbook and Adda247 reporting, the exam scheduled for 28 June 2026 was called off after a suspected paper leak, and a revised schedule will be published only on mahatet.in.

**Is MHTET the same as MAHATET?**

Yes. MHTET is a commonly mistyped short form of MAHATET, the Maharashtra Teacher Eligibility Test conducted by MSCE Pune. It is not the same as MHT CET, which is the Maharashtra entrance test for engineering and pharmacy admissions.

**Is MAHATET enough to get a government teacher job in Maharashtra?**

No. MAHATET only makes you eligible to be a teacher. To be recruited you must also clear MAHA TAIT, the Teacher Aptitude and Intelligence Test, which decides your merit rank, and then be placed through the Pavitra portal based on that rank and your preferences.

**What is the difference between MAHATET and CTET?**

MAHATET is the Maharashtra state teacher-eligibility test conducted by MSCE Pune, used for Maharashtra government and aided schools. CTET is the central teacher-eligibility test conducted by CBSE, used mainly for central schools and also accepted in Maharashtra. Both certify eligibility; neither gives a job on its own.

**Is the MAHATET certificate valid for lifetime?**

Yes. The MAHATET certificate is now valid for life, in line with the national move to lifetime validity for teacher-eligibility certificates. Once you pass, you do not need to re-sit the eligibility test for future recruitment cycles.

**What are the passing marks for MAHATET?**

General and open candidates need 90 out of 150 marks, which is 60 percent. Reserved candidates, meaning SC, ST, OBC, PwD, and EWS, need 82 out of 150, which is 55 percent. The same raw score can be a pass or a fail depending on category.

**Is there negative marking in MAHATET?**

No. MAHATET has no negative marking. It is an offline OMR-based test of 150 objective questions for 150 marks in 2 hours 30 minutes, so every question can be attempted without penalty.

**Can I apply for both Paper 1 and Paper 2 of MAHATET?**

Yes. Paper I is for teaching Classes 1 to 5 and Paper II is for teaching Classes 6 to 8. A candidate who wants to be eligible for both levels can apply for and sit both papers, subject to meeting the eligibility for each.

content:
AILET is the All India Law Entrance Test, conducted by National Law University Delhi for admission to its own programmes. It is the one national law entrance that sits outside CLAT, and NLU Delhi is the one national law university that does not admit through CLAT.

AILET 2026 was held on 14 December 2025, with applications open from 7 August to 10 November 2025. That admission cycle is complete. If you are reading this to plan an attempt, you are planning for the next cycle.

## What AILET is and why it exists separately

Twenty-something national law universities across India admit students through the Common Law Admission Test. NLU Delhi does not. It runs its own examination, on its own timetable, with its own paper.

For a candidate, that means AILET is an additional examination rather than an alternative one. Almost everyone who sits AILET also sits CLAT, because sitting AILET does not substitute for CLAT and NLU Delhi is a single institution.

The examination is held in December, which places it close to CLAT in the calendar. Preparation overlaps substantially, and the difference lies in the paper rather than in the syllabus.

## Programmes and intake

NLU Delhi admits through AILET to its five year integrated BA LLB (Hons), its one year LLM, and its PhD programmes.

The undergraduate intake is small relative to the applicant pool, which is the fundamental fact shaping how competitive AILET is. A single institution admitting a limited cohort, against a national applicant field, produces cutoffs that are demanding by any standard.

Reserved category seats and seats under specific provisions follow the university's published reservation policy for the cycle, which is set out in the prospectus rather than being uniform across law schools.

## Exam pattern

The AILET paper has been structured around 150 questions in recent cycles, and its character differs from CLAT in ways that matter for preparation.

For the BA LLB (Hons) programme the paper covers English language, current affairs and general knowledge, and logical reasoning. Legal aptitude has been treated differently across cycles, which is one reason the prospectus for the current cycle is the only reliable authority on the structure.

The distinguishing feature relative to CLAT is the treatment of comprehension. CLAT has moved firmly toward long passage-based questions across sections. AILET has retained a more direct question style in parts of the paper, which rewards a slightly different set of habits.

Negative marking applies. Confirm the exact deduction and the question count for the cycle you are sitting from the official prospectus, because NLU Delhi has revised the pattern between cycles and material describing an older AILET may not describe the current one.

That last point is not a formality. AILET has changed more often than most national entrance examinations, and candidates preparing from second-hand summaries have repeatedly prepared for a paper that no longer existed.

## How AILET differs from CLAT in practice

| | AILET | CLAT |
|---|---|---|
| Conducted by | NLU Delhi | Consortium of NLUs |
| Admits to | NLU Delhi only | Most other NLUs |
| Typical timing | December | December |
| Paper style | More direct questions in parts | Heavily passage-based |
| Applicant pool | Large, for one institution | Large, for many institutions |

The preparation overlap is high enough that no candidate should treat them as separate projects. English, current affairs, general knowledge and reasoning serve both.

What differs is exam-day technique. A candidate trained exclusively on long CLAT-style passages can find the pace of a more direct paper unfamiliar, and the reverse is also true. Practising both formats is the practical answer, and it costs little because the underlying knowledge is shared.

Sit both. There is no strategic reason to choose between them, and declining to sit AILET removes one institution from your options for no gain.

## Preparing for the next cycle

Since the 2026 cycle is complete, the useful content here is what to do if you are targeting the next one.

Current affairs and general knowledge reward daily accumulation and punish compression more than any other component. A candidate reading regularly across a year arrives with a base that no amount of late revision replicates. Static general knowledge and legal awareness sit alongside current affairs and need their own attention.

English rewards reading rather than drilling. Comprehension speed and vocabulary build from sustained reading of demanding prose, and candidates who only work through practice sets tend to plateau.

Logical reasoning is the most trainable component in the short term, which makes it worth concentrated work when time is limited.

Practise under timed conditions from early on. Law entrance papers are as much about pace and selection as about knowledge, and the ability to leave a question and move on is a trained habit rather than a natural one.

Work official past papers where available, and treat coaching material as supplementary. Past papers tell you what the examination actually asks; summaries tell you what someone thought it asked.

Track the NLU Delhi website directly for the notification. The university publishes on its own site, and applying to AILET requires watching for it rather than waiting to be told.

## The wider question of whether to target law

Candidates preparing for AILET are usually in Class 12 or shortly after, making a decision with long consequences, and it is worth being direct about the position.

A five year integrated law degree is a substantial commitment, and the outcomes vary enormously by institution. Graduates of the top national law universities have access to corporate law firms, litigation chambers, judicial services preparation and policy work on terms that graduates of weaker institutions do not.

That variance is the reason competition for NLU Delhi and comparable institutions is intense, and it is also the reason a candidate should think carefully before accepting a place at an institution whose outcomes they have not investigated.

Judicial services, which many law graduates target, is a separate examination conducted by each state with its own eligibility and its own preparation, and it is open to graduates of any recognised law school. A candidate whose goal is the judiciary is not foreclosed by not attending a top national law university, though the preparation environment differs.

None of that is a reason to avoid law. It is a reason to research specific institutions and specific career paths before committing five years, rather than treating admission anywhere as the goal.

## Building current affairs for a law entrance

Current affairs and general knowledge carry more weight in law entrance examinations than in most competitive papers, and candidates consistently underestimate how long the component takes to build.

The scope is wider than news headlines. It covers national and international events, awards and honours, appointments, sports, books and authors, summits and agreements, and a substantial legal awareness component covering landmark judgments, constitutional developments, important legislation and the structure of the judiciary.

The legal awareness portion is where law entrance diverges from general competitive examinations. A candidate reading a standard general knowledge compilation will cover the events and miss the legal material entirely.

What works is a daily habit maintained across a year rather than an intensive block. Read a serious newspaper properly, keep short notes organised by theme rather than by date, and revise those notes weekly. A month of intensive reading in November produces recall that decays before December.

Landmark judgments deserve separate treatment. Knowing the case name, the year, the core holding and why it mattered is the level generally required, and this is finite material that rewards systematic coverage.

Static general knowledge, covering history, geography, polity and basic science, sits alongside current affairs and is often neglected because it feels less urgent. It is examinable and it is stable, which makes it among the more reliable marks available.

## What the five year law course actually involves

Candidates commit to a five year integrated degree with limited information about what it contains, so a brief description is useful.

The integrated BA LLB combines undergraduate arts subjects with law subjects across five years, rather than requiring a separate bachelor's degree before law. That is the attraction: it saves a year against the three year LLB route taken after graduation.

The workload is reading-heavy in a way that surprises students from science backgrounds. Law is studied through cases, statutes and commentary, and the volume of reading is substantial and continuous rather than concentrated before examinations.

Moot courts, internships and research work sit alongside coursework at most serious institutions, and they matter for placement outcomes as much as grades do. Students who treat the degree as coursework alone tend to graduate with weaker options than peers who engaged with the wider programme.

Specialisation typically emerges in later years through electives and internship choices, covering corporate, constitutional, criminal, intellectual property, international and other fields.

The point of describing this is that law suits students who read willingly and argue carefully. A candidate choosing it because it is prestigious, without an appetite for sustained reading, is choosing five demanding years on weak foundations.

## Application and documents

Applications for AILET run online through the NLU Delhi portal during the notified window, which for the 2026 cycle was 7 August to 10 November 2025.

Register with a working email address and mobile number, since the university sends the admit card and later communication there and the same login carries through the process.

Prepare uploads before starting the form: a recent photograph, a signature, and any category or supporting certificate in the specified format and dimensions. Specification mismatches cause rejections that surface late.

Enter your name and details exactly as they appear on your certificates. Mismatches are checked at admission and cause genuine problems at a point where they are difficult to resolve.

Pay the fee online and confirm the transaction completed, because an application with a failed payment is not an application.

Do not submit on the closing day. Portals slow under load near deadlines without exception.

## A realistic plan for a December attempt

For a candidate targeting the next AILET cycle, the calendar shapes what is worth doing when.

The long run, from early in the year, belongs to the components that compound. Current affairs read daily, English built through sustained reading, and static general knowledge and legal awareness worked through systematically. None of these respond to intensity late on, and all of them separate candidates who started early from those who did not.

The middle stretch is for logical reasoning and for consolidating legal awareness into organised, revisable notes. Reasoning improves measurably with concentrated practice, which makes it the right place for focused effort once the reading habits are established.

The final two to three months are for timed full-length practice, in both AILET and CLAT formats, and for revision of your own notes rather than fresh material. This is where pace, question selection and the discipline of leaving a hard question are trained.

The last fortnight is revision only. Learning new material at that point displaces consolidation of what you already know, and it reliably costs more than it adds.

Through all of it, sit both AILET and CLAT practice papers rather than specialising in one format. The knowledge is shared and only the exam-day habits differ, so covering both costs little.

One caution on coaching. It can provide structure, material and a peer group, all of which help. It cannot substitute for the daily reading habit, and candidates who outsource their preparation to a class while not reading independently tend to plateau in exactly the components that matter most here.

## After the result

AILET results lead to counselling and admission conducted by NLU Delhi according to its published process for the cycle, which is set out in the prospectus rather than following the CLAT consortium's arrangements.

Candidates holding both an AILET result and a CLAT result face a genuine choice, and it should be made on the specifics rather than on general reputation. Compare the actual institutions available to you under each, their placement records, their faculty and their location, rather than treating one examination as inherently superior.

Keep documents assembled through this period: Class 10 and Class 12 certificates and mark sheets, identity proof, photographs matching the application, category certificate in the prescribed format where applicable, and the scorecard. Admission windows are short and a candidate assembling paperwork after an offer is at risk.

Candidates who are not admitted in a cycle have the option of attempting again, and many do. That decision deserves the same scrutiny as any repeat year: a clear diagnosis of what went wrong, a plan that addresses it, and an honest assessment of whether another year is the best use of the time.

## Frequently asked questions

**When was AILET 2026 held?**

On 14 December 2025, with applications open from 7 August to 10 November 2025. That admission cycle is complete, so candidates reading now are planning for the next one.

**What is the difference between AILET and CLAT?**

AILET is conducted by NLU Delhi for admission to its own programmes. CLAT is conducted by the Consortium of NLUs for admission to most other national law universities. NLU Delhi does not admit through CLAT, so AILET is an additional examination rather than an alternative, and almost all candidates sit both.

**Should I sit both AILET and CLAT?**

Yes. The preparation overlaps heavily, so sitting AILET costs little beyond the fee and the day, and declining it removes NLU Delhi from your options for no gain. There is no strategic reason to choose between them.

**What programmes does AILET admit to?**

The five year integrated BA LLB (Hons), the one year LLM, and PhD programmes at National Law University Delhi.

**What is the AILET exam pattern?**

The paper has been structured around 150 questions in recent cycles, covering English language, current affairs and general knowledge, and logical reasoning for the undergraduate programme, with negative marking. NLU Delhi has revised the pattern between cycles more often than most national entrance examinations, so confirm the structure from the prospectus for the cycle you are sitting rather than from a summary.

**Is AILET harder than CLAT?**

They test overlapping material with different paper styles rather than at clearly different difficulty levels. CLAT has moved firmly toward long passage-based questions while AILET has retained more direct questions in parts of the paper. The intake at NLU Delhi is small relative to the applicant pool, which makes AILET cutoffs demanding regardless of paper difficulty.

**How many seats does NLU Delhi offer?**

The undergraduate intake is small relative to the national applicant pool, which is the fundamental driver of how competitive AILET is. Exact intake and the reservation breakdown are published in the prospectus for each cycle.

**Is there negative marking in AILET?**

Yes. Confirm the exact deduction for your cycle from the official prospectus, since NLU Delhi has revised the marking scheme along with the pattern between cycles.

**How should I prepare for AILET?**

Read demanding prose regularly for English rather than only drilling practice sets. Accumulate current affairs and general knowledge daily across the year, since this component punishes compression more than any other. Work logical reasoning concentratedly, as it is the most trainable component in the short term. Practise under timed conditions from early, and use official past papers over coaching summaries.

**Where do I find the AILET notification?**

On the National Law University Delhi website. The university publishes its own notification and does not route it through the CLAT consortium, so candidates must watch the NLU Delhi site directly rather than assuming they will hear about it alongside CLAT announcements.

**Can I appear for AILET more than once?**

There is no cap on attempts. Eligibility is governed by the qualifying conditions in the prospectus rather than by an attempt limit, and candidates who are not admitted in one cycle commonly attempt again. That decision deserves a clear diagnosis of what went wrong and a plan that addresses it, rather than being taken as the default response to a disappointing result.

**Does AILET have a legal aptitude section?**

Legal aptitude has been treated differently across cycles, which is why the prospectus for the cycle you are sitting is the only reliable authority. What has been consistent is a legal awareness component within general knowledge, covering landmark judgments, constitutional developments and important legislation, and that material is distinct from what a general competitive-exam compilation covers.

**Is coaching necessary for AILET?**

Coaching can provide structure, material and a peer group, and those help. It cannot substitute for the daily reading habit that builds English and current affairs, which are the components that most separate candidates. Students who outsource preparation to a class while not reading independently tend to plateau in exactly those areas.

**What happens if I clear both AILET and CLAT?**

You choose, and the choice should be made on specifics rather than general reputation. Compare the actual institutions available to you under each result, their placement records, faculty and location. Neither examination is inherently superior: they admit to different institutions.

**Where can I find official AILET past papers?**

National Law University Delhi publishes past papers and related material on its own website. Use those in preference to coaching reconstructions, because past papers show what the examination actually asked while summaries show what someone believed it asked, and AILET's pattern has shifted enough between cycles that the difference is material rather than academic. Work them under timed conditions rather than reading through them, since pace and question selection are a large part of what the paper tests.

## Official sources

- National Law University Delhi: https://nludelhi.ac.in
- The AILET prospectus for the relevant cycle, which is the authority on the exam pattern, question count, marking scheme, intake and reservation policy

Where anything on this page conflicts with the prospectus, the prospectus is correct. AILET has revised its pattern between cycles more often than most national entrance examinations, so treat any pattern description not drawn from the current prospectus, including this one, as indicative rather than definitive.
