content:
## CDS 2 2026: Become an Officer in the Indian Army, Navy, or Air Force

The Combined Defence Services (CDS) exam is the civilian route into the Indian Armed Forces as a commissioned officer. You don't need to have been in NCC or studied at military school. A graduation degree and the right preparation is all it takes to get into the IMA, INA, AFA, or OTA.

CDS 2 2026 has **451 vacancies**. The exam is September 13, 2026. Application closed June 9.

---

## CDS 1 vs CDS 2: What Happened This Year

UPSC conducts CDS twice a year. Both cycles in 2026:

| Exam | Date | Status |
|---|---|---|
| CDS 1 2026 | April 12, 2026 | Conducted, result awaited |
| **CDS 2 2026** | **September 13, 2026** | **Upcoming: your current cycle** |

CDS 2 2026 notification was released on May 20, 2026. Application window was May 20 to June 9, 2026.

---

## Vacancies: 451 Posts Across 4 Academies

| Academy | Course | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| Indian Military Academy (IMA), Dehradun | 147th Course | 18 months |
| Indian Naval Academy (INA), Ezhimala | B.Tech (Naval Architecture) + Executive | 4 years (B.Tech) |
| Air Force Academy (AFA), Dundigal | No. 219 F(P) Course + Ground Duty | 74 weeks (Flying) |
| Officers Training Academy (OTA), Chennai | 124th SSC (Men) + 34th SSC (Women) | 49 weeks |

Total vacancies across these 4 academies: **451**. Academy-wise breakup is published in the official notification at upsc.gov.in.

---

## Eligibility: Academy by Academy

### IMA: Indian Military Academy (Army)
- **Gender:** Unmarried male only
- **Age:** Born January 2, 2003 to January 1, 2008 (19 to 24 years as on January 1, 2027)
- **Qualification:** Graduation from any recognised university: any stream (BA, BSc, BCom, B.Tech, all eligible)
- **Outcome:** Permanent Commission in the Indian Army as a Lieutenant

### INA: Indian Naval Academy (Navy)
- **Gender:** Unmarried male only
- **Age:** Born January 2, 2003 to January 1, 2008 (19 to 24 years)
- **Qualification:** Engineering degree (B.E. / B.Tech or equivalent): any engineering branch
- **Outcome:** Permanent Commission in the Indian Navy as a Sub-Lieutenant

### AFA: Air Force Academy (Air Force)
- **Gender:** Unmarried male only
- **Age:** Born January 2, 2003 to January 1, 2008 (19 to 24 years)
- **Qualification:** Graduation with **Physics AND Mathematics in Class 12**, OR B.E./B.Tech degree
- **Outcome:** Permanent Commission in the Indian Air Force as a Flying Officer (Flying Branch) or Group A Officer (Ground Duty)
- **Note:** Flying Branch candidates undergo additional AFCAT/PABT at AFB Dehradun and must meet strict medical standards for flying duties

### OTA: Officers Training Academy (Army Short Service Commission)
- **Gender:** Male (married/unmarried/widower/divorced) and Female (unmarried/widow/divorcee)
- **Age:** Born January 2, 2002 to January 1, 2008 (19 to 25 years: slightly wider range)
- **Qualification:** Graduation from any recognised university: any stream
- **Outcome:** Short Service Commission (SSC) in the Indian Army: initial 14-year service, extendable to permanent commission based on performance
- **Important:** OTA does NOT require the Elementary Mathematics paper: only English and GK

---

## Exam Pattern

### For IMA, INA, AFA (3 Papers)

| Paper | Questions | Marks | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| English | 120 | 100 | 2 hours |
| General Knowledge | 120 | 100 | 2 hours |
| Elementary Mathematics | 100 | 100 | 2 hours |
| **Total Written** | | **300** | |
| SSB Interview | | **300** | 5 days |
| **Grand Total** | | **600** | |

### For OTA (2 Papers Only: No Maths)

| Paper | Questions | Marks | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| English | 120 | 100 | 2 hours |
| General Knowledge | 120 | 100 | 2 hours |
| **Total Written** | | **200** | |
| SSB Interview | | **200** | 5 days |
| **Grand Total** | | **400** | |

**Negative Marking: 1/3 of marks per wrong answer in all papers.**

This is important for OTA aspirants, if you're only applying for OTA and have weak Maths, you have a significant advantage because you avoid the Maths paper entirely.

---

## Exam Syllabus

### English
Grammar: Tenses, articles, prepositions, conjunctions, voice (active/passive), narration (direct/indirect), sentence completion, error correction.
Vocabulary: Synonyms, antonyms, one-word substitution, idioms and phrases.
Comprehension: Reading passages with 5 to 10 questions per passage.

Most candidates score 60 to 80 out of 100 in English. It's manageable with 30 to 45 days of dedicated practice on previous CDS English papers.

### General Knowledge
- Current events (national and international), last 6 to 8 months
- Indian history, especially Freedom Struggle (1857 to 1947) and Constitution
- Indian geography and world geography
- General science, Physics, Chemistry, Biology (Class 10 NCERT level)
- Defence news and Indian military history

NCERT Class 9 to 10 textbooks are the GK backbone. For current affairs, use any standard monthly booklet.

### Elementary Mathematics (IMA/INA/AFA only)
- Arithmetic: Percentage, ratio, profit-loss, simple and compound interest, time-work, time-distance
- Algebra: Linear equations, quadratic equations, logarithms
- Geometry: Triangle theorems, circle properties, parallel lines
- Mensuration: Areas and volumes of standard shapes
- Statistics: Mean, median, mode, basic frequency distribution

CDS Maths is Class 10 level, not JEE, not even NDA level. But the negative marking means you must be accurate, not just fast.

---

## The SSB Interview: Equal to Written Marks

The SSB carries the same marks as the written exam. For IMA/INA/AFA, 300 marks written + 300 marks SSB = 600 total. For OTA, 200 + 200 = 400 total.

The SSB process unfolds over 5 days at SSB centres across India (Allahabad, Bhopal, Bangalore, Mysore, Kapurthala, Coimbatore, and others assigned based on your chosen academy):

**Day 1: Screening:**
- Officer Intelligence Rating (OIR) test, verbal and non-verbal reasoning
- Picture Perception and Discussion Test (PPDT), you describe a picture, write a story, and discuss it in a group

About 30 to 40% of candidates are screened in after Day 1. The rest are sent back the same day.

**Days 2 to 4: Psychological and Group Testing (for those who clear screening):**
- **TAT (Thematic Apperception Test):** You see 11 pictures + 1 blank slide, write a story for each in 4 minutes
- **WAT (Word Association Test):** 60 words flashed at 15 seconds each: write the first sentence that comes to mind
- **SRT (Situation Reaction Test):** 60 situations in 30 minutes: how do you respond?
- **SD (Self Description):** What does your family/friends/teachers say about you? What do you think of yourself?
- **Group Discussions:** 5 to 10 candidates, 2 rounds, defence and civilian topics
- **Group Planning Exercise:** Group solves a situation on a map
- **Progressive Group Task / Half Group Task:** Outdoor problem-solving activities with obstacles
- **Command Task:** You command your group to complete a task
- **Lecturette:** 3-minute talk on a chosen topic

**Day 5: Conference:**
All SSB officers discuss each candidate collectively. Final recommendation.

---

## Salary and Career After Commissioning

After completing training and commissioning:

| Rank | Pay Level | Basic Pay | MSP | Approximate Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lieutenant (Army) | Level 10 | ₹56,100 | ₹15,500 | ~₹80,000 to 1,00,000/month |
| Sub-Lieutenant (Navy) | Level 10 | ₹56,100 | ₹15,500 | ~₹80,000 to 1,00,000/month |
| Flying Officer (Air Force) | Level 10 | ₹56,100 | ₹15,500 | ~₹80,000 to 1,00,000/month |

In addition to salary: free accommodation, food allowance, medical benefits for family, Canteen Stores Department (CSD) facilities, and Group Insurance.

**IMA/INA/AFA → Permanent Commission:** Long-term career up to Colonel/Commodore/Group Captain or higher based on merit.

**OTA → Short Service Commission:** Initial 10 + 4 years (extendable). Option to apply for Permanent Commission after 5 years based on vacancies and performance. Many SSC officers transition to civil service or defence PSUs after service.

---

## Preparation plan for the September 13 exam

**Days 1 to 30: Foundation**
- English: Solve previous 5 years' CDS English papers. Note every grammar rule you missed. Use Wren & Martin for grammar reference.
- GK: Read NCERT Class 9 to 10 History, Geography, Science. Make short notes on each chapter.
- Maths (if applying for IMA/INA/AFA): Revise Class 9 to 10 NCERT Maths thoroughly. Solve R.S. Aggarwal or similar for practice.

**Days 31 to 60: Practice and Mock Tests**
- Solve 2 to 3 full CDS mock tests per week under timed conditions (2 hours per paper)
- Current affairs: Read monthly current affairs booklet for April, September 2026
- Focus on accuracy, CDS negative marking punishes random guessing

**Days 61 to 94: Revision and Accuracy Drills**
- Revise weak chapters identified from mock tests
- Focus on eliminating avoidable errors in English grammar and Maths calculations
- Physical fitness: Start running and basic fitness training if you haven't, SSB involves outdoor physical tasks

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: I'm a Commerce graduate. Can I apply for IMA?**
Yes. IMA requires any graduation, BA, BCom, BSc, B.Tech, LLB are all eligible. The CDS written exam tests English, GK, and Elementary Maths, none of which require a specific academic stream.

**Q: I want to be a pilot. Is CDS the right path?**
For Air Force pilots: AFA through CDS is one path. AFCAT (Air Force Common Admission Test) is another. Both lead to the Air Force Academy. Check AFCAT if you don't meet CDS age requirements or want a direct Air Force-specific route.

**Q: Can I apply for both IMA and OTA in the same application?**
No. You apply for specific academy/course choices in your preference order. You can indicate multiple preferences within one application, but your exam papers depend on which academies you've opted for (if OTA only = 2 papers; if IMA/INA/AFA = 3 papers).

**Q: What is the difference between Permanent Commission and Short Service Commission?**
Permanent Commission (IMA/INA/AFA) offers a full military career until retirement age (typically 54 to 60 years depending on rank). Short Service Commission (OTA) is a contractual term of service, 10 years initially, extendable by 4 more years (total 14 years). After 14 years you exit, or apply for PC conversion. Both are commissioned officer roles, the difference is career length.

**Q: I failed SSB once. Can I apply again?**
Yes. There is no restriction on the number of CDS/SSB attempts, as long as you meet the age and qualification criteria at the time of application.

---

## Official Links

- UPSC Official Site: [upsc.gov.in](https://upsc.gov.in)
- Apply Online (when open): [upsconline.nic.in](https://upsconline.nic.in)

---

*Disclaimer: All information is based on the official CDS 2 2026 notification released by UPSC on May 20, 2026. Academy-wise vacancy numbers and complete physical/medical standards must be verified from the official notification at upsc.gov.in.*
description: CDS 2 2026 exam is September 13 for 451 officer cadet vacancies across IMA, INA, AFA, and OTA. Graduate-level UPSC defence exam followed by SSB interview.

content:
## HTET 2026 status and what this guide covers

The Haryana Teacher Eligibility Test, HTET, is a real, long-running exam conducted by the Board of School Education Haryana (BSEH), Bhiwani, through its portal bseh.org.in. It is the eligibility test you must pass to become a teacher in Haryana government and aided schools. For the 2026 cycle, applications ran from 24 December 2025 to 5 January 2026 and drew around 2.45 lakh candidates, and the exam was postponed more than once, with 4 to 5 July 2026 among the last announced dates. Because BSEH revised the schedule, treat any forward date as tentative and confirm it on bseh.org.in.

This page is a full guide to how HTET works: the three levels, the eligibility for each, the exam pattern and qualifying marks, the lifetime validity of the certificate, and, most importantly, how HTET connects to the actual teacher recruitment in Haryana, which most sources blur. If you searched for HTET expecting a single exam that gives you a teaching job, the key thing to understand is that HTET is only the first step: it makes you eligible, and a separate recruitment then hires you.

## HTET, HPSC and HSSC: the two-step reality

This is the distinction that the whole search results page gets wrong, and getting it right saves you from a costly misunderstanding. Two separate things stand between you and a Haryana government teaching job.

First, you clear HTET, conducted by BSEH. This certifies that you meet the eligibility standard to teach. It gets you no job by itself.

Second, you apply to the actual recruitment, run by a different body. For Post Graduate Teacher posts this is the Haryana Public Service Commission (HPSC), and for Trained Graduate Teacher and primary posts it has historically been the Haryana Staff Selection Commission (HSSC). These bodies advertise vacancies and select candidates, and they require an HTET certificate as a prerequisite.

So the flow is: qualify HTET through BSEH, receive a certificate that is now valid for life, then apply to the HPSC or HSSC recruitment when it is advertised, and be selected by that body. HTET is the eligibility gate; HPSC and HSSC do the hiring.

## The three levels of HTET

HTET has three levels, matched to the classes you want to teach.

| Level | Post | Classes |
|---|---|---|
| Level 1 | PRT (Primary Teacher) | 1 to 5 |
| Level 2 | TGT (Trained Graduate Teacher) | 6 to 8 |
| Level 3 | PGT (Post Graduate Teacher) | 9 to 12 |

You sit the level or levels matching the classes you want to teach, and you can appear for more than one level if you meet the eligibility for each. A candidate who wants to keep options open across the primary, upper primary, and secondary levels, and who holds the qualifications for each, can appear for all three, though most candidates target the one or two levels that match their degree and career goal.

## Eligibility for HTET by level

The qualification you need rises with the level.

For Level 1, the Primary Teacher level, you need Senior Secondary, that is Class 12, with at least 50 percent, plus a two-year Diploma in Elementary Education, such as D.El.Ed or JBT, or an equivalent teacher-training qualification.

For Level 2, the Trained Graduate Teacher level, you need a bachelor's degree in the relevant subject with at least 50 percent, plus a recognised teacher-education qualification such as B.Ed or D.El.Ed.

For Level 3, the Post Graduate Teacher level, you need a postgraduate or master's degree in the concerned subject with at least 50 percent, plus a B.Ed from a recognised university.

Reserved categories usually get a 5 percent relaxation on the qualifying degree marks. Because the exact accepted qualifications and any final-year provisions can change between cycles, confirm them against the official notification.

## HTET exam pattern

The exam is offline and OMR-based, with objective multiple-choice questions, and the format is the same across the three levels.

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Questions | 150 |
| Marks | 150 |
| Duration | 2 hours 30 minutes |
| Negative marking | None |
| Medium | Hindi and English (bilingual) |

Each question carries one mark and there is no negative marking, so every question can be attempted without penalty. Level 1 covers Child Development and Pedagogy, languages, Mathematics, Environmental Studies, and general studies, while Levels 2 and 3 add a subject-specific component. Confirm the exact section-wise split against the official syllabus, since the internal weighting follows the standard eligibility-test template.

## Qualifying marks, with a worked example

To pass HTET you must reach the qualifying score, which differs by category and domicile. General and unreserved candidates need 60 percent, that is 90 out of 150. Scheduled Caste and Persons with Disabilities candidates who are Haryana residents need 55 percent, that is 83 out of 150. Candidates from those categories who are from other states need the general 60 percent bar.

A worked example makes the rule concrete. Suppose two candidates both score 88 out of 150. A general candidate with 88 fails, because the bar is 90. A Haryana-resident Scheduled Caste candidate with 84 passes, because their bar is 83, while a general candidate with 84 does not. So the same raw score can be a pass or a fail depending on category and domicile, which is why knowing your exact qualifying mark matters.

## HTET certificate is now valid for lifetime

One genuinely useful and well-sourced point: the HTET certificate is valid for life, not for seven years. The Haryana Government extended HTET validity from seven years to lifetime, a change that benefited a large number of candidates whose certificates would otherwise have expired. In practical terms, once you pass HTET, the certificate stays valid for future recruitment cycles and you do not need to re-sit the eligibility test. A candidate holding an older HTET certificate that had not lapsed before the extension can use it for recruitment advertised afterwards.

## Application fee and process

Application is online at bseh.org.in: register with a valid email and mobile number, fill the form with your personal, educational, and category details, choose your level or levels, upload your photograph and signature, pay the fee online, and submit before the last date. The fee for the 2026 cycle was reported as around Rs 1,000 for one level for general and other candidates and Rs 500 for Haryana-resident Scheduled Caste and Persons with Disabilities candidates, with higher amounts for two or three levels, but treat these as reported figures and confirm them on the official notice, since fees change between cycles. The 2026 application window has already closed, so the next window will open only when BSEH announces a fresh cycle.

## HTET versus CTET, and the Haryana twist

Candidates often ask whether CTET can be used instead of HTET in Haryana. The reported position, per teaching-exam sources, is that for Haryana government school teacher posts, HTET is the required eligibility test, and CTET is not accepted in Haryana, even though CTET is accepted almost everywhere else in the country. This is a strong, Haryana-specific claim, so verify it against the current HPSC or BSEH notification wording before relying on it, but the practical takeaway is clear: if your goal is a Haryana state or aided-school teaching job, plan for HTET, not [CTET](/entrance-exams/ctet-september-2026). CTET remains the route for central schools such as Kendriya Vidyalayas and Navodaya Vidyalayas and for many other states.

## Which exam do you actually need

Match your goal to the exam. If you want to teach in a Haryana government or aided school, you need HTET at the level for your target classes, and then you apply to the HPSC or HSSC recruitment when it opens. If you want to teach in central government schools or keep options open across states, CTET is the route. HTET certifies eligibility only within Haryana; it does not itself give a job, and it is not interchangeable with CTET for Haryana posts. Understanding this before you plan your preparation stops you from preparing for the wrong exam or assuming a single test leads straight to a posting.

## A second worked example on eligibility

To make the level-and-eligibility rules concrete, take a candidate with a master's degree in Physics at 58 percent and a B.Ed, who wants to teach Physics to classes 11 and 12. That candidate is eligible for HTET Level 3, the Post Graduate Teacher level, because they hold a master's in the subject above the 50 percent bar plus a B.Ed. If they instead held only a bachelor's degree with a B.Ed, they would be eligible for Level 2, the Trained Graduate Teacher level for classes 6 to 8, but not Level 3, since PGT posts need a master's. And a candidate with Class 12 and a JBT or D.El.Ed, but no degree, is eligible only for Level 1, the Primary Teacher level for classes 1 to 5. Matching your highest teaching qualification to the correct level before you apply is essential, because applying at a level you are not eligible for wastes the fee and the attempt.

## How the recruitment actually fills posts

Once you hold a valid HTET certificate, the job comes through a recruitment body's selection process. HPSC advertises Post Graduate Teacher vacancies and selects candidates through its own process, with the HTET or an equivalent qualification as a prerequisite. The HPSC PGT 2026 recruitment, for example, was advertised with its own application window and vacancy count, though the exact number of posts is reported inconsistently across sources, so confirm it on hpsc.gov.in. Trained Graduate Teacher and primary recruitment has historically run through HSSC. The point to hold onto is that your HTET pass qualifies you to apply, and the recruitment body's selection, not the HTET score alone, decides who gets appointed.

## Why HTET matters for a teaching career in Haryana

For anyone aiming to teach in a Haryana government or aided school, HTET is the foundation the whole career stands on. The Right to Education framework made a teacher-eligibility test mandatory for teaching appointments, and HTET is Haryana's version of that test across the three levels. Without a valid HTET certificate, you cannot be recruited through the state's process, no matter how strong your degree or your performance in a recruitment exam. That is why lakhs of candidates sit HTET each cycle, with the 2026 cycle drawing around 2.45 lakh applicants. The exam is pitched at the level a school teacher must actually master, testing whether you understand how children learn and can teach the school curriculum clearly, rather than testing advanced academic content. Passing it signals that you meet the professional standard Haryana sets for its classrooms, and thanks to lifetime validity, that signal now lasts your whole career.

## How to prepare for HTET

HTET rewards command of teaching pedagogy and school-level subject knowledge rather than advanced content, so the preparation is about breadth and clarity. Child Development and Pedagogy is common across levels and is the highest-return area because it is scoring and repeatable, so build a strong foundation in learning theories, child psychology, inclusive education, and assessment. The language sections reward comprehension and grammar practice plus a grasp of language teaching methods. For Level 1, the Mathematics and Environmental Studies sections stay at the primary-school level, so revise the concepts a primary teacher must explain clearly. For Levels 2 and 3, the subject component tests your teaching subject at the relevant depth, so revise your graduation or post-graduation syllabus to the level of the school curriculum you will teach. Because there is no negative marking, attempt every question, and practise full-length papers under the 2 hour 30 minute limit to build stamina and pacing. Previous HTET papers, available on the official site, are the best guide to the balance and difficulty the exam sets.

## Eligibility edge cases worth checking

Several eligibility situations trip up candidates, and it is worth checking them against the notification before you apply. Appearing or final-year candidates should confirm whether the cycle allows a provisional application before the qualifying result is out. For Level 2, candidates sometimes ask whether a B.Ed or a D.El.Ed is the right teacher-training qualification; both can be accepted, but the exact recognised list is in the notification. The minimum 50 percent degree requirement carries a relaxation for reserved categories, usually 5 percent, so a reserved candidate just below 50 percent may still qualify. Domicile matters for the qualifying-mark relaxation, since the lower 55 percent bar for Scheduled Caste and Persons with Disabilities candidates applies to Haryana residents, while candidates from those categories from other states face the general 60 percent bar. Checking your exact situation against these rules before applying avoids a rejection at verification.

## What the postponement means for candidates

If you had applied for the 2026 HTET, the postponement is frustrating but does not cancel your candidature. Your application stands, and BSEH announces a revised schedule on bseh.org.in when it is ready. The practical advice is to keep your admit-card login details ready, watch only the official portal for the new date rather than trusting the older dates still shown on aggregator sites, and use the extra time to strengthen your preparation, particularly Child Development and Pedagogy and your subject sections. A postponed exam usually returns with a firm new date once the board resolves whatever caused the delay, so the sensible approach is to stay prepared rather than wait for certainty.

## Common points of confusion

Several recurring confusions trip up candidates, and clearing them early saves wasted effort. The first is thinking HTET is a recruitment exam that leads directly to a job, when it is only the eligibility gate before the HPSC or HSSC recruitment. The second is assuming CTET can be used for Haryana government school posts, when the reported position is that Haryana requires HTET and does not accept CTET for its posts. The third is assuming the certificate expires after seven years, when Haryana extended validity to lifetime. The fourth is trusting the exam dates on aggregator sites, which still show the older postponed dates. The fifth is applying at the wrong level for the classes you want to teach, since Level 1, 2, and 3 map to specific class ranges. Getting these five straight puts you well ahead of a candidate working from the muddled information most sites still publish.

## Documents you will need

Keep these ready when the application window opens for a fresh cycle.

1. A recent passport-size photograph and a scanned signature in the specified format.
2. Your Class 12 marksheet and your graduation or post-graduation marksheet, depending on the level.
3. Your teacher-training qualification certificate, such as the D.El.Ed, JBT, or B.Ed.
4. A category and domicile certificate where you claim a fee concession or the lower qualifying-mark bar.
5. A valid photo ID and an active email and mobile number for exam alerts.

## How to track the real notifications

Given the postponement and the stale dates on aggregator sites, follow the primary sources. HTET notifications, admit cards, and results appear on bseh.org.in. HPSC teacher recruitment appears on hpsc.gov.in, and HSSC recruitment on the HSSC portal. CTET is on ctet.nic.in. Any HTET date not published on bseh.org.in should be treated as unconfirmed, especially since the 2026 exam was postponed more than once.

## Frequently asked questions

**Is HTET valid for a lifetime now?**

Yes. The Haryana Government extended HTET certificate validity from seven years to lifetime, benefiting a large number of candidates. Once you pass HTET, the certificate stays valid for future recruitment cycles and you do not need to re-sit the eligibility test.

**Is CTET valid in Haryana?**

For Haryana government school teacher posts, HTET is the required eligibility test, and CTET is reportedly not accepted in Haryana, even though CTET is accepted almost everywhere else. Verify this against the current HPSC or BSEH notification, but plan for HTET if you want a Haryana teaching job.

**Does qualifying HTET guarantee a government teaching job?**

No. HTET only makes you eligible to be a teacher in Haryana. To be recruited you must also apply to the actual recruitment, run by HPSC for Post Graduate Teacher posts and historically by HSSC for other levels, which selects candidates and requires an HTET certificate as a prerequisite.

**What is the difference between HTET Level 1, 2, and 3?**

Level 1 is for Primary Teacher posts (classes 1 to 5), Level 2 for Trained Graduate Teacher posts (classes 6 to 8), and Level 3 for Post Graduate Teacher posts (classes 9 to 12). You sit the level matching the classes you want to teach, and you can appear for more than one level if eligible.

**What are the HTET 2026 qualifying marks?**

General and unreserved candidates need 60 percent, that is 90 out of 150. Haryana-resident Scheduled Caste and Persons with Disabilities candidates need 55 percent, that is 83 out of 150. Candidates from those categories from other states need the general 60 percent bar.

**Is there negative marking in HTET?**

No. HTET has no negative marking. It is an offline OMR-based test of 150 objective questions for 150 marks in 2 hours 30 minutes, so every question can be attempted without penalty. The exam is bilingual, in Hindi and English.

**Who conducts HTET and who conducts the actual recruitment?**

The Board of School Education Haryana (BSEH), Bhiwani, conducts HTET, the eligibility test. The actual teacher recruitment is run by separate bodies: HPSC for Post Graduate Teacher posts and, historically, HSSC for Trained Graduate Teacher and primary posts.

**Can I apply for HPSC PGT with an HTET certificate?**

Yes. A valid HTET certificate, or an equivalent qualification, is a prerequisite for the HPSC Post Graduate Teacher recruitment. You clear HTET first, then apply to the HPSC PGT recruitment when it is advertised on hpsc.gov.in, and HPSC selects candidates through its own process.

content:
NTA declared the CUET UG 2026 result on 23 June 2026, and university counselling has been running since around August. If you sat the exam in May, the scorecard is out and the part that decides your admission is happening now.

One thing causes more confusion at this stage than anything else: NTA does not run counselling and does not publish cutoffs. Your score comes from NTA. Your admission does not.

## Where CUET UG 2026 stands

| Stage | Status |
|---|---|
| Exam | Conducted May 2026 |
| Result declared | 23 June 2026 |
| Scorecard | Available at cuet.nta.nic.in |
| Counselling | Running from around August 2026 |
| Cutoffs | Published by each university, not by NTA |
| Admission | Conducted by individual universities |

## The thing most candidates get wrong about counselling

NTA conducts the examination, processes the answer sheets and issues your scorecard. That is where its role ends.

It does not release a merit list for admission. It does not publish cutoffs. It does not allot seats. It does not run a single centralised counselling process that places every CUET candidate into a university.

Each participating university runs its own admission process using your CUET score. That means separate registrations, separate deadlines, separate cutoffs and separate counselling rounds, at every university you want to be considered by. Delhi University runs its own process. Banaras Hindu University runs its own. A state university runs its own. Applying to CUET does not apply you to any of them.

Candidates lose seats every year by assuming the scorecard triggers something automatic. It does not. If you have not separately registered with the universities you want, a strong CUET score achieves nothing.

The practical consequence is that August and September are administratively heavy months. You need to track each university's portal, registration window and document requirements independently, and those windows do not align with each other.

## Reading your scorecard

The CUET UG scorecard carries your name, roll number, application number, category, subject-wise marks, total marks, percentile score and rank.

The distinction between marks and percentile matters. Your marks are what you scored. Your percentile reflects where you sit relative to everyone who took that subject in that shift, after normalisation. Because CUET runs across multiple shifts and days for the same subject, NTA normalises scores so candidates who sat a harder shift are not penalised.

That is why your percentile can differ from what raw marks alone would suggest, and why comparing your marks against a friend who sat a different shift tells you little. Universities generally work from the normalised score.

Download the scorecard and keep multiple copies. Universities ask for it at registration, again at document verification, and sometimes again at admission. The NTA portal does not stay open indefinitely.

## How university cutoffs actually work

Cutoffs in CUET-based admission are not fixed in advance. They emerge from the applicant pool at each university in each round.

A university announces seats for a programme, candidates apply, and the cutoff settles at whatever score the last admitted candidate held once the seats fill. If seats remain, the university runs a further round at a lower cutoff. If demand is heavy, the first-round cutoff is high and later rounds may not happen at all.

This produces a few consequences worth planning around.

Cutoffs vary enormously between universities for the same programme, because they reflect that university's demand rather than a national standard. A score that is comfortable at one institution may be well short at another.

Cutoffs also vary between rounds at the same university, usually falling as rounds progress. Candidates who miss the first round should not conclude they are out.

And cutoffs vary by category, with separate lists for reserved categories, which means the relevant comparison is against your own category rather than the general list.

Previous year cutoffs are a rough orientation, not a prediction. They move with the applicant pool each year.

## What to do right now if you have your score

Shortlist universities honestly against your score, with a spread. Include a few where your score is comfortably above last year's level, several where it is around the mark, and one or two ambitious choices. A list made entirely of ambitious choices is how strong candidates end up unplaced.

Register separately at each one, inside its own window. Put the deadlines in a calendar, because they overlap and they are not extended for candidates who missed them.

Keep a document set ready and duplicated: Class 10 and Class 12 marksheets, the CUET scorecard, category certificate if applicable, identity proof, passport photographs and any programme-specific document. Verification is where admissions are lost on paperwork rather than on scores.

Read each programme's subject requirement carefully. Many programmes require specific CUET subjects, and a strong overall score in the wrong subject combination does not qualify you. This is a rule candidates discover at the wrong moment.

Track the fee payment deadline separately from the registration deadline. They are often different dates, and an unpaid seat is released.

## The exam itself, for candidates planning 2027

CUET UG is a computer based test conducted by NTA for undergraduate admission to central, state, deemed and private participating universities.

The paper is organised in sections. One set covers languages, with a large list of Indian and foreign languages available. Another covers domain subjects, spanning the common Class 12 streams including Physics, Chemistry, Mathematics, Biology, Accountancy, Business Studies, Economics, History, Political Science, Geography and others. A general test section covers general knowledge, current affairs, general mental ability, numerical ability and logical reasoning.

You select subjects according to what the universities and programmes you want require, which is why the subject choice needs to be made after checking programme requirements rather than before.

Eligibility for the test itself is a Class 12 pass or appearing, and NTA does not impose a minimum percentage or an age limit for CUET. Universities set their own eligibility on top, and those conditions are frequently stricter than NTA's. A candidate can be eligible for CUET and ineligible for a specific programme.

The test is conducted in multiple shifts across several days per subject, which is what makes score normalisation necessary.

## Normalisation, with an actual example

Normalisation is the part of CUET scoring that generates the most complaint and the least understanding, so it is worth working through concretely.

Suppose Physics is conducted across four shifts over two days. Shift 1 gets a paper that most candidates find manageable, and the average score lands around 120 out of 200. Shift 3 gets a harder paper and the average lands around 95.

Without adjustment, a candidate who scored 140 in Shift 3 would rank below a candidate who scored 145 in Shift 1, even though the Shift 3 candidate performed further above their shift's average and arguably did better. Normalisation corrects for that by converting raw scores into percentiles within each shift and mapping them onto a common scale.

The result is that your percentile answers a different question from your marks. Your marks say what you scored. Your percentile says what proportion of candidates in that subject you finished ahead of.

Two practical points follow. First, do not compare raw marks with someone who sat a different shift, because the comparison is meaningless. Second, do not assume a low raw score in a hard shift has sunk you, because the whole point of normalisation is that it should not have.

What normalisation cannot do is fix a genuinely weak performance. It adjusts for shift difficulty, not for preparation.

## Which universities accept CUET UG

CUET UG is accepted by central universities, a large number of state universities, deemed universities and participating private universities. The list has expanded across cycles as more institutions moved undergraduate admission onto the common test.

Acceptance does not mean uniformity. Universities differ in which CUET subjects they require for a given programme, what weighting they give to CUET score against Class 12 marks, whether they impose an additional eligibility bar, and how many counselling rounds they run.

Some programmes at some universities also use CUET as one component alongside an interview, a portfolio or an aptitude assessment, particularly in design, fine arts, performing arts and some professional courses.

The only reliable source for what a specific university wants is that university's admission prospectus for the current year. Aggregator lists of participating institutions are useful for building a shortlist and unreliable for programme-level detail.

Check also whether the university admits through CUET for the specific programme you want. An institution can participate in CUET for most undergraduate courses while admitting to a handful through a separate route.

## What CUET changed about undergraduate admission

Before CUET, undergraduate admission at most central universities ran on Class 12 board marks, which produced the well-documented problem of cutoffs approaching or reaching 100 per cent at the most competitive Delhi colleges.

That system disadvantaged candidates from boards that marked more conservatively, because a 92 per cent from a strict board competed directly against a 98 per cent from a lenient one. CUET replaced the board marksheet with a common test taken under the same conditions nationally.

The change is not without its own costs. Candidates now prepare for an additional examination on top of board exams in the same academic year, coaching has grown around it, and the administrative burden of applying separately to each university persists because the common test did not bring a common counselling process with it.

For a candidate planning ahead, the useful takeaway is that Class 12 marks still matter, because universities set eligibility conditions and some weight board performance, but they no longer decide admission on their own at CUET-participating institutions.

## Planning for CUET UG 2027

NTA had not announced the 2027 schedule as of 14 August 2026. The exam has historically been conducted in the first half of the calendar year, with registration opening several months ahead.

If you are in Class 11 or entering Class 12, the highest-return preparation is not exam-specific. Domain subjects test Class 12 syllabus content, so studying properly for boards is studying for CUET, and candidates who treat them as two separate preparations waste effort.

Where CUET does need separate work is the general test, which covers current affairs, general knowledge, mental ability, numerical ability and logical reasoning, none of which the board syllabus builds. That section rewards steady low-volume preparation across the year far more than a compressed effort near the exam.

Decide your target universities and programmes before you register, because the subject selection follows from what they require and the choice is not easily undone. This is the single most common planning failure and it happens at registration, months before anyone thinks about cutoffs.

Finally, budget for the administrative load in the admission season. Registering separately at eight universities, tracking eight sets of deadlines and assembling eight document sets is genuinely demanding work, and it lands at the same time as the result.

## Common mistakes across the CUET cycle

Assuming NTA handles admission. It does not, and this single misunderstanding costs more seats than any other.

Choosing CUET subjects before checking what the target programmes require. The subject combination gates your eligibility for specific courses regardless of your score.

Applying only to high-demand universities. Cutoffs at the most competitive institutions clear a narrow band of candidates, and a shortlist without safer options is a plan with one outcome.

Missing a university registration window while waiting for another university's result. The windows run in parallel and do not wait for each other.

Treating previous year cutoffs as a guarantee. They shift each year with the applicant pool and with the number of seats a university offers.

Underestimating document verification. Category certificates in the wrong format, name mismatches between certificates, and missing originals cause avoidable losses at the final step.

## Frequently asked questions

**Has the CUET UG 2026 result been declared?**

Yes. NTA declared the CUET UG 2026 result on 23 June 2026 at cuet.nta.nic.in. The scorecard is downloaded by logging in with your application number and password or date of birth, and carries subject-wise marks, total marks, percentile and rank.

**Does NTA conduct CUET counselling?**

No. NTA conducts the examination and issues the scorecard only. It does not run counselling, does not publish cutoffs and does not allot seats. Each participating university runs its own admission process using your CUET score, with its own registration, deadlines and counselling rounds.

**Do I have to apply separately to each university?**

Yes. A CUET scorecard does not register you anywhere. You must apply separately to every university you want to be considered by, within each one's own window. Candidates lose seats every year by assuming the process is automatic.

**What is the CUET UG cutoff for 2026?**

There is no single CUET cutoff. Each university publishes its own for each programme, category and counselling round, and those emerge from the applicant pool rather than being fixed in advance. Cutoffs generally fall across successive rounds as seats fill, and previous year figures are a rough orientation rather than a prediction.

**What is the difference between marks and percentile on the scorecard?**

Marks are what you scored. Percentile reflects your standing relative to everyone who took that subject, after normalisation. NTA normalises because CUET runs across multiple shifts and days for the same subject, so a candidate who sat a harder shift is not penalised. Universities generally work from the normalised score.

**Is there a minimum percentage or age limit for CUET UG?**

NTA does not set a minimum Class 12 percentage or an age limit for the test itself. Individual universities set their own eligibility conditions on top, and those are frequently stricter, so a candidate can be eligible for CUET and ineligible for a particular programme.

**What subjects should I choose in CUET UG?**

Choose according to what your target universities and programmes require, and check those requirements before selecting rather than after. Many programmes require specific CUET subjects, and a strong overall score in the wrong subject combination does not make you eligible.

**When will CUET UG 2027 be held?**

NTA had not announced the CUET UG 2027 schedule as of 14 August 2026. NTA publishes the notification and the registration window on cuet.nta.nic.in, and the exam has historically been conducted in the first half of the calendar year.

**What documents do I need for university admission?**

Class 10 and Class 12 marksheets, the CUET scorecard, a category certificate if applicable, identity proof, passport photographs and any programme-specific document. Keep duplicates, since universities ask at registration, at verification and again at admission. Name mismatches between certificates are a common cause of avoidable rejection.

**What if I miss the first counselling round?**

Universities generally run further rounds if seats remain, usually at lower cutoffs than the first. Missing the first round is not the end of the process, but you must be registered with that university to be considered in any round, and registration windows are separate from round schedules.

**Can I apply to a university if my CUET subject does not match the programme?**

Generally no. Many programmes specify which CUET subjects a candidate must have taken, and the requirement is checked at eligibility rather than being waived for a high scorer. A candidate with an excellent overall score in an unrelated subject combination will not qualify for a programme that requires specific domain subjects. Check requirements before selecting subjects at registration, since the choice cannot be revisited afterwards.

**Do Class 12 marks still matter with CUET?**

Yes, though not in the way they used to. Universities set their own eligibility conditions, and many require a minimum Class 12 percentage to be considered at all. Some also weight board performance alongside the CUET score. What changed is that board marks no longer decide admission on their own at participating institutions, which was the practice that pushed Delhi cutoffs toward 100 per cent.

**Is there negative marking in CUET UG?**

CUET UG applies negative marking, with a deduction for each wrong answer and no penalty for questions left unattempted. Confirm the exact marking scheme for your subject in the information bulletin for the relevant cycle, since NTA states it there and has adjusted the paper structure between cycles.

**How many universities should I apply to?**

Build a spread rather than a number. Include a few where your score sits comfortably above last year's level, several where it is around the mark, and one or two ambitious choices. A shortlist made entirely of the most competitive institutions is the most common way strong candidates end up unplaced, because those cutoffs clear only a narrow band.

**What happens if I am not satisfied with my CUET score?**

There is no re-examination within a cycle, and NTA does not offer score improvement mid-year. The options are accepting an admission at an institution where the score qualifies, or preparing for the next cycle. Candidates considering a repeat year should weigh it against the programme they can secure now, since a year is a real cost and cutoffs are not guaranteed to move in their favour.

## Official sources

- CUET UG portal, National Testing Agency: https://cuet.nta.nic.in
- Individual participating university admission portals, which are the authority on cutoffs, counselling schedules and programme eligibility

NTA is the authority on your score. Your university is the authority on your admission. Where this page conflicts with either, they are correct.

A closing point worth repeating, because it is the one that costs seats. The CUET scorecard is a qualification, not an application. Nothing happens automatically when it is issued, no central body places you anywhere, and no university will consider you because you scored well nationally. The admission belongs to whichever institutions you personally registered with, inside their own deadlines, with their own documents. Candidates who understand that in June do considerably better than candidates who discover it in September, when most of the good seats have already gone.

B.Ed is not the primary route for Varg 3 because the Supreme Court judgment of 11 August 2023 in Devesh Sharma versus Union of India removed B.Ed as a standalone qualification for primary teaching. ## MPTET 2026 Varg 3 at a glance

Madhya Pradesh Teacher Eligibility Test (MPTET) Varg 3, also called the Primary School Teacher Selection Test (PSTST), is the state-level qualifying exam for candidates who want to teach Classes 1 to 5 in Madhya Pradesh Government primary schools. The exam is conducted by the Madhya Pradesh Employees Selection Board (MPESB), formerly known as MPPEB or Vyapam, through its canonical portal esb.mp.gov.in. Many older sarkari sites and coaching blogs still link the deprecated peb.mp.gov.in URL, which now returns errors and cannot be used for registration or admit card download.

The 2026 cycle of Varg 3 is tentatively scheduled from 31 August 2026 onwards as per the MPESB Annual Calendar 2026. This follows Varg 2 (Middle School Teacher, Classes 6 to 8) which is slated for July 2026 and precedes Varg 1 (Higher Secondary Teacher, Classes 11 to 12) planned for the September to December 2026 window. The MP School Education Department has publicly indicated a target of roughly 30,000 total teacher posts across all three Vargs in 2026, and the Varg 3 share is expected to be the single largest chunk given the primary school vacancy backlog.

The most recent completed cycle, MPTET Varg 3 2025-26, has already produced a revised result on 15 July 2026 and TRC-MP counselling went live on 18 July 2026 at trc.mponline.gov.in. Original notified vacancies for that cycle were 18,650 posts and the revised Mains vacancy figure stands at 10,150 posts as reported by pw.live. Three facts most competitor pages miss or bury. First, the conducting body's canonical URL is now esb.mp.gov.in and the old peb.mp.gov.in is dead, so admit card and result checks must use the new URL. Second, the revised result of 15 July 2026 replaced an earlier provisional list, and TRC-MP counselling opened on 18 July 2026 rather than the September window that older articles still quote. Third, the MPTET certificate is valid for 7 years under the NCTE 2021 update, not lifetime, which is the exact opposite of UPTET and CTET.

## Timeline: notification, applications, admit card, exam, result

The full MPTET Varg 3 2026 timeline as published by MPESB and the MP School Education Department.

| Event | Date |
|---|---|
| MPESB Annual Calendar 2026 release | January 2026 |
| Notification (previous cycle, for reference) | 11 July 2025 |
| Application open (previous cycle) | 18 July 2025 |
| Application close (previous cycle) | 1 August 2025 |
| Correction window (previous cycle) | 5 to 10 August 2025 |
| Admit card (previous cycle) | Early September 2025 |
| Provisional result (previous cycle) | Q1 2026 |
| Revised result (previous cycle) | 15 July 2026 |
| TRC-MP counselling start (previous cycle) | 18 July 2026 |
| MPTET Varg 3 2026 notification (expected) | June or July 2026 |
| MPTET Varg 3 2026 application window (expected) | July to August 2026 |
| MPTET Varg 3 2026 admit card (expected) | Third week of August 2026 |
| MPTET Varg 3 2026 exam start (tentative) | 31 August 2026 onwards |
| MPTET Varg 3 2026 provisional answer key (expected) | Within 7 days of exam close |
| MPTET Varg 3 2026 result (expected) | November to December 2026 |
| TRC-MP counselling for 2026 batch (expected) | Q1 2027 |

The dates from the 2025-26 cycle matter for the 2026 candidate because the process template rarely changes across years. If the calendar holds, the notification-to-exam window is about 6 to 8 weeks, and the exam-to-result window is 10 to 12 weeks. Candidates should track esb.mp.gov.in and educationportal.mp.gov.in from mid-June 2026 for the fresh notification.

## Exam pattern: 150 questions, 150 minutes, no negative marking

MPTET Varg 3 is a computer-based test (CBT) of 150 objective multiple-choice questions carrying 150 marks in total, with a duration of 150 minutes (2 hours 30 minutes). Each question carries 1 mark and there is no negative marking, so every question can be attempted without penalty. The paper is bilingual in Hindi and English for most sections, with the Language 2 section offering a subject choice of English, Sanskrit, or Urdu depending on the candidate's declared teaching medium.

The question paper is split into 5 sections of 30 questions each. Section marks are equal at 30 per section and the candidate must attempt all sections. There is no optional section and no elective subject, which is different from Paper 2 style TET papers where a subject choice between Mathematics-Science and Social Studies is required.

Section-wise distribution.

| Section | Questions | Marks | Time (indicative) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Child Development and Pedagogy | 30 | 30 | 30 minutes |
| Language 1 (Hindi or English) | 30 | 30 | 30 minutes |
| Language 2 (English, Hindi, Sanskrit, or Urdu) | 30 | 30 | 30 minutes |
| Mathematics | 30 | 30 | 30 minutes |
| Environmental Studies (EVS) | 30 | 30 | 30 minutes |

MPESB conducts the exam in one or two shifts per day depending on the total registered candidate count. Shift 1 typically runs 9:00 am to 11:30 am and shift 2 runs 2:00 pm to 4:30 pm, with reporting time 90 minutes before the shift start. Candidates arriving after the shift start are denied entry per the admit card instructions and the MPESB CBT guidelines.

## Eligibility for Varg 3: age, education, D.El.Ed requirement

Age criteria. Minimum 21 years and maximum 40 years as on 1 January 2026 for general candidates. Guest teachers currently serving in MP Government schools get a relaxation up to 49 years for male candidates and 54 years for female candidates. SC, ST, OBC, and PwD candidates from Madhya Pradesh get standard state-level age relaxations that are applied at the recruitment stage rather than the eligibility stage.

Educational qualification for Varg 3 (Primary Classes 1 to 5). Class 12 with at least 50 percent marks (45 percent for NCTE-relaxed categories) plus one of the following: 2-year Diploma in Elementary Education (D.El.Ed), OR 4-year Bachelor of Elementary Education (B.El.Ed), OR 2-year Diploma in Education (Special Education). B.Ed is not the primary route for Varg 3 because Varg 3 targets primary teaching, and the Supreme Court judgment of 11 August 2023 in Devesh Sharma versus Union of India removed B.Ed as a standalone qualification for primary teaching across all state TETs. D.El.Ed or B.El.Ed remains the safe route for Varg 3 applicants.

Domicile. MPTET is open to candidates from any state of India for the eligibility test itself. Reserved category benefits (fee concession, reservation quota) apply only to MP-domicile candidates. Non-MP candidates are treated as unreserved for both fee and reservation purposes.

## Fee structure: general vs SC/ST/OBC/EWS/PwD MP resident

MPTET Varg 3 fee is a combined amount that includes the base application fee and a portal fee, both payable at the time of application. The MPOnline portal (portal.mponline.gov.in) is the fee gateway integrated with esb.mp.gov.in.

| Category | Base fee | Portal fee | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| General / OBC (non-MP resident) | Rs 500 | Rs 60 | Rs 560 |
| SC / ST / OBC (MP resident) | Rs 250 | Rs 60 | Rs 310 |
| EWS (MP resident) | Rs 250 | Rs 60 | Rs 310 |
| PwD (MP resident) | Rs 250 | Rs 60 | Rs 310 |

Payment channels accepted are net banking, credit and debit card (Visa or Mastercard or RuPay), and UPI through the MPOnline gateway. Kiosk payment is also permitted at any authorised MPOnline kiosk across MP with a small kiosk service charge. Fee refund is not available in any circumstance once payment has been confirmed and the application receipt is generated.

Correction of application form is permitted only during the correction window announced with the notification. Corrections after the window closes require a fresh application with a fresh fee, so candidates should recheck the form before final submission.

## Syllabus: five sections of 30 questions each

Section 1: Child Development and Pedagogy (30 marks). Covers principles of child development for the 6 to 11 age band, concepts of learning and motivation, individual differences and inclusive education, National Curriculum Framework (NCF) 2005 and NCF 2023, National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, assessment and evaluation, children with special needs, and pedagogy of teaching primary classes. Reference: NCERT textbook on Child Development and Pedagogy, RTE Act 2009, and NCTE resource material.

Section 2: Language 1 (30 marks). This is either Hindi or English, chosen at the time of application based on the candidate's declared teaching medium. Covers reading comprehension of unseen passages, grammar and syntax of the chosen language, principles of language teaching and language pedagogy, error correction, and vocabulary at the primary school level. Reference: NCERT Hindi or English textbooks Class 6 to 12, plus Vidyapeeth Hindi Vyakaran for Hindi and Wren and Martin for English.

Section 3: Language 2 (30 marks). The second language, chosen from English, Hindi, Sanskrit, or Urdu, distinct from the Language 1 choice. Covers reading comprehension, grammar, and language pedagogy at the primary level. Sanskrit and Urdu options are available for candidates who intend to teach in Sanskrit or Urdu medium schools respectively. English and Hindi are the default choices for most applicants.

Section 4: Mathematics (30 marks). Covers numbers and operations up to Class 5 level, place value, fractions and decimals, geometry (shapes, symmetry, patterns), measurement (length, weight, capacity, time, money), data handling, and pedagogy of mathematics at the primary level. Reference: NCERT Mathematics textbooks Class 6 to 8, plus RS Aggarwal for revision of arithmetic.

Section 5: Environmental Studies or EVS (30 marks). Covers family and friends, food and shelter, water and travel, things we make and do, plants and animals, the human body and its needs, our environment, and EVS pedagogy. Reference: NCERT EVS textbooks Class 3 to 5 (Looking Around) plus NCERT Science textbooks Class 6 to 8 for supplementary depth.

## Passing marks and merit list: 90 out of 150 for general, 75 for reserved

MPTET Varg 3 qualifying cutoffs are set by MPESB in line with the NCTE 2011 framework for teacher eligibility tests.

| Category | Qualifying marks (out of 150) | Percentage |
|---|---|---|
| General | 90 marks | 60 percent |
| SC | 75 marks | 50 percent |
| ST | 75 marks | 50 percent |
| OBC | 75 marks | 50 percent |
| EWS | 75 marks | 50 percent |
| PwD | 75 marks | 50 percent |

The 10 percentage point relaxation for reserved categories (60 percent for General, 50 percent for reserved) is the standard NCTE norm and is applied uniformly across all state TETs including UPTET, REET, and BTET. Widow, Ex-Servicemen, and Divorcee categories do not get a separate lower cutoff in MP.

Passing MPTET Varg 3 does not guarantee a teaching job. It only certifies eligibility for the primary teacher recruitment cycle. Actual selection depends on the Mains merit list prepared by MPESB using the Varg 3 marks plus the applicable reservation and category weightage. Merit list is issued district-wise and category-wise, and appointment orders are dispatched through the TRC-MP counselling process.

## Salary post-selection: Rs 25,300 basic + allowances

Selected candidates are appointed as Primary School Teachers in MP Government schools under the MP School Education Department. Salary structure follows the 7th Central Pay Commission with MP-specific allowances.

Basic pay. Rs 25,300 per month at entry level under Pay Level 6 of the 7th CPC pay matrix, with grade pay of Rs 2,400 (in the pre-7th-CPC nomenclature). Pay scale range is Rs 25,300 to Rs 80,500 across the career span. Annual increment is 3 percent of basic pay per NPS-linked rules.

Allowances. Dearness Allowance (DA) at the current Central rate applicable to MP Government employees. House Rent Allowance (HRA) at the applicable city category rate (Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur, and Gwalior are Y-category cities with 16 percent HRA on basic; other cities and rural areas are Z-category with 8 percent). Transport Allowance (TA) at Rs 1,350 plus DA on TA. Medical allowance as per MP Government norms.

In-hand salary. After deduction of NPS contribution (10 percent of basic plus DA), professional tax, and other statutory deductions, the in-hand salary for a Primary School Teacher at entry level is approximately Rs 41,478 per month at the Bhopal or Indore posting. Rural postings carry slightly lower HRA but no change to the basic pay structure.

Probation. 3 years of probation is standard for MP Government teacher appointments, with annual increment freeze during the first 2 years of probation. Permanent status is conferred after successful completion of probation and after clearing the departmental proficiency test.

## MPTET Varg 1 vs Varg 2 vs Varg 3: which one should you write?

MPTET is a three-tier exam and the correct Varg to apply for depends entirely on your target teaching level. All three are conducted by MPESB via esb.mp.gov.in with a shared portal login but separate application processes.

| Attribute | Varg 1 | Varg 2 | Varg 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full name | Higher Secondary Teacher Selection Test | Middle School Teacher Selection Test | Primary School Teacher Selection Test |
| Classes | 11 to 12 | 6 to 8 | 1 to 5 |
| Educational qualification | Post-graduation in relevant subject plus B.Ed | Bachelor's in relevant subject plus B.Ed or B.El.Ed | Class 12 with 50 percent plus D.El.Ed or B.El.Ed |
| Age (as on 1 Jan 2026) | 21 to 40 years | 21 to 40 years | 21 to 40 years |
| Paper structure | Subject-specific | Subject-specific | Common paper (5 sections of 30) |
| Total questions | 150 | 150 | 150 |
| Total marks | 150 | 150 | 150 |
| Duration | 3 hours | 2 hours 30 minutes | 2 hours 30 minutes |
| Passing (Gen / Reserved) | 60 / 50 percent | 60 / 50 percent | 60 / 50 percent |
| 2026 exam window (tentative) | September to December | July | 31 August onwards |
| Basic pay on selection | Rs 32,800 (Level 8) | Rs 29,200 (Level 7) | Rs 25,300 (Level 6) |
| Certificate validity | 7 years | 7 years | 7 years |

Practical guidance. A candidate with post-graduation plus B.Ed should target Varg 1 for the highest pay level and the secondary-classes teaching role. A candidate with a Bachelor's degree plus B.Ed should target Varg 2 for the middle school role. A candidate with Class 12 plus D.El.Ed should target Varg 3, which is also the largest hiring pool by post count in 2026. Candidates holding both D.El.Ed and B.Ed can apply for all three Vargs simultaneously provided they meet the age and educational thresholds for each.

## MPTET Varg 3 vs CTET, UPTET, REET, BTET side by side

The five main teacher eligibility tests that a candidate targeting Indian Government school jobs will consider.

| Attribute | MPTET Varg 3 | CTET | UPTET | REET | BTET |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Level | State (MP) | National (Central) | State (UP) | State (Rajasthan) | State (Bihar) |
| Conducting body | MPESB | CBSE | UPESSC | RSMSSB | BSEB |
| Frequency | Annual | Twice a year | Annual | Every 2 to 3 years | Annual |
| Age limit | 21 to 40 | No upper limit | No upper limit | No upper limit | 18 to 37 |
| Fee (General, single paper) | Rs 560 | Rs 1,000 | Rs 600 | Rs 550 | Rs 960 |
| Number of questions | 150 | 150 | 150 | 150 | 150 |
| Negative marking | No | No | No | Yes (0.33 per wrong) | No |
| Certificate validity | 7 years | Lifetime | Lifetime | 7 years | 7 years |
| Portal | esb.mp.gov.in | ctet.nic.in | upessc.up.gov.in | reet2024.co.in | bsebstet.com |
| Accepted for jobs in | MP Government schools | All Central and most state schools | UP schools plus CTET-accepting states | Rajasthan Government schools | Bihar Government schools |

Which one should an MP candidate hold. MPTET Varg 3 is the primary route for MP Government primary school jobs. CTET is a strong supplementary hold because it is accepted for Kendriya Vidyalaya (KVS), Navodaya Vidyalaya (NVS), Central schools, and many state Governments including MP. Holding both MPTET Varg 3 and CTET is the strongest position for an MP-focused candidate. UPTET, REET, and BTET are relevant only if the candidate plans to apply for teaching jobs in those specific states.

The certificate validity difference is worth noting. CTET and UPTET certificates are lifetime valid, but MPTET, REET, and BTET certificates expire after 7 years and require re-examination. This is one reason many MP-domicile candidates hold both MPTET and CTET, because the CTET certificate acts as a long-term fallback if the MPTET validity lapses.

## How to apply on esb.mp.gov.in (step by step)

Step 1: Visit esb.mp.gov.in and register. Use the New Registration link on the homepage. Register with a valid email ID and mobile number. The portal will send an OTP for verification. Do not use peb.mp.gov.in, which is the deprecated URL and does not accept new registrations.

Step 2: Fill in personal and educational details. Enter name exactly as on Class 10 marksheet, date of birth, category (General, SC, ST, OBC, EWS), domicile status (MP or non-MP), and educational qualification details including D.El.Ed or B.El.Ed marks and institution name.

Step 3: Upload documents. Recent passport size photograph (10 KB to 50 KB, JPG or JPEG format) taken within the last 3 months on a plain background. Signature scan (5 KB to 20 KB, JPG or JPEG format) done with black ink on white paper. Any mismatch between the upload and the physical appearance on exam day can lead to admit card cancellation.

Step 4: Choose exam city preferences. MPESB allows 3 city choices in order of preference. Popular centres include Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur, Gwalior, Ujjain, Sagar, Rewa, and Satna. City allotment depends on the total candidate count for each centre and is issued with the admit card.

Step 5: Pay the fee. Rs 560 for General and OBC non-MP candidates, Rs 310 for SC, ST, OBC, EWS, and PwD MP residents. Payment through net banking, credit or debit card, UPI, or MPOnline kiosk. Save the payment confirmation and transaction ID.

Step 6: Submit and download the confirmation. Once fee payment is confirmed, the portal generates an application confirmation with a unique application number. Download and save both the PDF confirmation and the application number, because these are needed for admit card download and result check.

Step 7: Track the admit card release. Admit cards are typically released 10 to 15 days before the exam date. For a 31 August 2026 exam start, admit cards are expected in the third week of August 2026 at esb.mp.gov.in.

## After the result: TRC-MP counselling from 18 July 2026

TRC-MP (Teacher Recruitment Counselling Madhya Pradesh) is the online counselling platform for MP Government teacher appointments, hosted at trc.mponline.gov.in. For the 2025-26 Varg 3 cycle, TRC-MP counselling went live on 18 July 2026 following the revised result of 15 July 2026.

TRC-MP process. Step 1: log in with the MPTET application number and date of birth. Step 2: fill in personal and category details for verification. Step 3: select district and school preferences in order of priority (up to 100 school choices are typically permitted). Step 4: upload supporting documents including MPTET result scorecard, D.El.Ed marksheet and certificate, Class 12 marksheet, category certificate, and domicile certificate. Step 5: pay the counselling fee of Rs 500 through the MPOnline gateway. Step 6: track the seat allotment result on the portal.

Seat allotment. Allotment is done through a merit-plus-preference algorithm. Higher-ranked candidates get their higher-preferred schools, and lower-ranked candidates fill the remaining vacancies. Multiple counselling rounds are held until all vacancies are filled, typically 2 to 4 rounds spread over 2 to 3 months.

After allotment. The selected candidate reports to the allotted school within 30 days of the appointment order. Document verification is done at the district Block Education Office (BEO). Joining letter and salary drawing paperwork are processed by the district education office. First salary credit typically arrives 45 to 60 days after joining because of the payroll onboarding cycle.

## Preparation strategy and previous year papers

Six-month preparation strategy for a first-time Varg 3 candidate. Month 1 to 2: cover NCERT textbooks for Class 6 to 12 for Mathematics and EVS, and the NCERT Child Development and Pedagogy textbook. Month 3 to 4: revise Hindi and English grammar from the standard reference books (Vidyapeeth for Hindi, Wren and Martin for English) and attempt 2 mock tests per week. Month 5: solve previous year MPTET Varg 3 papers from 2018, 2020, and the 2025-26 cycle. Month 6: full-length mock tests 3 times a week, focused revision of weak sections, and pedagogy revision.

Previous year papers. MPTET Varg 3 papers from earlier cycles are available on esb.mp.gov.in in the archive section and on major coaching platforms like Testbook, Adda247, PW (PhysicsWallah), and Oliveboard. Solving at least 5 previous year papers under strict 150-minute timing is the single highest-return preparation activity. Trend across recent cycles shows Child Development and Pedagogy and EVS sections carry the highest weightage of pedagogy questions, and Mathematics carries the highest weightage of application questions rather than pure calculation.

Coaching material to prioritise. NCERT textbooks are non-negotiable and cover roughly 70 percent of the syllabus. Adda247 Teaching Exam book covers pedagogy well. Testbook MPTET mock test series is popular for the CBT interface practice. Free Telegram groups run by teachers who cleared earlier cycles are a low-cost source of doubt clearance and past paper PDFs.

Time management on exam day. 150 questions in 150 minutes means exactly 1 minute per question, but the actual split should be 45 seconds for easy questions and 90 seconds for hard questions. Attempt all 150 questions because there is no negative marking. Do not leave any question blank, even if you have to guess on the last 10 to 15 hard ones.

## Common application rejection reasons and how to avoid them

MPESB rejects a portion of Varg 3 applications every cycle for avoidable process errors. The most common reasons per candidate feedback from the 2025-26 cycle.

Photo and signature mismatch. Uploaded photograph is more than 3 months old, taken with a background that is not plain white, or shows the candidate wearing spectacles that do not match the photo ID. Signature scan is done in blue ink instead of black, or is in a different style from the Class 10 record. Fix: use a photo taken within the last 30 days on a plain white background, and match the signature style to the one on your Class 10 marksheet.

Category certificate not valid. SC, ST, OBC, or EWS certificate is issued more than 5 years ago and has expired, or is issued by an authority not recognised by the MP Government (for example, an OBC certificate from Central format instead of MP state format). Fix: obtain a fresh category certificate from the SDM or Tehsildar office within 3 months of the application date, and ensure the format matches the MP state requirement.

Age proof mismatch. Date of birth on the application does not match the date on the Class 10 certificate. This is a hard rejection with no correction window. Fix: use the Class 10 certificate date of birth on all fields, even if other documents show a different date.

Educational qualification declared but not completed. Candidates who are in the final year of D.El.Ed or B.El.Ed at the time of application must confirm they will complete the course before the document verification date. Applications from candidates who cannot produce the final marksheet by the verification date are cancelled. Fix: apply only in the year of your D.El.Ed or B.El.Ed final year completion, not before.

Fee payment failure. Payment gateway timeout leads to money debit without application confirmation. This is not counted as a successful application even if the money is deducted. Fix: check the application status page 24 hours after payment. If the status shows unpaid, contact MPOnline support with the transaction ID for a refund or a manual application confirmation.

Domicile status error. Non-MP candidates who claim SC, ST, OBC, or EWS fee concession are rejected because reserved category benefits apply only to MP-domicile candidates. Fix: non-MP candidates should apply under the General category with the Rs 560 fee, even if they hold a reserved category certificate from another state.
