## Frequently asked questions
**When is MPTET Varg 3 2026 exam date?**
MPTET Varg 3 2026 is tentatively scheduled from 31 August 2026 onwards as per the MPESB Annual Calendar 2026 published in January 2026 on esb.mp.gov.in. The notification is expected in June or July 2026, applications will open shortly after the notification, and admit cards are expected in the third week of August 2026. The exam is a computer-based test of 150 questions and 150 marks in 150 minutes with no negative marking. Results are expected in November or December 2026.

**What is the passing mark for MPTET Varg 3?**
Qualifying cutoff for MPTET Varg 3 is 60 percent (90 marks out of 150) for General category candidates and 50 percent (75 marks out of 150) for SC, ST, OBC, EWS, and PwD categories. The 10 percentage point relaxation for reserved categories is the standard NCTE norm applied across all state TETs. Widow, Ex-Servicemen, and Divorcee categories do not get a separate lower cutoff in MP. Passing MPTET Varg 3 only certifies eligibility. Actual selection depends on the Mains merit list prepared by MPESB.

**Is MPTET Varg 3 certificate valid for lifetime?**
No. MPTET Varg 3 certificate is valid for 7 years from the date of issue, per the NCTE 2021 update. This is different from CTET and UPTET, both of which now have lifetime validity per the NCTE Notification dated 3 June 2020 and the retrospective UP Cabinet approval of November 2021. MPTET has not been extended to lifetime validity as of 2026. Candidates whose 7-year window is about to expire must re-appear for the exam to keep the certificate active.

**What is the age limit for MPTET Varg 3 2026?**
Minimum age is 21 years and maximum age is 40 years as on 1 January 2026 for General category candidates. Guest teachers currently serving in MP Government schools get relaxation up to 49 years for male candidates and 54 years for female candidates. SC, ST, OBC, and PwD candidates from Madhya Pradesh get standard state-level age relaxations applied at the recruitment stage. The age limit is one of the stricter aspects of MPTET compared to CTET and UPTET, which have no upper age limit for the eligibility test itself.

**What is the application fee for MPTET Varg 3 2026?**
Application fee for General and OBC (non-MP resident) candidates is Rs 500 base fee plus Rs 60 portal fee, totalling Rs 560. SC, ST, OBC, EWS, and PwD candidates from Madhya Pradesh pay Rs 250 base fee plus Rs 60 portal fee, totalling Rs 310. Payment is through the MPOnline gateway integrated with esb.mp.gov.in, accepting net banking, credit and debit card (Visa, Mastercard, or RuPay), and UPI. Fee refund is not available under any circumstance once payment is confirmed.

**Can B.Ed candidates apply for MPTET Varg 3?**
B.Ed is not the primary route for MPTET Varg 3 because Varg 3 targets primary teaching (Classes 1 to 5). The Supreme Court judgment of 11 August 2023 in Devesh Sharma versus Union of India removed B.Ed as a standalone qualification for primary teaching across all state TETs. The safe route for Varg 3 is Class 12 with at least 50 percent marks (45 percent for NCTE-relaxed categories) plus a 2-year D.El.Ed or 4-year B.El.Ed or 2-year Diploma in Education (Special Education). Candidates holding both D.El.Ed and B.Ed can apply for Varg 3.

**How many vacancies are expected in MPTET Varg 3 2026?**
The MP School Education Department has publicly indicated a target of roughly 30,000 total teacher posts across all three Vargs in 2026. Varg 3 is expected to be the single largest chunk given the primary school vacancy backlog, though the exact 2026 number will be confirmed with the notification. For reference, the previous 2025-26 cycle originally notified 18,650 posts, with the revised Mains vacancy figure at 10,150 posts as reported by pw.live after the 15 July 2026 revised result.

**What is the salary of an MP Primary School Teacher after Varg 3?**
Selected candidates are appointed as Primary School Teachers under Pay Level 6 of the 7th Central Pay Commission pay matrix. Basic pay is Rs 25,300 per month at entry level with a grade pay of Rs 2,400. Pay scale spans Rs 25,300 to Rs 80,500 across the career. After DA, HRA (16 percent for Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur, and Gwalior; 8 percent for other cities), TA of Rs 1,350, and NPS deduction, the in-hand salary at entry level is approximately Rs 41,478 per month for a Bhopal or Indore posting.

**Where is TRC-MP counselling done and when?**
TRC-MP (Teacher Recruitment Counselling Madhya Pradesh) is the online counselling platform at trc.mponline.gov.in. For the 2025-26 Varg 3 cycle, TRC-MP counselling went live on 18 July 2026 following the revised result of 15 July 2026. Candidates log in with the MPTET application number and date of birth, fill preferences for up to 100 school choices, upload supporting documents, and pay the counselling fee of Rs 500. Seat allotment is done through a merit-plus-preference algorithm across 2 to 4 rounds over 2 to 3 months.

**Is CTET accepted for MP Government teacher jobs?**
Yes. CTET (Central Teacher Eligibility Test conducted by CBSE) is accepted for MP Government primary and upper primary teacher recruitment on par with MPTET. Holding both MPTET Varg 3 and CTET is the strongest position for an MP-focused candidate because CTET certificate is lifetime valid while MPTET is only 7 years, and CTET is also accepted for Kendriya Vidyalaya (KVS), Navodaya Vidyalaya (NVS), Central schools, and many other state Governments. The higher qualifying score between the two is typically taken forward at the recruitment stage.

**What is the correct portal for MPTET Varg 3 application?**
The canonical portal for MPTET Varg 3 is esb.mp.gov.in, run by the Madhya Pradesh Employees Selection Board (MPESB), formerly known as MPPEB or Vyapam. The older peb.mp.gov.in URL is now deprecated and does not accept new registrations, admit card downloads, or result checks. Many older sarkari sites and coaching blogs still link the dead peb URL, so candidates should verify they are on esb.mp.gov.in before starting any application. Fee payment is routed through portal.mponline.gov.in and counselling is done on trc.mponline.gov.in.

**How many attempts are allowed for MPTET Varg 3?**
There is no cap on the number of attempts for MPTET Varg 3. A candidate can appear for the exam any number of times within the age eligibility window of 21 to 40 years. Each attempt requires a fresh application and fresh fee payment. There is also no restriction based on prior qualifying status. A candidate who has already cleared MPTET Varg 3 can re-appear to improve the score, and the higher of the two scores is used at the recruitment stage. The 7-year certificate validity means re-examination becomes necessary if the earlier certificate expires before the candidate secures an appointment.

content:
## AIBE 2026: a licence, not an admission

The All India Bar Examination, conducted by the Bar Council of India, is not an entrance examination. It is the test you take after completing your law degree, in order to be licensed to practise law in India.

That distinction matters because AIBE is routinely confused with CLAT and AILET, which are admission tests for law school. AIBE sits at the other end of the journey. You finish your LLB, you enrol with a State Bar Council, and then you pass AIBE to receive the Certificate of Practice that allows you to appear before courts.

The second thing to understand is that AIBE is qualifying rather than competitive. There is no rank, no merit list and no cutoff that shifts with the strength of the field. You need 45 per cent to pass if you are in the General or OBC category, or 40 per cent if you are SC, ST or a person with a disability. Everyone who reaches that mark passes. Nobody is competing against you.

And it is an open book examination. You may carry printed bare acts and study material into the hall.

Put those three facts together and AIBE is a very different proposition from the examinations that got you into law school. It is designed to confirm baseline professional competence, not to rank candidates, and it should be prepared for accordingly.

## Current cycle: AIBE 22

| Event | Date |
|---|---|
| Application form released | 19 August 2026 |
| Registration deadline | 27 October 2026 |
| Examination | 29 November 2026 |

The preceding cycle, AIBE 21, ran its registration from 11 February to 30 April 2026 and was held on 7 June 2026. So the Bar Council currently runs roughly two cycles a year, which means a candidate who misses one or does not pass has another opportunity within months rather than a year.

## Exam pattern

| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| Questions | 100 multiple choice |
| Marks | 100 |
| Duration | 3 hours 30 minutes |
| Mode | Offline, OMR based |
| Negative marking | None |
| Format | Open book |
| Subjects covered | 19 |
| Qualifying marks | 45 per cent for General and OBC; 40 per cent for SC, ST and PwD |

Three and a half hours for 100 questions is a little over two minutes per question, which is generous by the standards of any competitive examination. That generosity is deliberate: the open book format assumes you will spend time looking things up.

There is no negative marking, so every question should carry an answer. On a paper with no penalty and a fixed pass mark, leaving anything blank is simply discarding a chance at the marks you need.

## The open book rule, and its trap

You may carry printed bare acts and study material into the examination hall. You may not carry handwritten notes.

That restriction catches candidates every cycle, and it is worth being precise about. The Bar Council permits printed material, meaning published bare acts and commercially printed guides. Handwritten annotations and personally written notes are not permitted, and material found to breach the rule can be confiscated at the centre.

The practical consequence is that your preparation strategy has to work within printed material. Candidates who spend months making handwritten summaries arrive with material they cannot use.

What works instead is organisation of printed matter. Tabbing and indexing your bare acts so you can locate a provision in seconds is the single most useful preparation activity for this examination. An unindexed pile of bare acts is close to useless under a clock, however comprehensive it is; a well-tabbed set turns a lookup into a ten-second operation.

Check the current Bar Council notification before the examination, since the rules on permitted material are stated there and are the authority on what you may carry.

## Why open book does not mean easy

The common failure at AIBE is underestimating it precisely because it is open book, no negative marking and only 45 per cent to pass.

The paper covers 19 subjects. Nobody can look up 100 questions across 19 subjects in 210 minutes. If you have to search for every answer you will not finish, and the open book provision becomes a liability rather than an advantage because it encourages searching instead of knowing.

The realistic approach is to know enough to answer most questions directly, and to use the printed material for the ones where you need to confirm a provision, a section number or an exact wording. Treat the books as a safety net rather than as the primary source.

That is why tabbing matters more than volume, and why a candidate who has revised the major subjects and indexed their material well will finish comfortably, while one relying entirely on lookup will run out of time somewhere around question sixty.

## Subjects covered

AIBE spans 19 subjects drawn from the core of an Indian law degree.

The heavily weighted areas are typically Constitutional Law, the Indian Penal Code, the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Code of Civil Procedure, the Indian Evidence Act, the Indian Contract Act, Family Law, and the Professional Ethics and Professional Conduct rules along with the Advocates Act.

The remaining subjects carry fewer questions each and commonly include Administrative Law, Company Law, Environmental Law, Cyber Law, Labour and Industrial Law, Law of Tort including Motor Vehicles Act and Consumer Protection Law, Public Interest Litigation, Taxation Law, Intellectual Property Law, Alternative Dispute Resolution, and Land Acquisition Law.

The Professional Ethics component deserves specific attention. It is directly relevant to the licence you are seeking, it draws on the Advocates Act and Bar Council rules, and it is the area law graduates are least likely to have studied closely during their degree.

Since the exact subject-wise question distribution is published by the Bar Council with each cycle's notification, check that document rather than relying on a previous year's breakdown.

## Eligibility

AIBE is open to law graduates holding an LLB degree from a Bar Council of India recognised institution, whether through the three-year or the five-year integrated route.

Candidates must be enrolled as advocates with a State Bar Council before appearing. Enrolment comes first, then the examination, then the Certificate of Practice.

There is no age limit and no cap on the number of attempts. A candidate who does not reach the qualifying mark may sit again in a subsequent cycle, and since the Bar Council currently runs roughly two cycles a year, the wait is months rather than a year.

## What passing gives you

On passing, the Bar Council of India issues the Certificate of Practice, which is what entitles an enrolled advocate to practise before courts in India.

Without it, an enrolled advocate's right to appear is restricted. This is why AIBE matters practically for anyone intending to litigate, appear before tribunals, or work in roles where court appearance is part of the job.

It is worth noting what AIBE is not required for. Many law graduates work in corporate legal teams, compliance, policy, research, academia and legal process roles where court appearance is not part of the work, and those positions do not depend on the Certificate of Practice. Whether you need AIBE depends on the career you are entering, and it is reasonable to take it anyway as a keep-options-open measure, since the requirement is not onerous.

## How AIBE compares with the law entrance exams

Because this site also covers the entrance examinations, the distinction is worth setting out plainly.

| | [CLAT 2027](/entrance-exams/clat-2027) | [AILET 2027](/entrance-exams/ailet-2027) | AIBE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Admission to law school | Admission to law school | Licence to practise |
| Taken | After Class 12 or graduation | After Class 12 or graduation | After the LLB |
| Nature | Competitive, ranked | Competitive, ranked | Qualifying, pass or fail |
| Open book | No | No | Yes |
| Negative marking | Yes | Yes | No |
| Pass standard | Rank-based cutoff | Rank-based cutoff | Fixed at 45 or 40 per cent |
| Outcome | A seat at an NLU | A seat at NLU Delhi | Certificate of Practice |

The mental shift required between them is substantial. CLAT and AILET reward speed, precision under pressure and outperforming other candidates. AIBE rewards organisation, familiarity with the core statutes, and calmly reaching a fixed threshold that has nothing to do with how anyone else performs.

## Preparing for AIBE

Index your printed material first. Tab your bare acts by subject and by major provision so that any lookup takes seconds. This is the highest-return preparation activity and most candidates leave it too late.

Revise the heavily weighted subjects to the point where you can answer directly: Constitutional Law, IPC, CrPC, CPC, Evidence, Contract, Family Law and Professional Ethics. Aim to know these rather than look them up.

Give Professional Ethics and the Advocates Act genuine attention, since it is directly relevant, commonly under-studied, and the questions are answerable with modest revision.

Work past AIBE papers. The Bar Council's question style is consistent across cycles and previous papers show both the level and the recurring areas.

Practise with your actual materials under a clock. A timed mock using the exact books you will carry tells you whether your indexing works, which is something no amount of reading reveals.

Plan the paper: answer everything you know directly on a first pass, mark the lookups, then work through them with the time remaining. Attempting the paper in order while looking things up as you go is how candidates run out of time.

## How to index your bare acts

Since indexing is the highest-return preparation for this examination and almost nothing published explains how, here is a workable method.

Tab by statute first. Give each bare act you carry a distinct coloured tab on its cover edge so you can pull the right book without reading spines under pressure.

Within each act, tab the provisions that generate questions rather than every section. For the Indian Penal Code that means the general exceptions, the offences against the human body, offences against property, and the definitions. For the Criminal Procedure Code, arrest, bail, cognizance, charge, trial procedure and appeals. For the Civil Procedure Code, jurisdiction, pleadings, summons, interim orders, execution and appeals. For Evidence, relevancy, admissions and confessions, burden of proof, witnesses and estoppel. For the Constitution, fundamental rights, directive principles, the union and state executive and legislature, the judiciary, emergency provisions and amendment.

Write the tab labels in printed form, using printed labels or typed stickers, since handwritten annotation is not permitted.

Keep a printed contents sheet at the front of each act listing your tabs and their page numbers, which turns a two-step search into a one-step one.

Test the system before the examination. Take twenty past questions, time yourself locating the relevant provision for each, and fix whatever slows you down. A system that works on your desk at home is the one that will work in the hall.

## Common reasons candidates fail AIBE

Assuming open book means no preparation. The 19-subject spread makes pure lookup impossible within the time, and this is by some distance the most common cause of failure.

Carrying handwritten notes. They are not permitted, may be confiscated, and represent preparation time that produced nothing usable.

Carrying too much. A trolley of unindexed books is slower to use than three well-tabbed acts, because the search space is larger and the retrieval is no faster.

Neglecting Professional Ethics. It is directly relevant to the licence being sought, it is well represented in the paper, and it is the subject law graduates are least likely to have revised.

Attempting the paper in strict order with lookups as you go. The workable method is a first pass answering everything you know directly, then returning to the lookups with the remaining time.

Leaving questions blank. There is no negative marking and a fixed pass mark, so an unanswered question is a discarded chance at the marks you need.

## How to apply

Applications are filed on the official AIBE portal at allindiabarexamination.com.

1. Complete your enrolment with a State Bar Council first, since enrolment is a precondition for appearing.
2. Register on the AIBE portal with a valid email address and mobile number.
3. Fill the application with your degree and enrolment details exactly as on your documents.
4. Upload photograph, signature and the required documents in the specified format.
5. Pay the examination fee as notified by the Bar Council.
6. Select your examination centre preference.
7. Submit and save the confirmation, then download the admit card ahead of the examination.

For AIBE 22, the form is available from 19 August 2026 and the deadline is 27 October 2026, with the examination on 29 November 2026.

## Documents you will need

1. LLB degree certificate or provisional certificate from a Bar Council recognised institution.
2. LLB mark sheets for all years or semesters.
3. State Bar Council enrolment certificate and enrolment number.
4. Category certificate for SC, ST and OBC claims, and a PwD certificate where applicable.
5. Photograph, signature and a photo identity document matching the application.

## Frequently asked questions

**What is AIBE and how is it different from CLAT?**
AIBE is the All India Bar Examination conducted by the Bar Council of India, taken after completing your LLB in order to obtain the Certificate of Practice that licenses you to practise law. CLAT and AILET are admission tests taken before law school. AIBE sits at the other end of the journey, and unlike those examinations it is qualifying rather than competitive, with no rank and no merit list.

**When is AIBE 2026 and when does registration open?**
AIBE 22 is scheduled for 29 November 2026, with the application form released on 19 August 2026 and a registration deadline of 27 October 2026. The preceding cycle, AIBE 21, was held on 7 June 2026 with registration from 11 February to 30 April 2026. The Bar Council currently runs roughly two cycles a year.

**What are the AIBE qualifying marks?**
45 per cent, meaning 45 marks out of 100, for General and OBC candidates, and 40 per cent, meaning 40 marks, for SC, ST and candidates with a disability. There is no rank and no cutoff that moves with the strength of the field: everyone reaching the qualifying mark passes.

**Is AIBE an open book exam?**
Yes. You may carry printed bare acts and study material into the examination hall. However, handwritten notes are not permitted, and material breaching the rule can be confiscated at the centre. Check the current Bar Council notification for the authoritative statement of what is allowed, since the rules are set out there for each cycle.

**Can I carry handwritten notes to AIBE?**
No. Only printed material is permitted, meaning published bare acts and commercially printed guides. Handwritten annotations and personally written notes are not allowed. This catches candidates every cycle, and it means that months spent making handwritten summaries produce material you cannot use in the hall.

**Is AIBE easy because it is open book?**
No, and treating it that way is the common failure. The paper covers 19 subjects, and nobody can look up 100 questions across 19 subjects in 210 minutes. If you have to search for every answer you will not finish. The workable approach is to know enough to answer most questions directly and use the printed material to confirm provisions and section numbers, which is why indexing your bare acts matters more than the volume you carry.

**What is the AIBE exam pattern?**
100 multiple choice questions for 100 marks over 3 hours 30 minutes, offline in OMR mode, open book, with no negative marking, covering 19 subjects. At just over two minutes per question the timing is generous by competitive examination standards, which reflects the expectation that some lookup will happen.

**Is there negative marking in AIBE?**
No. Nothing is deducted for a wrong answer, so every one of the 100 questions should carry an answer. On a paper with no penalty and a fixed pass mark, leaving anything blank simply discards a chance at the marks you need.

**Which subjects are covered in AIBE?**
Nineteen subjects from the core of an Indian law degree. The heavily weighted areas are typically Constitutional Law, the Indian Penal Code, the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Code of Civil Procedure, the Indian Evidence Act, the Indian Contract Act, Family Law, and Professional Ethics with the Advocates Act. Others include Administrative Law, Company Law, Environmental Law, Cyber Law, Labour and Industrial Law, Law of Tort, Public Interest Litigation, Taxation, Intellectual Property, Alternative Dispute Resolution and Land Acquisition Law.

**Do I need to enrol with a State Bar Council before AIBE?**
Yes. Enrolment as an advocate with a State Bar Council is a precondition for appearing in the examination. The sequence is enrolment first, then AIBE, then the Certificate of Practice issued by the Bar Council of India on passing.

**How many attempts do I get at AIBE?**
There is no cap on attempts and no age limit. A candidate who does not reach the qualifying mark may sit again in a subsequent cycle, and since the Bar Council currently runs roughly two cycles a year, the wait is a matter of months rather than a full year.

**Do all law graduates need to pass AIBE?**
Only those who intend to practise before courts. The Certificate of Practice is what entitles an enrolled advocate to appear, so it matters for litigation, tribunal work and any role involving court appearance. Many law graduates work in corporate legal teams, compliance, policy, research, academia and legal process roles where it is not required, though taking it anyway is a reasonable way to keep options open given the modest demands.

**What is the best way to prepare for AIBE?**
Index your printed bare acts by subject and major provision so any lookup takes seconds, since that is the highest-return activity and most candidates leave it too late. Revise the heavily weighted subjects to the point of answering directly rather than searching, give Professional Ethics and the Advocates Act genuine attention as they are directly relevant and commonly under-studied, work past papers, and take at least one timed mock using the exact books you intend to carry to test whether your indexing actually works.

## SBI PO 2026 — Complete Guide

Getting into SBI as a Probationary Officer is one of the most sought-after career moves in Indian banking. The pay is excellent, the job security is iron-clad, and the career growth — from PO to Assistant General Manager — is structured and well-defined. Every year, over 20 lakh candidates apply for a few thousand PO posts. That alone tells you how much this exam matters.

The SBI PO 2026 notification is expected to be released in June 2026. The Prelims exam is likely in August 2026 and Mains in September 2026.

## Important Dates (Expected)

| Event | Date |
|---|---|
| Notification Release | June 2026 (Expected) |
| Application Opens | June 15, 2026 (Expected) |
| **Last Date to Apply** | **July 10, 2026 (Expected)** |
| Prelims Exam | **August 1–2, 2026 (Expected)** |
| Mains Exam | **September 12, 2026 (Expected)** |
| Group Exercise & Interview | October – November 2026 |
| Final Result | December 2026 |

*Dates are based on SBI's annual pattern. Official dates will be published at sbi.co.in/careers.*

## Eligibility

**Educational Qualification:** Any bachelor's degree from a recognized university. There is no minimum percentage requirement — just a pass is enough. Final year students can also apply.

**Age:** 21 to 30 years as on April 1, 2026. That means you should have been born between April 2, 1996 and April 1, 2005.

**Age Relaxation:**
- SC / ST: 5 years (upper limit becomes 35)
- OBC (NCL): 3 years (upper limit becomes 33)
- PwBD: 10 years

## Selection Process — 3 Stages

SBI PO is a three-stage exam. You must clear each stage to move to the next.

### Stage 1 — Prelims (Qualifying)
The Prelims is a 1-hour test with 100 questions across three sections. It is qualifying in nature — your Prelims marks are not counted in the final merit list. You just need to clear the cutoff.

| Section | Questions | Marks | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| English Language | 30 | 30 | 20 min |
| Quantitative Aptitude | 35 | 35 | 20 min |
| Reasoning Ability | 35 | 35 | 20 min |
| **Total** | **100** | **100** | **60 min** |

### Stage 2 — Mains (Counts in Final Merit)
The Mains is a full 3-hour objective paper plus 30 minutes of descriptive writing. This is what actually determines your rank.

| Section | Questions | Marks | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reasoning & Computer Aptitude | 45 | 60 | 60 min |
| Data Analysis & Interpretation | 35 | 60 | 45 min |
| General Economy & Banking Awareness | 40 | 40 | 35 min |
| English Language | 35 | 40 | 40 min |
| English Descriptive (Letter + Essay) | 2 | 50 | 30 min |
| **Total** | **157** | **250** | **210 min** |

The descriptive section requires you to write a letter and an essay in English. This is evaluated manually, so good writing skills matter here.

### Stage 3 — Group Exercise & Interview
Candidates who qualify Mains are called for a Group Exercise (20 marks) and a Personal Interview (30 marks). The final selection is based on Mains marks + GE + Interview combined.

## Salary and Perks

SBI PO starting salary is around **₹41,960 per month** (basic pay ₹36,000 + DA and other allowances). With DA and other benefits, the total Cost to Company (CTC) works out to approximately ₹8–8.5 lakh per year at the time of joining. There are also housing allowances, medical benefits, and loan concessions.

Over a 10–15 year career, a PO can move up to Senior Management roles with salaries crossing ₹25 lakh per year.

## Syllabus — What to Study

**Quantitative Aptitude:** Number Series, Simplification, Percentage, Ratio & Proportion, Average, Data Interpretation (Tables, Bar Graphs, Pie Charts, Line Graphs), Quadratic Equations, Time & Work, Pipes & Cisterns, Probability.

**Reasoning:** Seating Arrangement, Puzzles, Blood Relations, Direction Sense, Syllogism, Coding-Decoding, Input-Output, Inequality, Alphanumeric Series.

**English Language:** Reading Comprehension, Cloze Test, Error Spotting, Para Jumbles, Fill in the Blanks, Vocabulary.

**Data Analysis & Interpretation (Mains):** Advanced DI sets, Missing DI, Caselet DI, Data Sufficiency.

**General Economy & Banking Awareness (Mains):** RBI guidelines, banking terms, government schemes, economic news, budget highlights, current affairs of last 6 months.

## Application Fee

Around ₹750 for General/EWS/OBC candidates. SC/ST/PwBD candidates are exempt from the fee. Payment is online through debit/credit card or net banking.

## How to Apply

When the notification is out, go to sbi.co.in/careers. Register with your email ID and mobile number, fill in your educational details, upload your photo and signature, and pay the fee. Save the confirmation page.

## Official Website

sbi.co.in/careers — Watch for the notification in June 2026.

Marking: +1 for a correct answer, -0.25 for a wrong one, 0 for unattempted, a 4 to 1 ratio under which guessing carries a small positive expected value. Most candidates do not finish the paper, so puzzle triage and time management decide more outcomes than marking strategy.

## AILET 2027: one university, and a very different paper

AILET 2027, the All India Law Entrance Test conducted by National Law University Delhi, is on Sunday 13 December 2026 from 2:00 pm to 4:00 pm. Registration opened on 7 August 2026 on the university's official portal.

AILET exists because NLU Delhi is the one National Law University that does not use CLAT. Every other NLU admits through the Consortium's common test; NLU Delhi runs its own. So AILET is a single-university examination, admitting to its BA LLB (Hons), LLM and PhD programmes and nothing else.

The assumption most candidates make is that AILET is CLAT with a different name, and that preparing for one covers the other. It does not.

AILET has no Legal Reasoning section. It has no Quantitative section either. What it has instead is Logical Reasoning carrying 70 of its 150 questions, nearly half the paper. A CLAT-prepared candidate walking into AILET has spent months on legal principles that will not appear and arithmetic that will not be tested, while under-preparing the section that dominates the paper.

## Important dates

| Event | Date |
|---|---|
| Registration opens | 7 August 2026 |
| Examination | 13 December 2026, Sunday, 2:00 pm to 4:00 pm |

AILET falls one week after CLAT, which is on 6 December 2026. That spacing is convenient: sitting both is entirely practical, and the week between them is enough to shift emphasis from one format to the other.

## Exam pattern

AILET is an offline paper of 150 multiple choice questions in 120 minutes.

| Section | Questions | Share of paper |
|---|---|---|
| Logical Reasoning | 70 | About 47 per cent |
| English Language | 50 | About 33 per cent |
| Current Affairs and General Knowledge | 30 | 20 per cent |
| Total | 150 | 100 per cent |

Each correct answer carries 1 mark and each wrong answer costs 0.25 marks. Unattempted questions carry no penalty.

At 150 questions in 120 minutes you have 48 seconds per question, which is noticeably faster than CLAT's full minute. AILET asks more questions in the same time, so pace matters more here than it does a week earlier.

## Logical Reasoning is the exam

Seventy questions out of 150 sit in one section. No other law entrance examination weights a single section this heavily, and it should reshape how you allocate preparation time.

The section covers argument analysis, assumptions, inferences, conclusions and flaws; syllogisms and logical deductions; analytical reasoning through arrangements, sequences, orderings and puzzles; coding and decoding; blood relations and directions; series; and critical reasoning on short passages.

Two implications follow.

First, a candidate strong in logical reasoning has a structural advantage at AILET that they do not have at CLAT, where the same skill covers only about a fifth of the paper. If reasoning is your strength, AILET is the better bet of the two.

Second, the reverse is equally true. A candidate who is comfortable with legal reasoning and current affairs but slow at puzzles will find AILET considerably harder than CLAT, and should plan accordingly rather than treating it as a free second attempt.

Because analytical reasoning puzzles are time-expensive, set selection matters here in the same way it does in a data interpretation section. Recognising within thirty seconds whether a puzzle is tractable, and moving on when it is not, is worth more than raw solving ability on a paper this long.

## English Language

Fifty questions, a third of the paper, and a section where AILET tests more directly than CLAT does.

Expect reading comprehension passages with inference and tone questions, alongside vocabulary, synonyms and antonyms, idioms, grammar and error identification, sentence correction, para jumbles and cloze passages.

The distinction from CLAT is worth noting. CLAT's English section is almost entirely comprehension-based, with vocabulary tested in context. AILET retains direct vocabulary and grammar questions, which means the word lists and grammar rules that CLAT preparation has largely abandoned remain useful here.

## Current Affairs and General Knowledge

Thirty questions, the smallest section, covering national and international current affairs of roughly the preceding year, along with static general knowledge across history, geography, polity, economics, science, awards, sports and matters of legal significance.

At 20 per cent of the paper it deserves proportionate attention. A daily newspaper habit maintained through the autumn covers most of what is needed, and it serves CLAT simultaneously, which makes it efficient preparation across both examinations.

## Marking strategy

At +1 and −0.25 the ratio is 4 to 1, the same as CLAT.

A blind guess among four options yields on average one correct at plus 1 against three wrong at minus 0.75, netting plus 0.25. So guessing carries a small positive expected value and eliminating even one option makes attempting clearly worthwhile.

On a 150-question paper at 48 seconds a question, though, the realistic constraint is not whether to guess but whether you reach the questions at all. Most candidates do not complete AILET. Time management, and particularly the discipline of abandoning expensive puzzles, decides more outcomes than marking strategy does.

Reserve the closing minutes to fill anything unanswered, since blanks score nothing while guesses carry positive expected value.

## Eligibility

For the BA LLB (Hons) programme, candidates must have passed Class 12 or an equivalent examination with the minimum percentage prescribed by NLU Delhi, with relaxation for reserved categories as specified in the prospectus.

Candidates appearing in Class 12 in the current academic year may apply, subject to producing proof of passing at the time of admission.

For the LLM programme, an LLB degree or equivalent with the prescribed minimum marks is required, and for the PhD programme the conditions set out in the prospectus apply.

Because AILET is a single-university examination, the eligibility conditions are set by NLU Delhi rather than by a consortium, and candidates should read the current prospectus rather than assuming CLAT's conditions carry across.

## AILET compared with CLAT

The two examinations of December sit a week apart and are routinely treated as interchangeable. They are not.

| | [CLAT 2027](/entrance-exams/clat-2027) | AILET 2027 |
|---|---|---|
| Conducted by | Consortium of NLUs | NLU Delhi |
| Exam date | 6 December 2026 | 13 December 2026 |
| Questions | 120 | 150 |
| Duration | 120 minutes | 120 minutes |
| Time per question | 60 seconds | 48 seconds |
| Sections | Five | Three |
| Legal Reasoning | About 25 per cent | Not a section |
| Quantitative | About 10 per cent | Not a section |
| Logical Reasoning | About 20 per cent | About 47 per cent |
| English | About 20 per cent, comprehension-led | About 33 per cent, includes direct grammar and vocabulary |
| Admits to | 26 NLUs | NLU Delhi only |

Read that table properly and the strategic picture is clear. These examinations reward different profiles. CLAT spreads its weight across five areas and rewards the all-rounder with strong reading comprehension. AILET concentrates nearly half its marks in logical reasoning and rewards the candidate who is fast and accurate at puzzles and argument analysis.

Sitting both is still sensible for anyone serious about the NLUs, since the marginal preparation is manageable and NLU Delhi is among the most sought-after law schools in the country. But budget real time for AILET-specific reasoning practice rather than assuming CLAT preparation covers it.

## Preparing for AILET

Put logical reasoning first, and by a wide margin. At 70 of 150 questions it is where the paper is won, and it is a trainable skill that improves measurably with volume.

Practise puzzle triage explicitly. Take sets of analytical reasoning puzzles and train yourself to judge within thirty seconds whether one is worth starting. On a paper where most candidates do not finish, the ability to skip well is worth more than the ability to solve everything.

Retain vocabulary and grammar work. AILET tests these directly where CLAT does not, so if your preparation has been CLAT-led you have a gap here, and closing it is cheap: word lists and grammar drills produce marks quickly in a way that reading comprehension practice does not.

Keep current affairs running through a daily newspaper habit, which serves both examinations at once and is the most efficient preparation available across the December law season.

Take full 150-question mocks under the two-hour clock from October, and track how far through the paper you get rather than only your score. Reaching question 130 with 70 per cent accuracy beats reaching question 100 with 85 per cent.

Practise on paper, since AILET is an offline OMR examination. Candidates who have prepared entirely on screen sometimes lose time to the mechanics of an OMR sheet, and bubbling errors under time pressure are a genuine risk. Decide in advance whether you will bubble after each question or in batches at the end of a page, and rehearse it, because the batching approach saves time but goes badly wrong if the clock runs out with a page unmarked.

Use the week between the two examinations deliberately. CLAT is on 6 December and AILET on 13 December, and those seven days are best spent shifting emphasis rather than resting: heavier reasoning practice, a vocabulary and grammar refresh, and at least one full AILET-format mock on paper.

## What NLU Delhi offers

Since AILET admits to one university, it is worth knowing what you are competing for rather than treating it as an abstract target.

NLU Delhi is consistently among the highest-ranked law schools in India and sits in the national capital, which shapes the opportunities available during the degree. Proximity to the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, tribunals, regulatory bodies, ministries, policy organisations and the head offices of most major law firms means internships and court exposure are considerably easier to arrange than at an NLU in a smaller city.

The BA LLB (Hons) is a five-year integrated programme taken directly after Class 12. The intake is small compared with the combined intake across the 26 CLAT universities, which is precisely why AILET is competitive: a single university's seats against a national applicant pool.

Graduates move into litigation, corporate law firms, in-house legal teams, judicial services through state examinations, policy and research organisations, academia and the civil services. NLU Delhi's location and reputation make the corporate and policy routes particularly accessible.

For readers of this site tracking government careers specifically, the judicial services route is worth noting: state public service commissions and high courts recruit Civil Judges through their own examinations, for which the LLB is the qualifying degree, and a law degree is also a common foundation for the UPSC Civil Services Examination.

## Mistakes AILET candidates make

Assuming CLAT preparation covers it. The absence of legal reasoning and quantitative sections, and the concentration of nearly half the paper in logical reasoning, make these genuinely different examinations.

Treating AILET as a low-stakes second attempt. Because it admits to one university with a small intake, it is competitive in its own right rather than a softer alternative to CLAT.

Neglecting direct vocabulary and grammar. CLAT has moved away from testing these directly; AILET has not, and candidates prepared solely for CLAT arrive with a gap in a section worth a third of the paper.

Getting stuck on puzzles. At 48 seconds a question across 150 questions, a single analytical reasoning set consuming eight minutes can cost more marks elsewhere than it earns.

Preparing only on screen. AILET is an offline OMR examination, and OMR mechanics under time pressure cost minutes for candidates who have never practised on paper.

Measuring mocks only by score. On a paper most candidates do not finish, how far through you get is as diagnostic as your accuracy, and the two need tracking separately.

## How to apply

Applications are filed on the National Law University Delhi official portal.

1. Register with a valid email address and mobile number, both used for the admit card and all further communication.
2. Complete the application with personal and academic details exactly as on your certificates.
3. Select the programme you are applying to: BA LLB (Hons), LLM or PhD.
4. Choose your test city preference.
5. Upload photograph, signature and the required documents in the specified format.
6. Pay the application fee, noting the concession available to reserved category candidates and the provision NLU Delhi makes for candidates from economically weaker backgrounds.
7. Submit and save the confirmation, then download the admit card ahead of the 13 December examination.

Because AILET admits to a single university, there is no preference ordering to complete as there is with CLAT. The application is simpler, but the stakes on the day are concentrated: there is no alternative allotment if your score falls short.

## Documents you will need

1. Class 10 certificate as proof of date of birth.
2. Class 12 mark sheet and certificate, or evidence of appearing in the current year.
3. LLB degree and mark sheets for LLM applicants.
4. Category certificate in the prescribed format for reserved category claims.
5. PwD certificate where applicable.
6. Income or economic status documentation where applying under any provision for candidates from economically weaker backgrounds.
7. Photograph, signature and a photo identity document matching the application.

## Frequently asked questions

**When is AILET 2027 and when did registration open?**
AILET 2027 is on Sunday 13 December 2026 from 2:00 pm to 4:00 pm, and registration opened on 7 August 2026 on the National Law University Delhi portal. It falls one week after CLAT 2027, which is on 6 December 2026, so sitting both is practical.

**What is the AILET 2027 exam pattern?**
An offline paper of 150 multiple choice questions in 120 minutes across three sections: Logical Reasoning with 70 questions, English Language with 50, and Current Affairs and General Knowledge with 30. Marking is +1 for a correct answer and −0.25 for a wrong one, with no penalty for unattempted questions. That works out to 48 seconds per question.

**Does AILET have a Legal Reasoning section?**
No. Unlike CLAT, AILET has no Legal Reasoning section and no Quantitative section. Its 150 questions are divided between Logical Reasoning, English Language, and Current Affairs and General Knowledge only. A candidate who has prepared for CLAT has therefore spent time on legal principles and arithmetic that will not appear in AILET.

**Which university does AILET admit to?**
National Law University Delhi only, for its BA LLB (Hons), LLM and PhD programmes. NLU Delhi is the one National Law University that does not participate in CLAT; the other 26 admit through the Consortium's common test. So AILET is a single-university examination with no preference ordering and no alternative allotment.

**What is the difference between CLAT and AILET?**
CLAT has 120 questions in 120 minutes across five sections including Legal Reasoning and Quantitative Techniques, and admits to 26 NLUs. AILET has 150 questions in the same 120 minutes across three sections, with Logical Reasoning alone carrying about 47 per cent of the paper, and admits only to NLU Delhi. They reward different profiles: CLAT the all-rounder with strong reading comprehension, AILET the candidate fast and accurate at reasoning.

**How important is Logical Reasoning in AILET?**
It is the exam. Seventy of 150 questions, nearly half the paper, sit in that one section, which is a heavier concentration than any other law entrance examination applies. A candidate strong at reasoning holds a structural advantage at AILET that they do not have at CLAT, and one weak at puzzles will find AILET considerably harder.

**Is there negative marking in AILET?**
Yes, 0.25 marks are deducted for each wrong answer against 1 mark for a correct one, with nothing deducted for unattempted questions. That 4 to 1 ratio gives a blind guess a small positive expected value, so the closing minutes are best spent filling blanks rather than leaving them.

**Is AILET conducted online or offline?**
Offline, as a pen and paper OMR examination. Candidates who have prepared entirely on screen should practise on paper beforehand, since the mechanics of an OMR sheet cost time under pressure and bubbling errors are a real risk on a 150-question paper.

**What is the eligibility for AILET 2027?**
For BA LLB (Hons), Class 12 or an equivalent examination with the minimum percentage prescribed by NLU Delhi, with relaxation for reserved categories as specified in the prospectus, and candidates appearing in Class 12 in the current year may apply. For LLM, an LLB or equivalent with the prescribed minimum marks. Because AILET is a single-university test, conditions are set by NLU Delhi rather than a consortium, so read the current prospectus rather than assuming CLAT's rules apply.

**Should I take both CLAT and AILET?**
For anyone serious about the National Law Universities, generally yes. The examinations fall a week apart, NLU Delhi is among the most sought-after law schools in the country, and the current affairs and English preparation overlaps. But budget genuine time for AILET-specific reasoning practice rather than assuming CLAT preparation transfers, because the two papers reward different strengths.

**How should I manage time in AILET?**
By triaging puzzles ruthlessly. At 48 seconds per question across 150 questions, most candidates do not finish, so the decisive skill is judging within about thirty seconds whether an analytical reasoning puzzle is tractable and moving on when it is not. Track how far through the paper you reach in mocks, not just your accuracy, since reaching question 130 at 70 per cent accuracy beats reaching question 100 at 85 per cent.

**Does AILET test vocabulary and grammar directly?**
Yes, unlike CLAT. AILET's English section includes vocabulary, synonyms and antonyms, idioms, grammar and error identification, sentence correction, para jumbles and cloze passages alongside reading comprehension. CLAT-led preparation, which has largely moved away from direct vocabulary and grammar testing, leaves a gap here that is worth closing.

content:
## Choice filling closes on 13 August

NEET UG 2026 counselling is running now. The Medical Counselling Committee opened All India Quota Round 1 on 4 August 2026, and choice filling for that round is open from 8 August to 13 August 2026.

That is two days from the time of writing. If you have registered for All India Quota Round 1 and have not locked your choices, that is the task for today, not for the weekend.

MCC moved the choice filling start from 6 August to 8 August following a National Medical Commission notification on assessment guidelines for candidates with benchmark disabilities. The closing date of 13 August is what governs.

The rest of this page covers the full round schedule, the difference between the two quotas you should probably both be registered for, and the rules on accepting and exiting allotments, which is where candidates lose seats through procedure rather than through rank.

## The full 2026 counselling schedule

| Round | Process window | Joining deadline |
|---|---|---|
| All India Quota Round 1 | 4 to 17 August 2026, with choice filling 8 to 13 August | 22 August 2026 |
| State Quota Round 1 | 13 to 22 August 2026 | 28 August 2026 |
| All India Quota Round 2 | 24 August to 2 September 2026 | As notified |
| Round 3 | 10 to 18 September 2026 | As notified |
| Online Stray Vacancy Round | 28 September to 3 October 2026 | 10 October 2026 |

MCC revises this schedule during the season, as it already has once this cycle. Treat mcc.nic.in as the authority and check it before every round rather than working from a saved table.

Note how compressed the calendar is. From the opening of All India Quota Round 1 in early August to the final joining deadline on 10 October is about nine weeks, inside which four rounds run and several joining deadlines fall. Candidates who are slow to respond at any point can find a round has closed around them.

## Two quotas, and why you need both

This is the structural point that most affects your chances, and candidates routinely engage with only one side of it.

Medical seats divide into the All India Quota, which is 15 per cent of government medical college seats and is administered centrally by MCC, and the State Quota, which is the remaining 85 per cent and is administered by each state's own counselling authority.

MCC's process also covers deemed universities, central universities, ESIC and AFMS seats, and certain institutional seats, alongside the 15 per cent All India Quota.

The consequence is that most candidates should be registered in two parallel processes: MCC counselling for the All India Quota and central institutions, and their home state's counselling for the 85 per cent State Quota. These have separate registrations, separate fees, separate choice-filling windows and separate schedules.

A candidate who registers only for MCC is competing for 15 per cent of government seats. A candidate who registers only for their state is competing for 85 per cent of that state's seats but none elsewhere and none in the deemed or central institutions. Registering for both is the ordinary course, not an advanced strategy.

State Quota Round 1 runs 13 to 22 August this cycle, overlapping the tail of All India Quota Round 1, which is another reason the calendar needs watching rather than assuming the rounds are sequential.

## How a round actually works

Each round follows the same sequence.

Registration and fee payment on mcc.nic.in, within the stated window. Registration does not carry over automatically between rounds in every case, so check the requirement for each round rather than assuming your Round 1 registration stands.

Choice filling, where you select college and course combinations and place them in order of preference. This is the substantive decision of the round.

Choice locking. Unlocked choices may not be considered, and MCC auto-locks at the deadline in some rounds, which is not something to rely on.

Seat allotment, published after processing, showing the college and course you have been given, if any.

Reporting to the allotted college within the joining window, with original documents, to take up the seat.

The step candidates most often mishandle is locking. A carefully filled list that is never locked can be treated as incomplete, and the deadline passes without recourse.

## The rules that cost people seats

Rank determines what you are offered. The rules on accepting, resigning and exiting determine whether you keep it, and they differ by round in ways that are easy to get wrong.

Broadly, in the earlier rounds a candidate allotted a seat has options: to accept and report, to accept and remain in the process for a possible upgrade in a later round, or in some rounds to decline and continue. The specific options available, and their consequences for your security deposit and your eligibility in subsequent rounds, are set out in the MCC information bulletin for the cycle.

Two things matter most. First, the free exit provision is not available in every round. In later rounds, and particularly in the stray vacancy round, resigning from an allotted seat can carry forfeiture of the security deposit and debarment from further participation. Second, failing to report to an allotted college within the joining window is not a neutral act; it can be treated as forfeiture with the same consequences.

The stray vacancy round is the strictest. By that stage MCC is filling residual seats and a candidate allotted a seat there is generally expected to take it, with resignation heavily penalised.

Read the current bulletin before Round 1 closes rather than before the round in which it becomes urgent. These are decisions that cannot be undone, and by the time you need the rule you will not have time to research it.

## Choice filling: how to build the list

The preference order is the decision that shapes the next five and a half years, and it deserves more thought than it usually gets in the compressed window MCC allows.

Fill more choices rather than fewer. A short list risks going unallotted in a round where a longer list would have produced a seat somewhere acceptable. There is no penalty for listing many options, only for listing options you would not actually take.

Order by genuine preference, not by expected cutoff. The allotment engine works down your list and gives you the highest-placed option your rank reaches, so placing a less-preferred college above a more-preferred one only produces an outcome you like less.

Do not list a college you would refuse. If you are allotted it and decline, the consequences depend on the round's exit rules, and in later rounds they are severe.

Check the specifics of each college before listing it: the fee structure, which differs enormously between government, deemed and private institutions; the bond or service obligation, which several states attach and which can commit years after graduation; the hostel and infrastructure position; and the location, since you will live there.

Research previous years' closing ranks for the combinations you are considering. They are published and they tell you far more about your realistic options than any general advice.

Consider BDS alongside MBBS if your rank makes MBBS uncertain. Dentistry is a separate profession rather than a consolation, and a candidate who lists only MBBS options at a rank where they are marginal can end a round unallotted where a broader list would have produced a seat. Whether that trade is right is personal, but it should be a decision rather than an omission.

Finally, fill the list yourself rather than delegating it. Consultants and coaching centres offer choice-filling services, and while they can supply useful closing-rank data, the ordering encodes what you want from the next five and a half years, which nobody else can judge for you.

## Documents you will need

Assemble these before your allotment rather than after, since reporting windows are short.

1. NEET UG 2026 admit card and scorecard or rank letter.
2. Class 10 certificate as proof of date of birth.
3. Class 12 mark sheet and passing certificate.
4. Provisional allotment letter generated from the counselling portal.
5. Photo identity document, generally Aadhaar.
6. Passport size photographs, several copies.
7. Category certificate in the prescribed central government format for SC, ST, OBC-NCL and EWS claims, current as required.
8. PwBD certificate from a designated centre where applicable, noting that NMC issued a notification on assessment guidelines for benchmark disability candidates this cycle.
9. Domicile or nativity certificate where a state quota or state-specific claim is being made.
10. Migration and transfer certificates as required by the admitting institution.

A mismatch between a name or a date across documents is a common cause of trouble at reporting, and it is easier to resolve now than in a queue with a deadline. Keep both originals and several photocopy sets, since institutions retain some documents and ask for copies of others.

## Fees and deposits

Counselling registration carries a fee, and MCC also collects a refundable security deposit which differs between government institutions and deemed universities, the deemed university deposit being substantially larger.

The security deposit is refundable in defined circumstances and forfeited in others, which is precisely the point at which the exit rules above become financially concrete rather than abstract.

Beyond counselling fees, the tuition and other charges at the institution are separate and vary by an order of magnitude between a government college and a deemed university. A candidate listing deemed universities in their preferences should establish the actual annual cost before doing so, since an allotment you cannot afford to take up is worse than no allotment.

## Government, deemed and private: the cost difference

Because MCC's process covers all three, and candidates fill them into one preference list, it is worth being concrete about what separates them.

Government medical colleges charge the lowest fees by a wide margin, often a few tens of thousands of rupees a year, because the state funds the bulk of the cost. They are the most contested seats for exactly that reason, and closing ranks reflect it.

Deemed universities operate within the MCC process but charge fees on an entirely different scale, frequently in the range of lakhs per year across a five and a half year course, with hostel and other charges on top. The security deposit MCC requires for deemed university counselling is correspondingly larger.

Private colleges under state counselling occupy a middle and varied position, with management and NRI quota seats charging more again.

The practical instruction that follows is simple and often ignored: work out the total cost of the full course, not the annual fee, before placing a deemed or private college in your list. A five and a half year course at several lakhs a year is a commitment of tens of lakhs, and a family that discovers this after allotment is in a genuinely difficult position, because declining carries the round's exit consequences.

Education loans are available and widely used for this, but the loan needs arranging in advance rather than discovered as a necessity in a reporting queue.

## What happens after you take a seat

Reporting to the college with original documents completes the allotment, and the institution then conducts its own verification and admission formalities.

MBBS is a five and a half year course, comprising four and a half years of academic study followed by a compulsory rotating internship of one year. The internship is a requirement rather than an optional addition, and it is what makes a graduate eligible for registration and for postgraduate entrance examinations.

Original documents are generally retained by the institution during the course, which matters if you were considering holding a seat while pursuing something else.

Candidates who take a seat in an earlier round and are later allotted a better one through upgrade must follow the specific procedure MCC sets out for that, since simply reporting to a new college without completing the process at the old one creates problems.

And for anyone reading this while deciding whether to accept a seat they are unenthusiastic about: the alternative is a further year of preparation and a fresh attempt, which some candidates do successfully and others regret. The [NEET PG](/entrance-exams/neet-pg-2026) route later in a medical career, and the range of specialities available at that stage, means an undergraduate college that is not your first choice does not determine your eventual path as much as it feels like it does in August.

## Frequently asked questions

**When does NEET UG 2026 choice filling close?**
Choice filling for All India Quota Round 1 is open from 8 August to 13 August 2026. MCC moved the start from 6 August to 8 August following a National Medical Commission notification on assessment guidelines for candidates with benchmark disabilities, but the 13 August closing date governs. All India Quota Round 1 itself runs from 4 to 17 August 2026.

**What is the full NEET UG 2026 counselling schedule?**
All India Quota Round 1 runs 4 to 17 August with joining by 22 August. State Quota Round 1 runs 13 to 22 August with joining by 28 August. All India Quota Round 2 runs 24 August to 2 September. Round 3 runs 10 to 18 September. The Online Stray Vacancy Round runs 28 September to 3 October, with final joining by 10 October 2026. MCC revises this during the season, so check mcc.nic.in before each round.

**What is the difference between All India Quota and State Quota?**
The All India Quota is 15 per cent of government medical college seats, administered centrally by MCC, whose process also covers deemed and central universities, ESIC and AFMS seats. The State Quota is the remaining 85 per cent, administered by each state's own counselling authority. They have separate registrations, fees, choice-filling windows and schedules.

**Do I need to register for both MCC and state counselling?**
For most candidates, yes. Registering only for MCC means competing for 15 per cent of government seats. Registering only for your state means competing for 85 per cent of that state's seats but nothing elsewhere and nothing in the deemed or central institutions. Doing both is the ordinary course rather than an advanced strategy, and note that State Quota Round 1 overlaps the tail of All India Quota Round 1 this cycle.

**What happens if I do not lock my choices?**
Unlocked choices may not be considered in the allotment. MCC auto-locks at the deadline in some rounds, but relying on that is risky, and a carefully filled list that is never locked can be treated as incomplete with no recourse once the window closes. Locking is the step candidates most often mishandle.

**Can I leave a seat after it is allotted?**
It depends on the round, and this is where candidates lose seats through procedure rather than rank. In earlier rounds there are generally options to accept and report, accept and remain in the process for an upgrade, or decline and continue. In later rounds, and particularly the stray vacancy round, resigning can mean forfeiting the security deposit and being debarred from further participation. The MCC information bulletin for the cycle sets out the specific rules, and they should be read before Round 1 closes rather than when they become urgent.

**What happens if I do not report to an allotted college?**
Failing to report within the joining window is not a neutral act. It can be treated as forfeiture, carrying the same consequences as resignation for that round, which may include losing the security deposit and eligibility for later rounds. Joining deadlines are short, which is why documents should be assembled before an allotment rather than after.

**How many choices should I fill?**
More rather than fewer. A short list risks going unallotted where a longer one would have produced an acceptable seat, and there is no penalty for listing many options. The only thing not to do is list a college you would actually refuse, since declining an allotment carries consequences that vary by round and are severe in the later ones.

**Should I order choices by preference or by expected cutoff?**
By genuine preference. The allotment engine works down your list and gives you the highest-placed option your rank reaches, so placing a less-preferred college above a more-preferred one can only produce an outcome you like less. Use previous years' published closing ranks to judge what is realistic, but let the order reflect what you actually want.

**What is the stray vacancy round?**
The final round, running 28 September to 3 October 2026 with joining by 10 October, in which MCC fills residual seats left after the earlier rounds. It is the strictest round: a candidate allotted a seat there is generally expected to take it, and resignation is heavily penalised. It is an opportunity for candidates still without a seat, not a low-risk experiment.

**What documents do I need for NEET UG counselling?**
The NEET UG 2026 admit card and scorecard, Class 10 certificate as date of birth proof, Class 12 mark sheet and passing certificate, the provisional allotment letter from the portal, a photo identity document, several passport photographs, category certificate in the central government format where claimed, a PwBD certificate from a designated centre where applicable, domicile or nativity certificate for state quota claims, and migration and transfer certificates as the institution requires.

**What fees does NEET UG counselling involve?**
A counselling registration fee, plus a refundable security deposit which is substantially larger for deemed universities than for government institutions. The deposit is refundable in defined circumstances and forfeited in others, which is where the round-specific exit rules become financially concrete. Institutional tuition is entirely separate and varies by an order of magnitude between government colleges and deemed universities, so establish the actual annual cost before listing a deemed university in your preferences.

content:
## IBPS Clerk 2026 — Complete Guide

The IBPS Clerk exam is one of the most popular entry-level banking exams in India, and for good reason. It opens the door to a permanent government bank job in 11 public sector banks — and unlike IBPS PO, there is no interview. Your Mains marks are everything. Clear the Mains, meet the cutoff, and you get the job.

This is the 16th cycle — called CRP Clerks-XVI. The Prelims exam dates are already confirmed on the IBPS annual calendar: **October 10–11, 2026**. Mains is on **December 27, 2026**. The official notification with vacancy details is expected in July–August 2026.

## Important Dates

| Event | Date |
|---|---|
| Notification Release | July – August 2026 (Expected) |
| Application Opens | July 15, 2026 (Expected) |
| **Last Date to Apply** | **August 5, 2026 (Expected)** |
| Prelims Exam | **October 10–11, 2026 (Confirmed)** |
| Mains Exam | **December 27, 2026 (Confirmed)** |
| Provisional Allotment | February – March 2027 |

*Prelims and Mains dates are confirmed on the IBPS official annual exam calendar. Application dates are expected based on the previous year's pattern. Check ibps.in for the official notification.*

## Which Banks Recruit Through IBPS Clerk?

The same 11 banks that participate in IBPS PO also recruit clerks through this exam:
Bank of Baroda, Bank of India, Bank of Maharashtra, Canara Bank, Central Bank of India, Indian Bank, Indian Overseas Bank, Punjab & Sind Bank, Punjab National Bank, UCO Bank, and Union Bank of India.

## Eligibility

**Education:** Any graduate degree from a recognized university or equivalent. No minimum percentage is specified — a simple pass is enough. Students who have completed their graduation can apply even if convocation has not happened, as long as their results are out.

**Age:** 20 to 28 years. This is stricter than IBPS PO (which goes up to 30). Relaxation of 5 years for SC/ST, 3 years for OBC (NCL), and 10 years for PwBD candidates.

**Language:** You must have studied the official language of the state or UT you're applying to, either as a subject in Class 10 or Class 12, or in graduation. This is an important condition many candidates overlook.

## Selection Process — 2 Stages Only

IBPS Clerk is simpler than IBPS PO. There is no Group Exercise or Interview. You clear Prelims, then Mains, and that's it.

### Stage 1 — Prelims (Qualifying)

A 1-hour online test with 100 questions. You only need to clear the cutoff here — the marks don't count in the final merit.

| Section | Questions | Marks | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| English Language | 30 | 30 | 20 min |
| Numerical Ability | 35 | 35 | 20 min |
| Reasoning Ability | 35 | 35 | 20 min |
| **Total** | **100** | **100** | **60 min** |

Negative marking: -0.25 for each wrong answer.

### Stage 2 — Mains (Final Merit)

The Mains score is what decides your rank for allotment. It has four sections in 160 minutes.

| Section | Questions | Marks | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| General/Financial Awareness | 50 | 50 | 35 min |
| General English | 40 | 40 | 35 min |
| Reasoning Ability & Computer Aptitude | 50 | 60 | 45 min |
| Quantitative Aptitude | 50 | 50 | 45 min |
| **Total** | **190** | **200** | **160 min** |

Negative marking applies here too: -0.25 per wrong answer.

No interview after Mains — your scaled Mains score directly determines your allotment.

## Salary

A bank clerk's starting in-hand salary is around **₹26,000 to ₹29,000 per month** depending on the posting location (metro, urban, rural). The basic pay starts at ₹11,765 per month. Graduate candidates get two advance increments, which puts the effective starting basic at around ₹13,075. With DA, HRA, and special allowances added on top, the gross goes up significantly. With DA, HRA, special allowance, and other perks, the gross goes up significantly.

Clerks also get home loan concessions, medical benefits, and performance-based promotions (you can become an officer in 2–3 years through internal exams).

## What to Study

**Quantitative Aptitude / Numerical Ability:** Number series, simplification, approximation, quadratic equations, percentage, profit and loss, time and work, speed and distance, data interpretation.

**Reasoning Ability:** Seating arrangement, puzzles, syllogisms, inequality, coding-decoding, blood relations, direction sense, alphanumeric series.

**English Language:** Reading comprehension, cloze test, para jumbles, fill in the blanks, sentence correction, vocabulary.

**General/Financial Awareness (Mains):** Current affairs of last 6 months, RBI announcements, banking terms (REPO rate, CRR, SLR, NPA, PMJDY, etc.), government financial schemes, Union Budget highlights.

**Computer Aptitude (Mains):** MS Office basics, internet and networking terms, computer abbreviations, input/output devices, software and hardware basics.

## Application Fee

Approximately ₹850 for General/EWS/OBC candidates. SC/ST/PwBD candidates pay ₹175 (registration fee only). Payment accepted via net banking, debit/credit card, or UPI.

## Official Website

ibps.in — Exam dates (Prelims October 10–11 and Mains December 27, 2026) are already published on the IBPS annual calendar. Watch for the detailed notification in July–August 2026.
